News.title: UK pulls staff out of Iran as Trump escalates bombing blitzes & Tehran’s top dealmaker vows ‘no one will sell oil’
News.content:
BRITAIN has pulled any remaining staff from Iran as the “all or nothing” war with the US escalates.

The UK Foreign Office announced this evening: “Updated information on regional tensions, and due to the security situation, UK staff have been temporarily withdrawn from Iran.”

The UK government had already evacuated the ambassador and consular staff, and has since carried out diplomatic operations from outside the country.



It remains unclear who had remained in Tehran, and how many people have been pulled out.



This comes as the Head of Iran’s negotiating team, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said: “The equation of this war is clear, all or nothing. In a region where we do not sell oil, no one will sell oil.

“If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe, and the key to the security of the strait lies in the absence of American forces.”

For 12 consecutive days, the US has carried out mass airstrikes across the country.



Donald Trump has also threatened to bomb Pickaxe Mountain, a fortified underground site that the US and Israel suspect could be used for nuclear activity.

“We’ll be hitting that area very probably pretty soon,” he said on Tuesday.

“There’s not a thing they can do about it. You know, normally I wouldn’t say that. If I thought they could do something about it, I would never say that.

“But we’ll be hitting that area pretty soon, and very heavily.”

News.title: Joseph Stalin’s chilling death mask hits auction as fans of tyrant who killed millions set to spend thousands
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KILLER'S END Joseph Stalin’s chilling death mask hits auction as fans of tyrant who killed millions set to spend thousands

A CREEPY mask of Joseph Stalin is set to be auctioned off with excited collectors set to spend thousands.

The “death mask” of one of history‘s most notorious killers will go on sale next month.



The dark green likeness is one of 12 created from the original plaster cast taken as the Soviet dictator lay motionless on his deathbed in 1953.

The mask comes with two bronze casts of Stalin’s hands.



The left is withered from an injury he sustained as a child when he was hit by a horse-drawn carriage near his home in Gori, Georgia.

Stalin was supposedly self-conscious about his hand and would often hide it in photographs.



Who was Joseph Stalin? Joseph Stalin was the leader of the Soviet Union from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953.

Born in Georgia, he rose through the Bolshevik Party after the Russian Revolution.

He transformed the Soviet Union into a major industrial power through rapid industrialization and collectivized agriculture.

These policies came at an enormous human cost, contributing to widespread famine, forced labor, and millions of deaths.

Stalin established a highly centralized dictatorship that relied on censorship, surveillance, and political repression.

During the Great Purge of the 1930s, countless perceived opponents were imprisoned, exiled, or executed.

He led the Soviet Union through World War II, playing a decisive role in the Allied defeat of Nazi Germany.

Born into a poor family, Stalin was a revolutionary who led the Soviet Union from 1924 until his death.

His regime was defined by terror, resulting in the death of millions.

The “death mask” was originally purchased by the seller at a Sotheby’s auction in 1993.

Valuers at Canterbury Auction Galleries have now put a guide price of between £8,000 and £12,000 on the item.



The extraordinary item goes under the hammer on August 4 in an online auction.

This is the last of a four-day auction, which features hundreds of lots from jewellery and porcelain to furniture and collectibles.

The first two days are dedicated to the Peter Firmin studio sale.

It features 500 lots of his children’s artwork and toys.

News.title: When will it rain? Latest UK weather forecast from the Met Office – and how long the dry spell has been
News.content:
THIS summer Britain has felt like a different continent, with temperatures rising up to 35C at least once in all of the last three calendar months.

Over the last few weeks there has been a substantial dry spell as the heat has only continued – but when will we next see rainfall?

When is it expected to rain?

Although the summer sunshine has been enjoyable and a big treat for sun-seekers, many are now wondering when the temperature will begin to drop.



Especially given the ongoing hosepipe bans affecting around 23 million people across England and Wales.



Given the ban, people will be hoping rainfall is approaching, as it’s getting harder to keep lawns green and prevent flowers from wilting – affecting gardens all over the UK.

However, a change in temperature has already started, as cooler Atlantic air has pushed its way across the country, sweeping away the heat and bringing a shift in the weather pattern.

The Met Office says this week we shall expect short, settled periods before topsy-turvy weather could hit, bringing longer spells of rain that could again turn heavy and thundery.



Looking further ahead to the next week, from Monday, July 27 into the first week of August, the weather is set to be a total mixed bag.

Forecasters say changeable weather patterns are on the cards, meaning Brits will be dodging showers and longer spells of rain. And there’s a risk of more booming thunder.

Crucially, the Met Office predicts temperatures will remain firmly above normal for the time of year, with the door open for more hot spells as we head into August.



How long has the dry spell lasted?

The current dry spell in the UK has lasted what feels like a lifetime, with many parts of England receiving virtually no rainfall for over three weeks.

According to the National Drought Group, there are now multiple parts of the country in “prolonged dry weather”, which is the final stage before drought.

Among these locations are East Anglia, the West Midlands, Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Hertfordshire and London, Wessex, Thames, Solent and the South Downs.

The latest announcement takes into account the lack of rainfall and has confirmed that over 20 million people will be living under hosepipe bans by the end of this week.

News.title: Fugitive who goaded cops with ripped selfie after they shared rounder pic of him for appeal is back behind bars
News.content:
ABS-CONDER Fugitive who goaded cops with ripped selfie after they shared rounder pic of him for appeal is back behind bars

A FUGITIVE who mocked the police with a shirtless pic of his ripped body has been thrown back behind bars.

Greater Manchester Police shared an appeal on Facebook to find Nathan Muir, 32, who was on the run.



In response to the appeal, Muir posted in the comment section a photo of him shirtless, writing “Could of done a better pic”.

The force has since caught the runaway, saying “while his famous abs appear to have escaped justice, he didn’t”.



Muir was being hunted down by GMP’s Wythenshawe division as he was wanted “on recall to prison”, according to Manchester Evening News.

The man, who has links to Wythenshawe, Hale and Altrincham, was less than impressed with the photo the force used in its appeal to locate him.

Logging onto Facebook, he replied in the comment section and posted a shirtless photo of himself with his abs showing.

The reply began to receive hundreds of likes, as Muir taunted officers online.



But in a turn of events, GMP Wythenshawe uploaded another Facebook post on Tuesday saying: “Remember Nathan Muir who wanted a ‘better pic’ on his recall to prison appeal?

“Good news, Muir was arrested this morning at an address in #Stockport following extensive enquiries and has been sent back to prison.

“We’d like to thank those who shared our appeal.”

In the unexpected post by the force, it included a photo of Muir appearing to have put on weight and with no abs in sight.

One person commented under the post saying: “Looks like the prison gym just got its star member back, back to getting a free membership with no cancellation fees”.

News.title: Nicolas Maduro jokes & laughs in court as ‘slimmed down’ ex-dictator has trial date set after Trump’s special ops arrest
News.content:
NICOLAS Maduro bantered his way through his court appearence today where a judge set a June 2027 date for his narcoterrorism trial.

Venezuela’s former president and his wife Cilia Flores, who were captured by US Special Forces in a daring raid on his fortified Caracas compound in January, have been holed up in a Brooklyn jail ever since.



Sporting a beige uniform and a pair of glasses, he looked slimmed down – but in jovial spirits.

His hair was shaved tightly at the sides, making his face look even thinner.



As he was led into ​the packed Manhattan courtroom, the toppled leader cracked several jokes – telling his lawyer that he looked “very serious.”

He then waved to the public and even got a smile from his lawyer Barry Pollack as he cracked another gag.



Neither Maduro nor his wife spoke during the tense 15-minute hearing – the third one since their capture.

Both have pleaded not guilty to charges that include narcoterrorism conspiracy and possession of machine guns and destructive devices.

They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to ship thousands of tons of cocaine into the US.

Prosecutors argue Maduro colluded with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.



“I am not guilty,” the fallen dictator said in Spanish during his arraignment hearing in January.

“I am a decent man, the constitutional president of my country.”

The court heard that Maduro will try to claim “sovereign immunity”, likely because he was a head of state when he was seized in Venezuela.



His lawyer said that they expected to keep the June 1, 2027, trial date, that is unless there are issues with classified material.

Pollack further added that he expects to contest the legality of Maduro’s “military abduction” – something that the Trump administration has been defending, describing it as a “surgical law enforcement operation”.

Maduro, a socialist who had an antagonistic relationship with the US while leading Venezuela from 2013 until his capture, referred to ⁠himself as a “prisoner of war” during his January 5 appearance.

He has long accused the US of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the OPEC nation’s vast oil reserves.

Meanwhile, the US branded him a corrupt dictator whose mishandling of the economy led to an economic collapse, and accused him of rigging his reelection votes in 2018 and 2024.



It stopped recognizing him as Venezuela’s legitimate president in 2019.

In an advisory opinion ahead of the January raid, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel said it would be lawful for Donald Trump to order the raid because it served an important national interest and ‌did not rise to the level of a war that would require congressional authorization.

The next court date was set for November 17.

News.title: Villagers’ fury as giant wind turbines threaten to RUIN idyllic Yorkshire countryside made famous by David Hockney
News.content:
WINDING UP Villagers’ fury as giant wind turbines threaten to RUIN idyllic Yorkshire countryside made famous by David Hockney

VILLAGERS are furious over plans to build giant wind turbines that would ruin their idyllic countryside that inspired David Hockney.

The 492 ft high structures are expected to be erected in Woldgate, near Burton Agnes.



But locals are challenging the green move, saying that it would “ruin” the landscape popularised by artist Hockney’s paintings.

Former art teacher Nancy Miller, 75, who lives in the nearby village of Carnaby, said: “I’m a huge champion of green energy and the fight against climate change.



“It’s all a matter of placement and minimising negative impact.

“We all understand from its physical size and functionality the chosen location is always going to be rural, impact wildlife and alter the landscape forever.



“This site unfortunately pushes the impact to another level.

“The recent loss of David Hockney has made his depictions of the landscape under discussion even more irreplaceable.



“If the project goes ahead on this site it shows a huge lack of respect for national artistic heritage, let’s face it, there are other fields that haven’t been painted by one of the most iconic artists in modern history.

“The battle against climate change doesn’t have to be a war on culture.”

A member of campaign group Keep Wind Off Woldgate, Rob Booth, 58, said: “Residents are absolutely appalled that the developer has said these turbines can be ‘accommodated within the host landscape’ and would not result in significant adverse effects, when East Riding Council’s own pre-application assessment concluded precisely the opposite.

“The council planners described this part of the Yorkshire Wolds as a ‘highly sensitive area’ and found that the wind farm would cause ‘harm to the landscape, heritage assets and living conditions’.

“It went on to state that those harms would ‘significantly and demonstrably outweigh the benefits‘.



“We will continue to fight these plans and encourage everyone who values this unique destination to submit their objections.”

The developers, Ridge Clean Energy, said the six wind turbines it has earmarked for the Yorkshire countryside would “offset emissions” and “contribute to the national legislation of net zero emissions by 2050”.

They had submitted the proposal just days before the death of Bradford-born artist David Hockney.

Hockney, who died last month aged 88, painted a range of famous artworks of Woldgate Woods, near where the turbines are planned to be erected.

One of his pieces titled “Woldgate Woods” sold for £9.4million in New York in 2016.



It will be part of the Three Oaks Renewable Energy Park, which includes a solar farm and battery storage.

The turbines, which will span across a 5.4-hectare area, are estimated to produce enough power to supply 24,000 UK households annually.

In response to the local backlash, Ridge Clean Energy has offered a “community benefit fund” of around £126,000 a year.

It said the money would go towards supporting community led initiatives.

If the plans are approved, construction will begin in early 2028 and take eight months to complete.



Local councillor Denise Howard said: “Woldgate is not an anonymous stretch of countryside.

“It is one of the most recognisable landscapes in Yorkshire, celebrated internationally through the work of David Hockney and treasured by the communities that live here.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Along with Burton Agnes Hall and the Rudston Monolith, this area is crucial to our tourism economy.

“We support renewable energy in the right place, but this is certainly not the right place.”

News.title: Woman SLAPS two passengers riding train in late night attack as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to
News.content:
SLAP ATTACK Woman SLAPS two passengers riding train in late night attack as cops share CCTV of person they want to speak to

POLICE have released a CCTV image of a woman they want to speak to after two females were slapped at a train station.

The force said that the woman approached the pair at around 11.40pm on Saturday at Preston station and slapped them both before fleeing.



Officers have released a picture of a woman they wish to speak to as part of their investigation.

They have asked for anyone who recognises the woman to contact British Transport Police by texting 61016 or calling 0800 40 50 40, quoting reference 27 of 21 June.

News.title: Netflix slammed for ‘cash grab’ Idaho murders doc with viewers begging to ‘let families heal’ as new trailer is released
News.content:
NETFLIX is facing widespread criticism from viewers for a plan to release a new documentary on the murders of four college students in Idaho.

The streaming platform shared a trailer for the upcoming release, which will detail the murders of the four University of Idaho students at the hands of Bryan Kohberger.



The Netflix documentary, titled The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare, will be released on July 29.

It will recount the murders of Kaylee Goncalves, 21, Madison Mogen, 21, Xana Kernodle, 20, and Ethan Chapin, 20, who were fatally stabbed in an off-campus house in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022.



Weeks after their bodies were found by police, Bryan Kohberger was arrested and charged with four counts of first-degree murder.

The Netflix trailer was released and shared on social media on Wednesday, and people quickly responded to the new documentary with both praise and criticism.

“Still profiting off this? Enough with these already, let these families heal,” one X user wrote, while another said, “Cash grab for Netflix, Profiting off Serial killers is evil.”

Another viewer asked, “Why is everything a documentary. Let these kids rest.”

Peacock released a documentary entitled The Idaho Student Murders in 2025, while Amazon released a documentary titled One Night in Idaho: The College Murders the same year.

Someone else questioned how the new documentary would differ from others that have already been released.



“Bro it’s been a BUNCH of docs already about this incident. What more can yall even say about it?” another user wrote in response to the Netflix trailer.

“Unless you’re actually showing the police search footage of the bodies unblurred and things in that nature, it’s nothing left to really reveal with this,” the commenter continued.

The trailer for the new documentary begins with bodycam footage of police arriving at the house where the four students were stabbed to death.



Kaylee’s mother, Kristi Goncalves, was interviewed for the documentary and is seen in the trailer, saying, “I knew something bad had happened.”

While others criticized the number of documentaries about the case, some still stated that they were looking forward to watching the new one on Netflix.

“What is this the 17th doc on it? And yes I will still watch it,” one user commented.



“So many documentaries on this, but I’mma still watch it,” another wrote.

Kohberger pleaded guilty to the murders just before his trial was set to start in July 2025 and received four life sentences.

The horrific murders and subsequent hunt for Kohberger attracted global attention from the media and true crime fans from across the world.

Many shared different theories, and police received thousands of tips throughout their investigation.

News.title: Man found guilty of murder after previously killing sister in shooting accident
News.content:
Man found guilty of murder after previously killing sister in shooting accident

Dublin’s Central Criminal Court found Derek Boyd of Scribblestown Place, Finglas, Dublin guilty of the murder of Mark Carroll on June 9, 2024

View 2 Images Derek Boyd was found guilty of murder (Image: DublinLive)

A man has been found guilty of stabbing a man to death while he was already serving a suspended sentence for the manslaughter of his sister.

‌



Derek Boyd fatally stabbed another man in the chest at his north Dublin home while serving the suspended part of his sentence for the manslaughter of his sister.

‌



Dublin’s Central Criminal Court found Boyd guilty of murder this afternoon.

‌



The two men and their partners had been drinking together at Boyd’s home when a late-night row broke out. In the following altercation Mr Carroll suffered three stab wounds which killed him.

Prosecuting Counsel Sean Guerin said Boyd had run away to the UK after the attack. However his defence said this did not mean he was guilty of murder but because the fact he was already serving a suspended sentence meant he would go back to prison.

View 2 Images Mark Carroll died of a stab wound to the chest (Image: DublinLive)

‌



The 31-year-old, of Scribblestown Place, Finglas in north-west Dublin had pleaded not guilty to murdering Mark Carroll, 34, at his home on June 9, 2024.

He was also charged with assaulting the deceased man’s girlfriend, Megan Rock on the same occasion, causing her harm. Boyd also pleaded not guilty to this charge.

Boyd's girlfriend Chantelle Harcourt, 34, stood accused of impeding her partner's prosecution, Dublin Live reports.

Article continues below

Ms Harcourt, of Primrose Grove, Darndale in Dublin 17 had pleaded not guilty on the same date at Blanchardstown Garda Station, in circumstances where another person had committed an arrestable offence, namely murder, and knowing or believing that person to be guilty of that offence or of some other arrestable offence, did without reasonable excuse an act with intent to impede the apprehension or prosecution of the said person.

The 11 jurors returned today unable to reach a verdict on Boyd’s alleged assault on Megan Rock or Harcourt’s alleged charge of assisting an offender.

Boyd will be sentenced next Tuesday to the mandatory sentence of life in prison.

News.title: 'Close neighbour' 70, charged with murder of Brit expat Karen Carter in Dordogne
News.content:
'Close neighbour' 70, charged with murder of Brit expat Karen Carter in Dordogne

View 2 Images Karen Carter, 65, was found stabbed to death in the Dordogne region of south west France (Image: Facebook)

A woman who was ‘a close neighbour’ of a British mother-of-four stabbed to death at her home in France has been charged with her murder.

‌



The 70-year-old suspect, who has not yet been formally named, is said to have carried out the killing of Karen Carter, 65, in the village of Trémolat, in the Dordogne, in April 2025.

‌



Jacques-Édouard Andrault, the state prosecutor in nearby Périgueux, said the suspect was on Wednesday in custody and being held under suspicion of ‘premeditated murder,’ which can be punished with a life prison sentence.

‌



It follows claims that Ms Carter, who lived alone, was the victim of a feud related to her love life.

She was on the verge of divorcing her South Africa-based husband, Alan Carter, now 66, while seeing Jean-François Guerrier, a 75-year-old retired executive who lived close to her French property.

In turn, those upset by the relationship included Marie-Laure Autefort, now 70, and another near-neighbour.

‌



View 2 Images Karen Carter was killed in a ‘savage attack’ (Image: Facebook)

Mr Guerrier and Ms Autefort were arrested after the killing, before being released without charge.

Philippe Monribot, Ms Autefort’s brother, has confirmed she was in love with Mr Guerrier, and deeply upset by his affair with Ms Carter, but said the thought of her murdering someone was preposterous.

‌



‘It’s a catastrophe,’ he said. ‘The police messed up at the start of the investigation and when you get it wrong at the beginning, it’s difficult to get it right afterwards.’

Mr Guerrier had hosted a wine tasting party on the day Ms Carter died, and later followed her to her home in his car.

When he got there he found her lying in a pool of blood, before she was declared dead at the scene by emergency workers.

‌



Mr Guerrier first said he was concerned that his lover had not telephoned him on reaching her house, which was just 10 minutes away from his.

Then, Mr Guerrier told police that he ‘had come to spend the night at Karen’s,’ leaked interview notes reveal.

It was Mr Guerrier who told detectives to investigate Ms Autefort. The police record states: ‘During his brief custody period, Jean-François Guerrier directed them to Marie-Laure Autefort, a resident of Trémolat who lives only about a ten-minute walk from the victim’s home, cutting across the fields.

‌



‘He described her as a woman who had fallen madly in love with him the previous year, to the point of divorcing the father of her children after several decades of marriage.

‘She was then terribly frustrated when she realised that this budding passion was not reciprocated.’

The words guaranteed Ms Autefort’s arrest, but she was said to have provided an alibi, and vehemently denies any wrongdoing.

‌



Both Ms Autefort and Mr Guerrier are among those who have given DNA samples to police, along with some 15 guests at Mr Guerrier’s wine tasting party.

None provided a match to forensic evidence found at the crime scene, where the only apparent witness was Ms Carter’s puppy, Haku, who remained in her car.

The prosecutor confirmed that the woman charged with murder had first been taken into custody on April 30 – the day Marie-Laure Autefort was arrested.

‌



The suspect was ‘a near-neighbour’ who knew Karen Carter well, he said.

Mr Andrault said the 70-year-old was formally charged with premeditated murder on July 2, and was currently under ‘judicial supervision’ because of her age.

This means she is under constant surveillance by judicial police, while not having to stay in a cell.

‌



Mr Andrault confirmed she was a resident of Trémolat, but was not currently permitted to stay in the village.

While detectives investigated the crime, Karen Carter’s widower and four adult children had a strong feeling about who was to blame.

Their lawyer, Reda Hammouche, said on April 29 this year – the one year anniversary of the crime – that they had ‘a hunch, an opinion on the matter.’

‌



He said it followed a detailed examination of ‘the case file that we discuss – me and them – in the privacy of our meetings.’

Mr Hammouche continued: ‘So they have a hunch, but I won’t elaborate further on the subject.

‘I obviously can’t go into detail since the confidentiality of the investigation prevents me from divulging such information, but numerous leads are being explored, many actions are being taken, and so,indeed, daily, as I speak to you, actions are being carried out.

Article continues below

‘And they hope that all of this will be resolved by identifying the perpetrator of this murder and by justice being served for Karen.’

News.title: Family pooch dies after unlicenced dog boarder leaves him unattended on hot day
News.content:
Family pooch dies after unlicenced dog boarder leaves him unattended on hot day

Charlotte Sutton, who carried out an animal boarding business without the required licence, abandoned pooch Hero at an address in Braintree, Essex for a "significant period"

View 3 Images Leighanne Ship was left devastated following Hero's death (Image: Braintree District Council / SWNS)

A rogue dog boarder was spared jail after a beloved family pooch died when he was left unattended on a hot day.

‌



Charlotte Sutton, 26, left pooch Hero alone at her property for a "significant period." A court heard Sutton, 26, was operating as a home dog boarder at the time despite not having a licence.

‌



She operated the home despite repeated attempts by Braintree District Council to explain the legal requirements to her. She was prosecuted by the council and appeared before District Judge Williams at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on July 15.

‌



Sutton was later found guilty of causing unnecessary suffering under the Animal Welfare Act 2006. She went on to plead guilty to carrying out an animal boarding business without the required licence.

View 3 Images Hero, a 10.5-stone Leonberger, died after being left alone at the home of an unlicensed dog boarder. (Image: Braintree District Council / SWNS)

‌



Killer elephant leaves dad devastated after stalking and murdering four members of his family in chilling attacks READ MORE :

But Sutton's 26-week prison sentence, suspended for two years. She was ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work, must play £10,000 towards Braintree District Council's prosecution costs, and a £154 victim surcharge.

Speaking after the sentencing this week, Hero's devastated owner Leighanne Ship said the conviction had finally secured justice for her much-loved pet. Hero died nearly two years ago - on August 2, 2024 - but it had taken some time to reach court.

View 3 Images Leighanne said she wanted to share the experience if it could help another family (Image: Braintree District Council / SWNS)

Article continues below

Leighanne said: "We are incredibly grateful to Braintree District Council for taking on this case and pursuing it through to a successful prosecution.

"Whilst nothing will ever bring Hero back, we finally have justice for him and some measure of closure. We hope Hero's story serves as a reminder of the importance of using properly licensed animal boarding providers and of the immense responsibility that comes with caring for someone else's beloved pet.

"If sharing our experience prevents even one family from suffering the heartbreak, uncertainty and anguish that we have endured, then Hero's legacy will continue to protect others."

News.title: Homeless man who killed pensioner in Remembrance Day knife rampage was 'very unwell'
News.content:
Homeless man who killed pensioner in Remembrance Day knife rampage was 'very unwell'

Musse Ali, 68, stabbed pensioner Hilkiah McLeggan to death and attacked two other people during a frenzied attack outside an East London market on Remembrance Sunday

View Image (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

A homeless man who killed a 77-year-old pensioner and stabbed two others during a rampage in a market on Remembrance Sunday has been sentenced to an indefinite hospital order.

‌



Musse Ali, 67, pleaded guilty to the manslaughter of Hilkiah McLeggan and to wounding Ho Man Yau and Baheru Nadew Bartura with intent during an attack at East Street market in Walworth, south London, on Sunday, November 10, 2024.

‌



A sentencing hearing at the Old Bailey heard that Ali has previously been diagnosed with a schizoaffective disorder, and experiences symptoms associated with both schizophrenia and bipolar.

‌



The defendant had not been taking his medication at the time of the attack, and Mr McLeggan’s grieving relatives said his life choices have left their family “devastated”.

Ali, who was born in Somalia but moved to the UK in 1990 after seeking asylum, previously pleaded guilty to manslaughter by diminished responsibility, having an article with a blade, and wounding with intent.

He was sentenced at the Old Bailey on Wednesday after admitting manslaughter by diminished responsibility, wounding with intent and having an article with a blade.

‌



His Honour Judge Nigel Lickley KC said: “This case concerns the tragic events on the 10th of November 2024 when three members of the public were attacked by the defendant, who had armed himself with a large kitchen knife.

“Mr Ali was mentally very unwell at the time with his long standing illness as the main driver in his horrific offending that day, when he stabbed and killed Hilkiah McLeggan and seriously injured Ho Yau and Baheru Bartura .

“A life was lost and many lives changed as a consequence.”

‌



The judge said that Ali’s offending caused “serious alarm and distress” and that there is “no doubt” that he is a “dangerous” individual.

He accepted the evidence of two experts that “the reason Mr Ali behaved in the very violent way he did was because he was very unwell at the time”.

Prosecutor Allan Compton KC explained how Ali was caught on CCTV entering the market and going into a shop at around 10.30am, following an 'unremarkable' bus journey.

‌



He then proceeded to jump over a counter appeared to steal a knife, the court heard. The shop manager, thinking Ali had tried to steal vapes, pushed him out of the store, only to realise the defendant was holding a blade.

Ali then stabbed three people in "quick succession," the court heard. The first victim, Mr Yau, was walking through the market when Ali “ran at him” and “stabbed him a number of times”, the prosecution said.

In a witness statement, Mr Yau said the defendant “looked crazy”, adding: “His eyes were wide and scary, looking directly at me. He looked unclean, like he hadn’t had a shave or a shower in a while.”

‌



The defendant then stabbed Mr Bartura from behind before fatally stabbing Mr McLeggan, while panicked onlookers shouted "he has a knife," the court heard.

Ali then "lunged" at other members of the public before he was disarmed and restrained.

Mr McLeggan died at the scene from a stab wound to the back, the court heard. The other two victims were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

‌



While at Brixton police station, Ali stated that he “did not intend to murder”.

Scotland Yard said at the time the incident was not being treated as a terrorist attack.

In a victim impact statement, Mr Bartura said the incident “changed my life”, adding: “In a matter of seconds, the attack shattered my physical health, psychiatric well-being, independence and hopes for the future.”

‌



He said that since the assault, he has become dependent on his wife and children, adding: “Without their support I’m effectively housebound because of the overwhelming anxiety, post-traumatic stress and a constant fear of being attacked again.

“No sentence imposed by the court can restore my health or return the life that was taken from me on November 10 2024… However, I hope the court can understand the life-long impact this violent attack has had on me.”

Delivering a victim impact statement to the court, Mr McLeggan’s daughter Laura said: “Mr Ali’s life choices have left our family devastated.”

‌



She said Ali was “sound of mind when he made a decision, a conscious decision, to end his medication”.

Ms McLeggan said he made “the choice to abscond from supported living and withdraw from mental health services”.

She said that Ali has shown “no remorse”, adding: “The murder of our father was preventable.”

‌



Sarah McLeggan, who is also a daughter of the victim, said: “It’s soul-destroying to think that he will never have the mental capacity to take account for what he did and understand the impact on not just our family and friends but those other victims who were hurt on that horrible day.”

She described her father as a “dear friend, confidant, go-to guy when things went wrong” who was “everything to everyone”.

The responsible clinician for Ali told the court that the defendant has a “serious and treatment-resistant” form of the schizoaffective disorder.

Article continues below

He said that in his view, Ali would not have offended and the event would not have taken place if he did not suffer the illness.

News.title: 'People think I'm crazy when I eat my Doc Martens, but there's a delicious secret'
News.content:
Mum-of-two Karen Geraghty has found a way to have her cake and eat it. For these Doc Marten boots are made for eating, not walking - as are the killer heels and even the ‘Jimmy Choos.’ A self-taught baker she can recreate virtually anything, using icing and her eagle eye for detail.

Karen, 55, started following her fondant fancies in 2010, when she was a full-time mum to her boys Josh, then nine, and Max, six, after a busy career working in clinical management. She says: "One day, a school mum who knew I loved baking and decorating cakes for my family, asked me to make her a bespoke Christmas cake. I was thrilled to oblige.

"I made a fruit cake topped with sugar paste penguins and icebergs. The mum absolutely loved it and it fired-up something creative inside me. I began experimenting and creating. I had absolutely no formal training and everything I knew was completely self-taught.

View 6 Images Karen, who lives in Dublin, says her family love her cakes (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



“I watched cake decoration tutorials for hours on end and began buying lots of different modelling tools. I honestly was like a kid in a sweet shop. Everything was trial and error. My husband, Robert, then 45, would come home from work and frown as I showed him another gadget.”

At first she just tried out her creations on her family. She says: "For my husband’s birthday I made a model of him sitting in a chair with his guitar. He absolutely loved it.

"My mother loved gardening, so for her birthday I made a model of her holding a trowel, digging the garden and with hanging baskets.”

View 6 Images Good enough to eat! One of Karen's amazing shoe cakes (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



Looking for a more creative career that would allow her to work around being a mum, she started her own business making cakes and cake toppers. And the orders came flooding in.

Karen, of Dublin, Ireland, says: "I began getting all sorts of requests. One customer wanted a cake topped with a sugar stiletto. I thought it was a real challenge, but I liked a challenge and to be taken out of my comfort zone.

"Needing a template, I got to work. I looked around my kitchen and wondered what I could use. I ended up using one of my own stilettos to create the template."

View 6 Images Karen's cakes absolutely delight her customers (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



Karen will never forget the delighted look on the birthday girl’s face when she saw her stiletto cake. She adds: "Seeing her so astonished and happy with her stiletto gave me a real buzz and I wanted more.”

Soon requests for shoe cakes and cake toppers were flooding in and Karen began experimenting and making all sorts of posh stilettos with sparkles, pearls and glitter. She adds: "It wasn't long before I began working on my own designs, like an owl, a unicorn and even a tropical pair of shoes.”

With the shoe toppers - each taking four hours to make - they have to be made in stages. And each part has to dry completely before moving on to the next bit.

View 6 Images Karen hard at work on one of her creations

‌



Karen, who prices each creation individually, continues: "In 2019, I entered a cake competition with the theme of footwear. I made a cake in the style of a pair of Dr Marten’s black boots with dog eyes and teeth.

"I got the idea for them as I was singing alone in the car to the song Who Let the Dogs Out? With shoes in mind and being a lover of puns, I was changing the words to 'Shoe let the dogs out?'

“I had to show techniques of carving cake, painting with edible dusts and paints. “Every piece of the shoe was edible. I was beyond thrilled when I won the competition."

View 6 Images Karen created hyperrealistic dogs on a pair of her shoe cakes (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



Since then, Karen has made hundreds of cakes, from replica edible handbags to a superhero version of ET. She says: "People often ask me where I get my crazy and wacky ideas from. I guess I get inspiration from everything around me.”

Now concentrating on making edible cake toppers, business is booming. She says: "I’m very grateful for each day. Life really couldn’t be sweeter."

*For more information about Karen’s creations go to www.facebook.com/bakecakecreate

News.title: William Shatner, 95, and daughter Melanie, 61, diagnosed with stage 4 cancer at same time
News.content:
William Shatner, 95, and daughter Melanie, 61, diagnosed with stage 4 cancer at same time

William Shatner and his daughter Melanie were both being treated for stage four cancer at the same time as the pair reveal how it made them feel at the time

View 2 Images Melanie Shatner and father William Shatner (Image: WireImage)

William Shatner has revealed both he and his daughter faced stage four cancer together. The pair were both diagnosed around the same time, with the Star Trek legend diagnosed with stage four malignant melanoma which spread to his lungs and brain.

The 95-year-old's diagnosis in June 2023 came just as his daughter Melanie was in the final stretch of her treatment for stage four breast cancer. She had received her diagnosis in 2022.

And the legendary actor has now opened up on his health journey and the worries the duo both faced. He admitted he first became concerned after a lump grew on his cheek.

View 2 Images William Shatner holding his daughter when she was a baby (Image: Bettmann Archive)

He revealed a doctor initially told him it was a blocked salivary gland and told him to “just massage it”. But as the concern continued to grow, he was told a a month late by a plastic surgeon friend that he “better get it out” after he noticed it was a tumour.

He had surgery and two years of immunotherapy followed to target the cancer in his lungs and brain. At the same time, his daughter was facing her own battled.

Article continues below

But Melanie told People that her dad "kept working and moving forward,” despite his condition. Melanie's own woes came after she discovered a lump on her breast in 2022.

She initially thought it was a bug bite after having a clear mammogram five months earlier. But she admitted that “something pushed me back” to get checked. And when the doctors carried out an examination, it confirmed she had cancer that had spread to her lymph nodes in her chest.

William told the publication he was "devastated" when he found out. But after his own diagnosis, Melanie revealed she panicked.

She said: “I remember vividly thinking, ‘I don’t have the strength to take care of myself and lose my father at the same time’.”

The pair both received the good news that they are now cancer free. And Melanie admits the journey "changed my life”. She said she is “not so afraid anymore” of what life might bring.

Dad William added: "We’re a very together family. We’re bonded by all kinds of difficulties that we’ve overcome.”

And he confessed to feeling healthier than he has in years. Two years before his diagnosis, the Captain James T Kirk actor headed into space. He became the oldest person to fly in space after being a passenger aboard Blue Origin NS-18.

As he continues to try out new things, he revealed last week that he is set to play his first heavy metal performance later this year. It comes as part of his newly formed band The *uckers.

The band will take to the stage at Riot Fest in Chicago in September after the punk rock festival spent more than a decade trying to get him to perform.

Article continues below

Like this story? For more of the latest showbiz news and gossip, follow Mirror Celebs on TikTok, Snapchat, Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, YouTube and Threads.

News.title: Trump lawyers in uproar as judge rules they must hand his financial records to BBC in defamation case
News.content:
Trump lawyers in uproar as judge rules they must hand his financial records to BBC in defamation case

The judge said that, in order to show the 'reputational and financial injury' to Trump from the 2024 Panorama documentary, his legal team must hand over financial records to the BBC's lawyers

View Image The president's lawyers are not happy at the decision (file photo) (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

A judge has ruled that Donald Trump must hand over his financial records to the BBC as part of his 10 billion dollar (£7.5 billion) defamation case against the broadcaster.

‌



Trump’s legal team has tried to block the move, calling the ruling “premature, improper, and especially burdensome”.

‌



It comes after Trump sued the UK broadcaster in a Florida court over the editing of a Panorama documentary from 2024 about the US Capitol riots.

‌



BBC lawyers had asked for the financial documents from the Donald J Trump Revocable Trust, which holds the president’s business interests and assets. Judge Enjolique Lett granted the request for access to records from the trust, which is managed by Trump’s eldest son.

Trump’s representatives had called the BBC team’s request a “fishing expedition”, a claim rejected by BBC lawyers, who said the details were needed to assess the financial impact of the programme.

‌



The court papers stated: “Defendants have requested information from these entities only because plaintiff alleges without limitation that his financial interests have been impacted by defendants’ actions and because plaintiff is the sole beneficiary of a trust that owns or is associated with nearly 400 entities.”

The trust, which is also represented by Mr Trump’s lawyers, had sought to resist the demand previously arguing: “Although plaintiff has alleged that his businesses have suffered damages as a result of the documentary, that alone does not give defendants carte-blanche to obtain sweeping financial discovery from hundreds of non-parties.”

Trump’s lawsuit alleged that the Panorama episode, broadcast shortly before the 2024 presidential election he won, caused him reputational and financial injury. Criticism has been levelled at the show claiming it gave the impression the US president had encouraged his supporters to storm the Capitol building on January 6 2021 after he lost the election to Joe Biden.

Article continues below

BBC director-general Tim Davie resigned in the wake of the allegations and BBC chairman Samir Shah apologised on behalf of the broadcaster over an “error of judgment”. Mr Shah accepted the editing of the programme gave “the impression of a direct call for violent action”.

But the corporation is fighting to have the case thrown out of court, claiming that it will have a “chilling effect” it would have on “robust reporting on public figures and events”.

It has also challenged the jurisdiction of a Florida court to hear the case given the programme was never aired in the state or the US.

News.title: Donald Trump threatens to blow up 'bridge or power plant' every time Iran hits ship
News.content:
Donald Trump threatens to blow up 'bridge or power plant' every time Iran hits ship

US President Donald Trump has thrashed out plans for Iran ground invasion as he warned Tehran he will blow up a bridge or a power depot every time they hit a ship in the Strait of Hormuz

View 3 Images Donald Trump speaks during a reception with FIFA President Gianni Infantino last week (Image: AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

US President Donald Trump has threatened to blow up a power plant or bridge every time Iran hits a ship in the latest Middle East crisis escalation.

‌



It came as it emerged Pentagon war-planners are drafting a scheme for a partial ground invasion of Iran if the Tehran regime refuses to back down. The President has not green-lighted a ground assault on key Kharg Island but it is one of the options for escalation with which he has been presented.

‌



Mr Trump stormed: "From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by missile, rocket, drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy one bridge or power plant, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran."

‌



In recent weeks, the Republican leader has made repeated threats against civilian infrastructure as he became frustrated with Iran’s defiance.

Zelensky fires Ukraine's military chief after widespread protests READ MORE :

View 3 Images A plane being prepared for war (Image: X)

But Iran has hit back with warnings of their own escalation, claiming they could attack US bases and even kidnap US soldiers, whisking them back to Tehran. And Tehran’s military even threatened that it America does occupy Khark Island then Iran would go ahead and bomb its own territory. Former Iranian Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki, now a member of parliament, said Iran should go further than striking US bases in the region and consider capturing American soldiers.

‌



He stormed: "The US threats have intensified, and it has said that it will seize Kharg Island and take control of Iran's oil facilities. I have been advocating for a ground war for a long time. We should seize one of the US bases in the region, capture its forces, and bring them back to our country.’ An Iranian army spokesperson warned Iran would bomb its own territory rather than allow US forces to occupy it, as threats of a ground operation grown.

Brigadier General Mohammad Akrami-Nia said on Iranian state television: “If America occupies our territory, we will even bomb our own territory. This is the logic of war." The remarks came as US Central Command marked the tenth consecutive day of strikes against Iranian targets. US President Donald Trump is expected to decide in the coming days how to proceed, with the prospect of a US ground operation or seizure of Iranian territory now openly discussed.The Pentagon is preparing options for ground operations in Iran that would fall short of a full invasion but could involve thousands of troops and take weeks or months.

View 3 Images Bridge hit by US in Iran strikes (Image: ISNA/AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

The White House said the Pentagon was working to give the president "maximum optionality" but that "this does not mean the president has made a decision." Iranian MP Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a former member of the parliamentary National Security Commission, said Tehran could launch ground attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain if the US invaded Iranian territory. On the prospect of a US assault on Kharg Island, he said Washington might take it for a day but could not hold it. He said: "Iranian missiles from Semnan, Zahedan, Isfahan and elsewhere can reach it. Occupying Kharg Island would turn it into a target for Iran.”

And it is possible Iran could make a bold move to take territory, including the taking of Bubiyan Island which is owned by Kuwait. The island, with an area of 700 square mikles, is Kuwait's largest and sits at the northern end of the Persian Gulf close to Iraq. Some Iranian political figures and social media accounts have considered the scenario in response to a potential US seizure of Kharg, suggesting the IRGC could use regional proxies and its Saberin special forces unit to launch a ground operation through southern Iraq if Washington moved on Iranian territory.

The Saberin unit is an elite IRGC formation with extensive combat experience across Iran and neighbouring countries. Reports of Iranian military movements toward the Kuwaiti border have circulated online. Kuwait hosts US forces and has been among the most heavily targeted countries in the latest wave of Iranian strikes. Earlier reports in March and May alleged that IRGC commandos had targeted Bubiyan and engaged against Kuwaiti forces.

News.title: PC Harper's widow criticises early prisoner release plan as Burnham to review scheme
News.content:
The widow of PC Andrew Harper has described the possible early release of prisoners as "deplorable", following reports that two of his killers could be freed early.

Lissie Harper said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier said he would review the Sentencing Act policy that from September would see thousands of offenders in England and Wales eligible to be released earlier.

Speaking on Wednesday, Burnham said: "I can't say that I can change the policy completely, but I will look at it in detail before we go further forward."

He acknowledged that there was "pressure on prisons places" and that a failure to invest in the prison system in the past had created "an unacceptable situation".

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but could be released early under the new Sentencing Act.

PC Harper was killed after he was dragged to his death behind their getaway car. The car's driver, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for manslaughter but would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham's comments came after the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said the potential early release of two of her son's killers felt like an "insult".

In a separate statement released later on Wednesday, PC Harper's widow Lissie Harper said: "It has taken me years to rebuild a life that was torn apart in a matter of moments. Years to pick up the pieces left behind by three men whose actions robbed Andrew of his life and stole our future.

"It is deplorable to me that we have reached a point where releasing prisoners early is even considered acceptable. We speak of justice, accountability and standing with victims, yet decisions like this do the opposite."

The overcrowding of the prison estate has been a problem for several years and successive governments have released prisoners early in a bid to free up space.

Tens of thousands of inmates have been let out of prison to create more space in jails since 2024.

The Sentencing Act, which was passed by Sir Keir Starmer's government earlier this year, was designed to ease pressure on prisons, and will see some offenders spend less time in prison before release.

Burnham said: "I want to assure myself that everything has been looked at before this policy proceeds, and I can give that assurance that every single part of this I will look into with the justice secretary."

Concerning the case of PC Harper, he said: "I feel for the family it's an appalling crime that was committed."

He said the "main perpetrator" of his death would not be eligible for early release.

Burnham also said it was not acceptable to joke about early releases and that it was right Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had apologised for comments he made that were caught on camera.

News.title: Most bus fares in England to be capped at £2 from January
News.content:
The bus fare cap in England will revert to Â£2 from January, new prime minister Andy Burnham has announced.

The government says the policy, which is expected to cost more than Â£500m, will "help with the cost of living and give people the breathing space they need".

At the start of last year, the England-wide bus fare cap rose to Â£3 under Sir Keir Starmer's Labour government, although in Liverpool and Manchester fares were held at Â£2.

Burnham said affordable transport links were an essential, adding: "Lower fares will help people get to where they need to."

The measure gives people "a little bit of hope" in a time when many are grappling with higher living costs - especially after fuel costs spiked as a result of the US-Iran war, transport secretary Heidi Alexander told the BBC's Today programme.

However, she admitted the measure was "not the whole solution".

The new cap will take effect from January next year for fares on participating buses outside of London. The cost of a non-discounted single bus journey in London is Â£1.75.

The Burnham government said going back to a Â£2 cap should particularly help passengers in rural and coastal areas, where single fares can be higher.

The Campaign for Better Transport said rural areas were still suffering from fewer bus routes and services, adding that such areas had been more affected by council cut backs in the last decade than urban zones.

Services in those areas - as measured by vehicle miles - decreased by 18% between 2019 and 2024, according to the County Councils Network, which represents 39 unitary and county councils across England.

"What we need to see is the replacing of those lost services which have particularly affected those in rural areas," Campaign for Better Transport's Michael Solomon Williams said.

News.title: Ex-Southern Water boss among four charged over alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests
News.content:
The ex-chief executive of Southern Water has been charged with three others over an alleged plan to manipulate water quality tests to avoid paying financial penalties of about Â£45m, it can now be reported.

Matthew Wright is accused of conspiring to defraud the Environment Agency (EA) and water regulator Ofwat between 2012 and 2017, along with Philip Barker, Clive Massey and Mark Gregory, who also worked at the firm.

Wright's solicitor says he "denies all wrongdoing and has co-operated fully" with the EA's investigation.

Southern Water said the charges related to "a historic set of failures" uncovered in an internal investigation. It said it was a "completely different" company to a decade ago.

The EA asked a judge to issue a summons against the four, charging them with the offence, last year, but Wright launched a legal challenge, dismissed by two senior judges on Wednesday.

Massey, Gregory and Barker did not appear at the hearing in London and were not represented.

According to court documents, the allegations include arranging for wastewater to be removed from facilities by tankers in order to create "no flow" results.

This had been "with a view to covering up pollution and deceiving those whose function is to protect the public from such harm", prosecutors allege.

In his legal challenge, Wright's lawyers argued at the High Court in June that the EA did not have the power to issue the summons and it should be thrown out.

But the judges dismissed his claim and ruled restrictions previously preventing reporting of the legal challenge should be lifted.

Separate court listings showed the case against 60-year-old Wright, of Haslemere, Surrey; Barker, 57, of West Chiltington, West Sussex; Massey, 64, of Brandhill, Shropshire; and Gregory, 63, of Southampton, were scheduled to be heard at Medway Magistrates' Court on 14 July.

The four are accused of conspiring between 2012 and 2017 to defraud those conducting the environmental and financial regulation duties of Southern Water, including the EA and Ofwat, by "the implementation of artificial no-flow events at wastewater treatment works".

News.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The ChatGPT-maker said its agent - an AI system which can operate alone after human instruction â was being tested in a controlled environment but, after finding weaknesses, was able to escape the test limits.

They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.

OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was conducting an investigation alongside Hugging Face, whose boss Clement Delangue said in a post on X it was "mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously".

"The investigation is ongoing, and we'll share more learnings from what might be the first incident of its kind," Delangue added.

A government spokesperson said the UK's AI Security Institute was studying the behaviour from the AI system seen in the incident and was continuing to work with OpenAI and other labs to improve safeguards.

They said organisations should step up their cyber-defences by taking steps such as enrolling in the government-backed Cyber Essentials certification scheme.

News.title: Prince George enjoys coastal fun in new video as he becomes a teenager
News.content:
A new video of Prince George has been released by Kensington Palace to mark his 13th birthday.

The video, external, showing a smiling prince waving at the camera in his sunglasses, playing cricket on the beach and climbing rocks, was accompanied by the caption: "Thank you for all the birthday wishes for George today!"

The video was shot in Cornwall at Easter, and follows a new photograph of George which was also published on social media on Wednesday.

George, the elder son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is second in line to the throne.

News.title: Police formally investigate woman, 70, after Brit stabbed to death in French village
News.content:
A woman has been placed under formal investigation over the death last year in France of a British-South African mother-of-four.

Karen Carter, 65, was found lying near her car with stab wounds by a friend in TrÃ©molat, the Dordogne village where she had lived for over a decade and managed two holiday rental homes.

Prosecutors say the 70-year-old woman was originally taken into custody in 2025 as part of preliminary inquiries before being released.

Jacques-Edouard Andrault, the investigating judge in the case, said in a statement on Wednesday that "the investigations conducted as part of the judicial inquiry opened on 7 May, 2025, have led the investigating judge to formally charge her".

Being placed under formal investigation in French law means an investigating judge has to decide whether or not there is enough evidence for the case to go to trial.

At the time of the killing in April last year, Karen Carter's husband, Alan, said that he first heard of her death through a cousin who had read about it on a local community Facebook page.

He said he received confirmation of the death after his assistant phoned local police.

Describing his wife as an outgoing, friendly person who "wouldn't hurt a fly", he said her death has been "traumatic" for his family.

"I'm an introvert, and she's the exact opposite. She's an extrovert, she loves people, she loves to have fun. People love her, she has a good heart," he said.

"She's the one who would bring home the lost dog, or cat, or whatever. She's that sort of person. Everyone liked her. That's why I married her. She's just lovely."

News.title: Natalie Fleet leaves 'triggering' safeguarding minister role
News.content:
Natalie Fleet says she has stepped down as safeguarding minister after finding the role "overwhelmingly triggering", telling the BBC that it was making her ill.

The Labour MP, who was groomed and raped as a teenager, added she told the team of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham that she "sadly couldn't stay" in the job.

Fleet described it as the "bravest thing I've ever done" and offered her support to her successor.

She was appointed to the role on 12 May this year following the resignation of Jess Phillips, who said opportunities for progress had been "stalled and delayed" under the leadership of then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Announcing her departure on the social media platform X, external, Fleet said: "Honour of lifetime to be minister for safeguarding. Quickly found contents overwhelmingly triggering."

She added: "Victims deserve someone at their best."

She told BBC News the nature of the role as safeguarding minister means "you hear the worst of humanity", saying: "I understand what it is like not to be seen and not to be heard."

"I know how important this job is and I know how much it needs a good and competent minister. It quickly became apparent how ill it was making me."

She received support from the Home Office while in post, she said.

"But even with that [support] the nature of the job means that you hear the worst of humanity.

"Anybody would struggle hearing that but not everyone would react in the same way as someone who has gone through what I have.

"For me it is one of the most important jobs in government. It was the honour of my life to be able to do it.

"Nothing can compare to being asked to make a difference to the lives of women and girls. It was incredible."

Fleet was elected MP for Bolsover in July 2024, succeeding Labour stalwart Dennis Skinner.

She has spoken openly about her experiences as a teenager, including in an interview with GB News in 2024.

Fleet said she became pregnant at the age of 15 after being groomed and raped by an older man, adding she has "weekly nightmares" about what she said happened to her.

"I didn't know we were having unprotected sex," she told the broadcaster. "I was a child and (it) is statutory rape."

The MP said she fell pregnant and gave birth to her daughter, who she described as the "absolute love of my life".

In her maiden speech in the House of Commons in October 2024, Fleet said it was her "duty" to speak up for women in her Derbyshire constituency "whose stories are not being told".

News.title: Liverpool issue bans as £1.2m seized from ticket touts
News.content:
Liverpool have issued over 400 lifetime bans after more than Â£1.2m of assets relating to the illegal selling of tickets was seized by police.

The club worked with Merseyside Police to seize the assets from organised ticket touts.

The police operation focused on the laundering of criminal proceeds from illicit ticket sales and took place alongside the club's crackdown on ticket touting, both online and in the ground.

The club has since issued 432 lifetime bans to the guilty parties, as well as 115 indefinite suspensions.

Detective Chief Inspector Nick Suffield said: "This is a fantastic example of partnership working between ourselves and Liverpool Football Club for the good of the fans and the general public.

"We will always take action to protect genuine fans who fall victim to touts when all they are trying to do is simply purchase tickets to support their team."

From the assets seized, the money was split between Merseyside Police and the Home Office.

Last year, BBC Sport revealed Liverpool had shut down 145,000 ticket accounts over the previous two years as part of a crackdown on touting.

And last season alone, Liverpool analysed almost 700,000 ticket registrations, with 67,663 suspected fake accounts blocked or cancelled, and a further 121,379 accounts currently under investigation.

A further 3,847 tickets were cancelled for suspicious purchase activity in the 2025-26 season. They were put back on sale as general admission tickets, increasing the number available for genuine fans.

There was also a significant increase in targeted stops carried out on matchdays by the club, who prevented access to the turnstiles for accounts with suspicious activity.

These stops were carried out at Anfield â an average of 300 per home game â and at away games both in the Premier League and in Europe.

News.title: Burnham rebukes ministers after prisoner releases joke
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has rebuked some of his cabinet ministers after they were caught on camera sharing a joke about releasing prisoners.

In the footage, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting can be heard telling Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood that new Justice Secretary Alex Norris "wants to let them all out".

Streeting apologised for the remarks, which were first published by Metro journalist Craig Munro, after critics suggested he had been joking about the government's early prisoner release scheme.

Asked whether it was appropriate for his ministers to be joking about early release, Burnham told reporters: "No it's not, and certainly that's been acknowledged and apologies have been made."

The moment was captured on Tuesday, when broadcasters were invited to film members of Burnham's cabinet chatting ahead of their first meeting.

In the footage, Mahmood can be seen chatting with Streeting before breaking off to greet Norris, a former minister at the Home Office who was promoted to justice secretary by Burnham on Monday.

Streeting can then be heard joking to Mahmood that Norris is "the enemy now", to which she replies "no he's not".

Streeting goes on to say "he wants to let them all out", before Mahmood replies "You know who's boss!" and the pair share a laugh.

In a post on X, Streeting said he had been referencing a joke Theresa May used to make about Ken Clarke when the two of them occupied the same cabinet posts as Mahmood and Norris respectively in a Conservative government.

May has previously said that when she was home secretary, she would joke about Clarke: 'I locked 'em up and he let 'em out'".

He added: "I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new justice secretary.

"But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity."

Mahmood released a similar comment, adding: "I appreciate this is an extremely serious issue and do not want anyone to mistake this moment of levity for a lack of serious intent."

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the pair of making light of the government's scheme to release some prisoners early to ease prison overcrowding, announced in 2024 when Mahmood was justice secretary.

"While Andy Burnham's cabinet are joking about letting criminals out of prison early, Conservatives are listening to victims and will continue to fight this disgusting policy," she wrote on X.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said it was "right" that Streeting had apologised.

"Those remarks don't reflect the seriousness with which all of them will approach matters relating to public safety and the prison system".

Shortly after coming to power in 2024, the Labour government announced emergency measures to release prisoners in England and Wales early to ease overcrowding, in a scheme that was later expanded.

Under the Sentencing Act, due to come into effect in September, some prisoners let out after serving a third of their sentence, while those who would previously have served two-thirds will instead be released after serving half of their sentence.

News.title: No helicopters to fight wildfires as 'crisis management' plans activated in Wales
News.content:
The Welsh government has activated "crisis management arrangements" due to the number of wildfires across the nation.

It comes amid criticism from residents over a lack of resources like helicopters to tackle the fires, some of which have been burning for days across north and south Wales.

The Welsh government said North Wales Fire and Rescue had received extra resources but aerial support was not available anywhere in the UK.

However, it said "urgent discussions are now underway both within Wales and at a UK level to identify how this can be resolved".

Meanwhile, firefighters are tackling a big blaze in south Wales for a third day, with the smoke travelling 30 miles (48km) away.

News.title: Over £100,000 raised for boy, 3, in croc attack
News.content:
More than Â£100,000 has been raised for a three-year-old boy who was attacked in a crocodile enclosure.

The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst near Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 18 June when he was attacked by at least one of the animals.

A fundraising page has raised Â£105,000 for the boy and his family after the three-year-old was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital, where he has undergone seven surgeries.

Cambridgeshire Police arrested and bailed a 30-year-old man from Norfolk on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident.

News.title: Mid-air 10-person brawl halts easyJet   flight
News.content:
A mid-air brawl involving around 10 passengers forced a Liverpool-bound easyJet plane to fly back to Tenerife, according to air traffic control.

The captain decided to return to the Spanish island about 30 minutes after departure "due to the danger" the fight "posed to the safety of the flight", the air traffic controller said.

Police met flight EZY3352 when it touched down at Tenerife South airport on Tuesday evening, per the crew's request.

The 186-passenger aircraft then continued to Liverpool.

The air traffic controller said in its statement, originally written in Spanish: "Our full support goes out to the crews and passengers who are increasingly having to endure these situations."

EasyJet said the plane "returned to the airport and was met by police due to a group of passengers behaving disruptively.

News.title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
News.content:
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.

Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.

Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.

June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: 'No secrecy' over asylum camp decision, court told
News.content:
The Home Office did not act in secrecy over its decision to house asylum seekers at a former military training camp in East Sussex and engaged with relevant bodies beforehand and afterwards, the High Court has heard.

Community interest company Crowborough Shield is taking legal action over the government's use of Crowborough Training Camp to house up to 540 men.

The group claims the Home Office failed to exercise its powers with the openness required.

James Strachan KC, for the Home Office, said the Secretary of State engaged with the police, NHS and councils and once the decision was taken, a forum was established for people to address any issues.

News.title: Former Lloyd's of London boss's relationship breached rules, firm says
News.content:
Lloyd's of London's former boss's close relationship with another director breached compliance rules, the insurance market has said after an internal investigation.

Former chief executive John Neal and former corporate affairs director Rebekah Clement's relationship was "sufficiently close... that it could be viewed as creating a perceived conflict of interest", the firm said.

Lloyd's said the pair breached compliance rules by not disclosing their relationship but found no conclusive evidence they had a romantic relationship while at Lloyd's.

Neal said all parties can now move on. Clement's lawyer said she is considering legal action.

"Rebekah is hugely disappointed with Lloyd's conduct over the course of this investigation, the nature and length of which have caused her unnecessary stress and significant reputational damage relative to its 'findings'," Clement's lawyer added.

"She is not surprised that Lloyd's found no evidence of an inappropriate relationship with John Neal, nor any evidence of any failings in her promotion. She also co-operated with the investigation throughout.

"Yet, Lloyd's has still chosen to find against Rebekah, on the pretext of 'perception', the source of which was rumour, gossip and innuendo."

Neal said: "I am pleased, but not at all surprised, that the investigation found there was no inappropriate relationship.

"I would have hoped less time and resource had been spent in reaching a conclusion on the central question that was, in truth, never in doubt.

"I am disappointed with the other findings and do not accept them."

Lloyd's said on Wednesday that it first received "certain whistleblowing reports" in November 2023 but that it didn't act on them.

It said its chairman Sir Charles Roxburgh judged this to be a governance failure and informed the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) about it in October 2025.

Lloyd's said it could not share the nature of these allegations or the identities of the people involved.

In November 2025, Lloyd's said Sir Charles became aware of "new information related to an alleged personal relationship" between Neal and Clement and "immediately launched an expanded investigation into the matter".

Lloyd's said its investigation was hampered by the fact that Neal and Clement had both left the company and refused to answer questions, but Lloyd's said it interviewed nearly 40 witnesses in its probe.

It added that it has kept the FCA informed throughout the process.

Sir Charles said on Wednesday: "Based on the findings of this investigation, we have concluded that the conduct of the former chief executive fell significantly below the standards expected of him."

He added the investigation "established serious failings in the governance standards and in following processes, most worryingly in the handling of whistleblowing reports. These were serious failures that should never have been allowed to happen."

Lloyd's history as a City institution stretches back well over 300 years, with its first recorded mention appearing in 1688.

News.title: Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to restore fire-hit Mackintosh building
News.content:
Glasgow School of Art says it cannot fully restore the city's iconic Mackintosh Building to its former state without additional financial support.

The art school previously insisted it was committed to a faithful reinstatement of the building, which was designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh but wrecked by two fires in 2014 and 2018.

However it now says "financial clarity", provided by an insurance settlement regarding the 2018 blaze, has shown it "cannot take forward the faithful reinstatement on its own."

Instead it suggests the building has potential to be an anchor for a "creative and cultural production innovation district".

But this claim that has attracted scorn from figures in the art world.

News.title: Wild moment shirtless driver leaps head-first off bridge after being pulled over for speeding by police
News.content:
A driver in Missouri leapt head-first off a bridge after being pulled over by police in a bizarre incident captured on dashcam.

Stone County Sheriff’s deputies attempted to stop Gavin Thor Lundgren, 26, in Kimberling City in the early hours of Saturday (July 18) after he was clocked doing 75mph in a 45mph zone.

After leading them on a chase, Lundgren slowed down, exited his car and jumped off the Kimberling City bridge into the water below, leaving his driver’s license in the vehicle.

Lundgren allegedly headbutted two officers while they were taking him into custody after locating him in the water.
