A Story That Refuses to Age

Jonathan Larson’s RENT did not just win a Pulitzer Prize and four Tony Awards. It redefined what a Broadway musical could sound like and who it could speak for.

Set in the shadow of the HIV/AIDS crisis in New York’s East Village, the show follows a year in the lives of a group of friends fighting to make art, pay the rent, and hold onto each other.

The musical broke ground in the 1990s by bringing rock music, queer characters, and raw social issues onto a mainstream stage. Its arrival in Bogotá marks a cultural milestone for a city whose appetite for ambitious international theater has grown steadily over the past decade.

Why RENT Still Connects Three Decades On

The musical premiered in 1996, yet its central question feels startlingly current: how do you build a life of meaning when the world feels fragile and uncertain?

Songs like “Seasons of Love” have become anthems far beyond the theater, measuring a year not in money or milestones but in love. That emotional directness is why audiences return to it, and why a Bogotá season makes profound sense right now.

The show’s themes of community, displacement, and creative survival resonate across languages. A local Colombian cast will bring their own texture to characters that have been played everywhere from Tokyo to São Paulo.

For Bogotá, a city that has weathered its own cycles of uncertainty and renewal, the story of young people clinging to art and each other carries a particular weight. The production arrives at a moment when live performance is being embraced again with fresh intensity across Latin America.

The Practical Details: When, Where, and How Much

The season runs from August 7 to August 28, 2026, at the Centro Cultural Gimnasio Moderno, a well-regarded cultural space located at Carrera 9 # 74-99 in Bogotá.

Tickets are priced between US$21 and US$57. The production is mounted by 2 Productores, a local company, and marks the first time RENT has been staged in the Colombian capital.

The venue is easily reachable from the Chapinero and Zona G neighborhoods, making it a straightforward evening out for both residents and visitors staying in the city’s central corridor.

Given the limited four-week run and the show’s global fanbase, early booking is strongly advised. The intimate scale of the Centro Cultural Gimnasio Moderno means seating is finite, and a sold-out season is a realistic possibility.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and Visitors

For the foreign community in Bogotá, this production offers a rare taste of a Broadway classic without the need for international travel. It is a chance to enjoy a familiar cultural touchstone while experiencing the city’s own theatrical energy.

The decision to mount RENT locally, rather than importing a touring company, signals growing confidence in Colombia’s creative sector. For investors watching the entertainment and hospitality space, it is another data point suggesting Bogotá’s cultural infrastructure is maturing.

Visitors planning an August trip can build an evening around the show with ease. The surrounding Chapinero area is dense with well-reviewed restaurants, cafes, and bars that cater to international tastes, making a pre-show dinner or post-show drink a seamless part of the outing.

The US$21 to US$57 ticket range also makes the production accessible by international standards. A comparable seat at a Broadway house would cost several times more, meaning a night of professional musical theater here delivers strong value for dollar-earning visitors.

A Night Out With Staying Power

For expats and long-time Bogotá residents alike, this is a rare chance to see a canonical work of musical theater without boarding a plane. The local production promises the full score and emotional weight of the original.

It is also an invitation to experience Bogotá’s growing theater scene. The city has steadily built a reputation for ambitious stage work, and hosting a title like RENT signals confidence in that momentum.

Whether you know every lyric or are walking in fresh, the show offers something increasingly precious: a live, collective moment that asks you to feel something real.

As Bogotá continues to position itself as a cultural destination in South America, productions like this one help redraw the map for travelers who might once have looked only to Buenos Aires or São Paulo for world-class theater.

What Happens Next

The four-week window means word of mouth will spread quickly once the first performances land. Expect social media and expat forums to light up with reactions, which could drive last-minute demand even higher.

If this local staging succeeds, it may open the door for more major musical titles to receive Colombian productions in the years ahead. For now, the focus is squarely on August, when Bogotá finally gets its chance to measure a year in love.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this a touring Broadway production of RENT?

No. It is a local Colombian production by 2 Productores, performed in Bogotá for the first time, not a stop on an international tour. This means the cast, crew, and creative direction are all Colombian, offering a distinct local interpretation of the material.

What language will the Bogotá production of RENT be performed in?

The production is locally mounted, and while the exact language choice has not been detailed, local productions of major musicals in Bogotá are typically performed in Spanish. Audiences familiar with the English lyrics will still recognize the music and emotional arc immediately.

How do I get tickets for RENT in Bogotá?

Tickets are available through the venue’s official channels and ticketing partners. Prices range from US$21 to US$57, and early booking is recommended given the limited four-week run. Check the Centro Cultural Gimnasio Moderno website or authorized platforms for the most direct purchasing route.

World.title: Peru Passport Rule Now Strictly Enforced at Key Airports
World.content:
Latin America · Expats

Key Facts —Peru's rule. A passport must be valid for at least six months from the date you enter the country. —Enforcement start. Peruvian border officials began strict, immediate enforcement on January 1 of this year. —Affected airports. The rule is enforced at Lima's Jorge Chávez International Airport and Cusco's Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport. —Airline role. Airlines can and do deny boarding at your departure gate if your passport does not meet Peru's validity requirement. —Mexico and Colombia. Mexico requires a passport valid for the length of your stay; Colombia asks travelers to check a minimum of three to six months.

Travelers heading to Peru need to check their passport right now, because a long-standing entry rule is being enforced with new rigor at the country’s busiest airports. Starting January 1, Peruvian migration officers began turning away visitors whose travel documents fall short of a strict six-month validity window.

Passports are mandatory identification documents for crossing international borders by air.

What the Peru Passport Rule Actually Says

Peru requires every foreign visitor to carry a passport that is valid for at least six months from the date of entry. This is not a new law, but a rule that migration authorities are now applying without exception.

If your passport expires five months and three weeks after you land in Lima or Cusco, you can be refused entry on the spot. The U.S.

State Department and Peru’s own migration authority both confirm the six-month floor is absolute.

Which Airports Enforce the Rule and When It Started

The two main gateways are Lima’s Jorge Chávez International Airport, the country’s primary hub, and Cusco’s Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport, the entry point for Machu Picchu. Both locations apply the same standard.

Peruvian border officials began strict enforcement on January 1 of this year, and the change was immediate. There was no grace period, and the policy is now a fixed part of every entry inspection.

What Happens Before You Even Board the Plane

Airlines are the first line of defense. Carriers flying to Peru can deny boarding at your departure gate if your passport does not satisfy the destination’s validity rule.

This means a traveler can be stopped in Miami, Madrid, or São Paulo before ever setting foot on Peruvian soil. The financial hit from a lost flight often falls entirely on the passenger.

Why the Six-Month Passport Rule Exists in Latin America

Many countries across Latin America and the world use a six-month validity buffer to avoid situations where a traveler’s passport expires during an unexpected extended stay. This precaution protects both the visitor and the host country’s immigration system.

Peru’s rule is part of a broader regional patchwork. While Peru draws a hard line at six months, other popular destinations set different standards, which can confuse travelers planning multi-country trips.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

Foreign residents holding a Peruvian residency card are not exempt from the six-month passport rule when re-entering the country. A document that falls below six months can disrupt a return trip even if your residency status is fully valid.

For investors and business travelers who make frequent short trips, the stakes are high. A single denied boarding can mean missed meetings, lost deposits, and a scramble for emergency passport renewal services abroad.

Practical Steps for Expats and Tourists Right Now

Open your passport and find the expiration date. If you have a trip to Peru booked and fewer than six months remain after your arrival date, renew your passport immediately before traveling.

Expats living in Peru should verify their passport validity before any departure and re-entry. A document that falls below six months can disrupt a return trip even if you hold a residency card.

For other Latin American destinations, the rule changes. Mexico requires a passport valid for the duration of your stay, not six months.

Colombia asks travelers to confirm a minimum of three to six months, so check with your airline before booking.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens if my passport expires five months after I land in Peru?

You will likely be denied boarding by your airline or refused entry by Peruvian migration officials at the airport. The six-month rule is enforced without exceptions, and border officers are applying it strictly at Lima and Cusco airports.

Does the six-month rule apply to expats with a Peruvian residency card?

Yes. Expats re-entering Peru must still hold a passport with at least six months of validity, or their travel plans can be disrupted even with valid residency. The residency card alone does not override the passport validity requirement.

Is the six-month rule the same for Mexico and Colombia?

No. Mexico only requires a passport valid for the length of your stay, not a fixed six-month window. Colombia asks travelers to verify a minimum of three to six months, so rules vary by country and you should always check before booking.

World.title: Metropolitan Opera Opens Laffont Auditions to South America
World.content:
Latin America · Culture

Key Facts —What it is. The Eric and Dominique Laffont Competition is the Metropolitan Opera’s program to discover and develop exceptional young opera singers. —Who can enter. Vocalists aged 20 to 30 from Argentina, Chile, and Colombia can audition with a video of an operatic aria. —The prize path. District winners advance to a South America final in Santiago, then to New York semifinals and a Grand Finals Concert at the Met. —Cash awards. Semifinalists receive US$5,000, finalists US$10,000, and Grand Finals winners earn US$20,000 each. —First winners. Chilean soprano Camila Romero and Argentine mezzo-soprano Valeria Delmé were the inaugural South America winners in 2026.

The Metropolitan Opera has quietly opened a new door for young Latin American singers, launching a dedicated South America pathway for its Eric and Dominique Laffont Competition that lets talent from Argentina, Chile, and Colombia audition closer to home.

The Metropolitan Opera is a New York City institution dedicated to grand opera performances.

What the Laffont Competition Actually Is

The Eric and Dominique Laffont Competition is the Metropolitan Opera’s long-running young-singer audition program, formerly known as the National Council Auditions. It exists for one reason: to find exceptional emerging opera voices and move them toward Met-level visibility and career opportunities.

Singers progress through district rounds, regional finals, New York semifinals, and a Grand Finals Concert staged on the Met’s legendary stage. At every step, they perform for Met artistic staff and industry judges who can change a career with a single decision.

How the South America Pathway Works

Beginning with the 2025–26 season, the Met established a South America Region based in Santiago, Chile, with districts in Argentina, Chile, and Colombia. The inaugural district registration opened in September 2025, with district competitions running from October 2025 through January 2026.

District winners then advance to a South America Region final in Santiago. The region’s top singers earn a trip to the National Semifinals in New York, which took place on March 15, 2026, followed by the Grand Finals Concert on March 22.

How a Singer from the Region Can Enter

The competition invites vocalists aged 20 to 30 from the participating countries. The first step is submitting one video recording of an operatic aria during the qualifying application window, which ran July 1 through July 31, 2025, with results announced on September 1.

The recording must be free of any sound or video enhancement. For district and region rounds, singers must prepare four operatic arias in two or more languages.

Oratorio, musical theater, concert arias, and zarzuela are not permitted.

Why the Metropolitan Opera Competition Matters

Advancing in this competition places a young singer on the Met’s stage in front of the very people who cast major roles. The visibility alone can launch an international career, and the cash prizes are substantial: semifinalists receive US$5,000, finalists US$10,000, and Grand Finals winners earn US$20,000 each.

The inaugural South America winners proved the pipeline works immediately. Chilean soprano Camila Romero and Argentine mezzo-soprano Valeria Delmé became the region’s first singers to reach the New York semifinals in 2026, putting their countries squarely on the Met’s radar.

A Continent Rich in Opera Talent Finally Gets a Closer Stage

South America has long punched above its weight in classical music, producing world-class voices that often had to travel to the United States or Europe just to be heard in a formal audition setting. The new Santiago-based region removes a significant financial and logistical barrier that kept many promising singers from even trying.

The Met’s decision to carve out a dedicated South America pathway also signals that the institution sees the region as more than a source of occasional talent. It is a strategic investment in a pipeline that can feed the company’s future casts for years to come.

What This Means for Expats, Investors, and Culture Watchers

For foreign residents and investors with an eye on Latin America’s cultural sector, the Met’s expansion is a quiet but meaningful vote of confidence in the region’s artistic infrastructure. Santiago now joins a small list of global cities that host official Metropolitan Opera audition hubs, which can boost local opera companies, music schools, and performance venues.

Tourists and culture-focused travelers may also start seeing more South American singers on the Met’s stage in New York, creating a virtuous cycle of exposure. When a Chilean soprano or Argentine mezzo-soprano wins in New York, it draws international attention back to the theaters and conservatories that trained them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to travel to New York to enter the competition?

No. The first rounds happen in your home district within Argentina, Chile, or Colombia, and the South America Region final takes place in Santiago. Only the region’s winners travel to New York for the semifinals and Grand Finals, which significantly reduces upfront costs for young artists who might otherwise never audition.

What kind of repertoire must I prepare?

You need four operatic arias in two or more languages for the district and region rounds. Musical theater, oratorio, zarzuela, and concert arias are not accepted. The initial qualifying round requires just one video-recorded aria with no audio or video enhancement, so the first hurdle is accessible from anywhere with a decent recording setup.

What do winners actually receive?

Beyond career-changing visibility, there are direct cash awards. Semifinalists receive US$5,000, finalists US$10,000, and approximately four to six Grand Finals winners each receive US$20,000. The finals concert is also broadcast nationwide on the Met Opera Radio Network, giving winners a national audience in the United States.

World.title: Medellín Tourism Hit US$2.8 Billion in 2025, Stirring Debate
World.content:
Colombia · Business

Key Facts —Estimated 2025 tourism revenue. Close to COP$9 trillion (approx. US$2.3 billion), based on card transactions and excluding cash. —Visitor growth in H1 2025. 954,632 visitors arrived, a 12.4% increase from the same period in 2024. —Top source market. The United States remained the leading country of origin for foreign tourists. —Main economic beneficiaries. Lodging, gastronomy, local transport, shopping, and entertainment sectors. —Short-term rental impact. In 2024, 85% of Airbnb-linked spending in Colombia stayed in neighborhood businesses, not with hosts.

Medellín generated an estimated COP$9 trillion (approximately US$2.8 billion) in tourism revenue during 2025, a figure that underscores the sector’s powerful economic pull even as it fuels a growing debate over the city’s social fabric.

Medellín is a Colombian city that attracts visitors with its mild climate and cultural transformation.

The Scale of Medellín's Visitor Economy

The estimate comes from the city’s Tourism and Entertainment Intelligence System (SITE), which draws on card transaction data from Credibanco, a major Colombian payment processor, and analytics firm CityData. The calculation extrapolates from roughly COP$4 trillion (approx.

US$790 million) in recorded card spending, based on Credibanco’s coverage of about 45% of local card transactions.

The final figure does not capture cash payments, meaning the true economic footprint is likely larger. In the first half of 2025 alone, the city welcomed 954,632 visitors, a 12.4% jump year-on-year.

Who Is Coming and Where They Spend

International travelers made up 59% of arrivals during that period. The top feeder markets were the United States, Panama, Mexico, Peru, and Costa Rica, with the U.S. consistently leading the list of foreign visitors throughout the year.

City officials say the spending flows most heavily into lodging, internal transport, gastronomy, shopping, and leisure. A September 2025 snapshot showed 184,929 visitors that month, with 59.9% foreigners and 11.9% Colombians living abroad.

The Engine Behind Medellín's Growth

The boom rests on a transformed global image, improved security, a mild climate, and a growing reputation as a hub for digital nomads and remote workers. Direct flights from major U.S. cities and Panama have made access easier than ever.

Local authorities frame tourism as a core pillar of economic development, linking it directly to jobs for families in hotels, restaurants, transport, and neighborhood shops. The city’s innovation district and cultural calendar have also widened its appeal beyond traditional vacationers.

A Sober Look at the Social Tensions

The rapid growth has sharpened a debate over mass tourism. Critics point to rising bureaucratic costs tied to promotion and regulation, alongside visible pressure on housing and public space in popular neighborhoods.

Short-term rentals sit at the center of the friction. Data cited by Airbnb shows that in Colombia, the economic impact of guests and hosts surpassed COP$10.6 trillion (approx.

US$3.3 billion) in 2024, with 85% of that spending staying in neighborhood businesses rather than going to hosts.

Yet the platform describes Medellín as one of Latin America’s epicenters for short-term renting, which feeds local concerns about gentrification, rising long-term rents, and the transformation of quiet barrios into transient zones.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and property investors, the revenue figures confirm Medellín’s status as a maturing destination with a diversified visitor base. The strong U.S. connection, in particular, supports a steady pipeline of short-term rental demand and service-sector opportunities.

However, the same data should prompt caution. The growing political sensitivity around housing and neighborhood change means tighter regulations on platforms like Airbnb are a real possibility, a trend already seen in other global cities facing similar growing pains.

What Happens Next

City officials are likely to face increasing pressure to balance promotion with protection, crafting policies that safeguard residential communities without killing a vital economic engine. The SITE data system itself may become a tool for more targeted, data-driven regulation.

For now, the 2025 numbers give both sides ammunition: proponents can point to billions in spending and thousands of jobs, while critics can highlight the social costs that the raw revenue figures conveniently leave out. The conversation in Medellín is only getting louder.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much tourism revenue did Medellín generate in 2025?

The city estimates roughly COP$9 trillion, or about US$2.8 billion, based on card transactions tracked by its SITE system. The figure excludes cash spending, so the real total is likely higher.

Which countries send the most tourists to Medellín?

The United States is the top source market, followed by Panama, Mexico, Peru, and Costa Rica. In some months, the Dominican Republic and Spain also rank among the top five.

Why is tourism growth controversial in Medellín?

While the sector creates jobs and income, rapid expansion has sparked concerns over housing pressure, gentrification, and the conversion of residential neighborhoods into short-term rental zones. The debate centers on how to balance economic benefits with protecting local communities.

World.title: Ex-Army Chief: Milei Weakens Argentina’s Malvinas Claim
World.content:
Argentina · Politics

Key Facts —Who spoke. Former Argentine Army chief Diego Luis Suñer made the remarks on 2 June 2023, the anniversary of the 1982 war. —What he said. Suñer called the Malvinas a permanent and non-negotiable national objective for Argentina. —Government position. President Javier Milei reaffirmed the sovereignty claim while calling for mature dialogue with the UK. —UK response. Downing Street said sovereignty rests with the UK and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount. —Why it matters. The dispute remains tied to Argentine nationalism and the memory of the 1982 conflict.

The Malvinas remain “a permanent and non-negotiable national objective,” former Argentine Army chief Diego Luis Suñer declared, reviving a politically charged debate over sovereignty just as President Javier Milei’s government attempts to balance a firm claim with pragmatic diplomacy toward London.

Argentina maintains a longstanding territorial dispute with the United Kingdom over the islands.

A General’s Uncompromising Words

Suñer, who once led Argentina’s ground forces, spoke on 2 June 2023 to mark the anniversary of the 1982 war with the United Kingdom over the South Atlantic archipelago.

His phrasing echoed the most traditional wing of Argentine nationalism, which views any softening on the islands as a betrayal of the 649 soldiers who died in the ten-week conflict.

Milei’s Balancing Act on the Malvinas

President Javier Milei, a libertarian economist who took office in December 2023, has walked a careful line on the issue that stirs deep emotion across Argentina’s political spectrum.

On 25 April 2026, Milei posted on social media that the islands “were, are, and will always be Argentine,” a statement that came days after Reuters reported he had called for direct negotiations with Britain.

His official 2 April 2026 statement reaffirmed the sovereignty claim, argued the 1982 war “did not alter the legal nature of this dispute,” and urged “mature and sincere dialogue” with the United Kingdom.

At the same time, Milei warned Argentina would take “all the necessary diplomatic measures” in response to oil exploration activity around the islands.

Why the Islands Strike Such a Deep Nerve

For Argentines, the Malvinas are far more than a territorial claim. The archipelago, known internationally as the Falkland Islands, sits about 480 kilometres off the Patagonian coast and has been under British administration since 1833.

The 1982 war, launched by the military dictatorship then ruling Argentina, ended in defeat after 74 days. The conflict still evokes strong emotions and is woven into school curricula, political rhetoric, and national identity.

Sovereignty over the islands is enshrined in Argentina’s constitution, and successive governments have treated the recovery of the territory as a unifying national cause.

Any perceived retreat from that position can trigger swift backlash from opposition parties and veterans’ groups, as Milei discovered when his early comments were branded too conciliatory.

Government Insists No Policy Shift Has Occurred

After Milei’s remarks drew criticism, cabinet officials moved quickly to insist there had been no change in Argentina’s long-standing policy.

The government’s formal position remains a demand for bilateral negotiations with London, a path the United Kingdom has consistently rejected unless the roughly 3,500 islanders consent.

Downing Street responded by stating that sovereignty “rests with the UK” and that the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount.

The diplomatic friction intensified after reports emerged of a possible US review of support for Britain’s position, a development Milei seized upon to amplify his sovereignty message.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and investors in Argentina, the renewed Malvinas rhetoric is a reminder of how quickly nationalist sentiment can reshape the political climate.

While Milei’s government has prioritized economic liberalization and attracting foreign capital, the sovereignty dispute remains a non-negotiable pillar of Argentine identity that can flare up and dominate headlines overnight.

Expats should understand that the islands are a universally sensitive topic across Argentine society, and questioning the country’s claim—even in casual conversation—can provoke strong reactions.

For investors, the diplomatic tension with the UK is unlikely to derail Milei’s pro-market reforms, but it adds a layer of political risk to watch, particularly if the dispute escalates and affects bilateral trade or international perceptions of Argentina’s stability.

What Happens Next

The immediate outlook points to continued diplomatic stalemate, as the UK shows no sign of entertaining sovereignty talks without the islanders’ consent.

Milei is likely to keep using the Malvinas issue to shore up nationalist credentials at home while quietly pursuing a less confrontational relationship with London on trade and investment.

The reported US review of support for Britain’s position introduces a new variable, though any concrete shift in Washington’s stance remains uncertain and would likely face strong pushback from UK allies.

For now, the Malvinas will stay exactly where they have been for decades: at the center of Argentine national identity, and far from any diplomatic resolution.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are the Malvinas so important to Argentina?

The islands represent a deeply emotional sovereignty claim tied to nationalism, the 1982 war, and a constitutional mandate to recover the territory peacefully. For many Argentines, the Malvinas are a symbol of national unity and a reminder of the lives lost in the conflict, making the issue far more personal than a typical territorial dispute.

What is the United Kingdom’s position?

The UK maintains that sovereignty rests with Britain and that the islanders’ right to self-determination, expressed clearly in a 2013 referendum where 99.8 percent voted to remain British, must be respected. London has consistently refused to enter sovereignty negotiations unless the roughly 3,500 islanders themselves request them.

Has President Milei changed Argentina’s policy on the islands?

His government says no. Milei has reaffirmed the sovereignty claim while pursuing a more pragmatic tone, calling for dialogue rather than confrontation. Cabinet officials insist there has been no policy shift, even as the president balances his pro-Western economic agenda with the nationalist expectations of his domestic audience.

World.title: Chile Joins UNITAS 2026 Naval Exercise Hosted by Peru
World.content:
Chile · Defense

Key Facts —What is UNITAS? The longest-running annual multinational maritime exercise in the world, conceived in 1959 and sponsored by U.S. Southern Command. —Who is hosting 2026? Peru is the host nation for UNITAS 2026, with the planning conference concluding in Lima on March 5, 2026. —Which countries are participating? Eleven nations: Peru, the United States, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, and Panama. —What will the exercise cover? Maritime, amphibious, Amazon, cyber defense, and highlands training phases focused on interoperability and humanitarian assistance. —What is the state of Chile-Peru naval ties? Both nations are recurring UNITAS participants, reflecting ongoing professional cooperation rather than confrontation.

Chile will deploy naval forces to Peruvian waters later this year as part of UNITAS 2026, the world’s longest-running multinational maritime exercise, marking another chapter in the professional military relationship between the two neighboring countries.

The Chilean Navy is the maritime branch of Chile's armed forces, responsible for national defence.

What UNITAS Means for the Hemisphere

UNITAS is an annual naval exercise conceived in 1959 and first held in 1960, making it the oldest continuous multinational maritime drill on the planet. Sponsored by U.S.

Southern Command, it rotates host-nation duties each year among partner countries in the Americas.

The exercise aims to strengthen interoperability, enhance operational readiness, and build enduring partnerships among participating navies. It also demonstrates a shared commitment to maritime security, crisis response, and humanitarian assistance capabilities across the region.

Chile and Peru: Neighbors Training Together

Chile and Peru have a long history as recurring UNITAS participants, with integrated naval operations dating back to the exercise’s earliest editions. The 2026 planning conference in Lima included both nations among the eleven confirmed delegations, signaling routine professional cooperation.

The Chilean Navy’s deployment to Peruvian territory for UNITAS reflects the institutional maturity of bilateral military ties. Such exercises allow both countries to practice common operating procedures and improve technology standardization in a structured environment.

Inside UNITAS 2026: Phases and Participants

The Initial Planning Conference concluded in Lima on March 5, 2026, with the signing of a memorandum of understanding among the participating delegations. Exact dates for the at-sea exercise have not yet been published, though UNITAS typically runs for several weeks in the second half of the year.

Training will span five distinct phases: maritime operations, amphibious landings, Amazon riverine maneuvers, cyber defense drills, and highlands exercises. The diverse geography reflects Peru’s unique terrain and the exercise’s goal of preparing forces for joint response across multiple domains.

A Routine Signal of Regional Stability

For foreign investors and expatriates following Latin America, UNITAS offers a quiet but reliable indicator of how regional navies manage their relationships. The presence of Chile at a Peru-hosted exercise underscores that professional military channels remain open and functional.

The exercise also includes Bolivia, a landlocked country, and the Dominican Republic, alongside major regional navies like Brazil and Colombia. This broad participation reinforces UNITAS as a platform for hemispheric security dialogue rather than a narrow alliance.

Background: A Six-Decade Tradition of Naval Cooperation

Since its inception during the Cold War, UNITAS has evolved from a primarily U.S.-South American anti-submarine warfare drill into a comprehensive multi-domain exercise. The name “UNITAS” comes from the Latin word for “unity,” reflecting the original vision of fostering hemispheric solidarity through naval cooperation.

Over the decades, the exercise has adapted to new security challenges, incorporating humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and cyber defense into its training curriculum. For Chile, participation in UNITAS has been a near-constant feature of its naval calendar, reinforcing its reputation as one of Latin America’s most professional and capable maritime forces.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For the international community living and doing business in Latin America, multinational exercises like UNITAS serve as a barometer of regional stability. When neighboring countries with complex histories, such as Chile and Peru, routinely train together, it signals that diplomatic and military institutions prioritize cooperation over conflict.

This professional engagement helps ensure the safety of key maritime trade routes along the Pacific coast of South America, which are vital for the export of copper, lithium, agricultural products, and other commodities. Investors with exposure to Chilean or Peruvian markets can view such exercises as a stabilizing factor in the broader geopolitical landscape.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the purpose of the UNITAS naval exercise?

UNITAS strengthens interoperability and operational readiness among Western Hemisphere navies while fostering partnerships for maritime security, crisis response, and humanitarian assistance missions. It also increases warfighting proficiency and improves common operating procedures and technology standardization across participating fleets.

How often do Chile and Peru train together militarily?

Chile and Peru participate together regularly in UNITAS and other regional exercises, maintaining professional naval cooperation despite occasional diplomatic tensions over historical border issues. Their joint involvement dates back to the earliest editions of UNITAS in the 1960s.

When and where will UNITAS 2026 take place?

Peru will host UNITAS 2026, with the initial planning conference completed in Lima on March 5, 2026. The exact exercise dates are pending official announcement, though UNITAS typically occurs between September and October and runs for several weeks.

World.title: SQM and Wesfarmers Double Down on Australian Lithium
World.content:
Chile · Business

Key Facts —Total investment. Each partner is contributing up to US$500 million for the Mt Holland expansion. —Output target. Production will double to 760,000 tonnes of spodumene concentrate per year from 2030. —Joint venture. The project is owned 50/50 through Covalent Lithium, a partnership between SQM and Wesfarmers. —Technology upgrade. A new ore-sorting facility will recover 3 million tonnes of previously unusable stockpiled material. —Market context. The decision comes as spodumene prices hovered near US$2,890 per tonne in May 2026.

SQM, the world’s second-largest lithium producer, and Australian conglomerate Wesfarmers have approved a final investment decision to double output at their Mt Holland lithium project in Western Australia, committing up to US$500 million each to the expansion.

SQM is a Chilean mining company that extracts lithium for batteries and other products.

What the Mt Holland Expansion Delivers

The partners will build a second concentrator and an integrated ore-sorting facility at the remote mine site, roughly 500 kilometers east of Perth. The upgrade lifts annual spodumene concentrate production from 380,000 tonnes to 760,000 tonnes on a 100% basis, with the first new tons expected by 2030.

Wesfarmers pegged its nominal share of capital expenditure at A$645 million to A$715 million (US$450 million to US$500 million). The ore-sorting unit alone will unlock roughly 3 million tonnes of additional spodumene concentrate over the life of the mine by processing material once considered waste.

Why a Chilean Miner Is Growing in Australia

For SQM, the Covalent Lithium joint venture is a deliberate hedge. The Santiago-based company built its reputation on the Atacama salt flat in Chile, where it extracts lithium from brine.

Adding a hard-rock Australian asset diversifies its geographic footprint and shields the firm from political or operational risks in any single country.

Industry analysts describe Mt Holland as SQM’s first major step into Australian lithium. The project gives the company a long-life, low-cost source of spodumene concentrate, the raw material that feeds the battery supply chains of electric vehicle makers across Asia and North America.

Betting on a Price Rebound

Both partners frame the decision as a cost play. Doubling output lowers the unit cost of each tonne produced, which improves margins even if prices stay flat.

The move also positions Covalent to capture cash flow quickly when a sustained recovery in electric vehicle demand tightens the global lithium market.

How SQM Fits into the Global Picture

SQM’s lithium business spans Chile, Australia, and China, supplying giants like LG Energy Solution and Tesla. The company has been racing to expand capacity while rivals pull back, a contrarian bet that it can serve a market expected to triple in size by 2035.

The Mt Holland expansion reinforces that strategy. By securing more hard-rock supply, SQM complements its brine operations and builds a portfolio that can respond flexibly to shifts in battery chemistry and customer demand.

For foreign investors watching Latin America’s commodity champions, the message is clear: SQM is no longer just a Chilean story.

What This Means for Expats and Investors

For expatriates and foreign investors with ties to Latin America, SQM’s Australian expansion signals a maturation of the region’s commodity giants into truly global players. The company is using cash generated from its Chilean brine operations to fund growth in a stable, mining-friendly jurisdiction, which could reduce the risk profile of its overall business.

Investors who track SQM on the New York Stock Exchange should note that the Mt Holland project adds a hard-rock pillar to a portfolio long dominated by brine extraction. This diversification may offer a buffer against regulatory changes in Chile, where lithium nationalization debates have periodically rattled markets.

The expansion also ties SQM more closely to Asian battery supply chains that depend on Australian spodumene.

What Happens Next

Construction on the second concentrator and ore-sorting facility is expected to ramp up over the next several years, with first production targeted for 2030. In the near term, the partners will focus on detailed engineering and procurement contracts, while continuing to operate the existing concentrator at full capacity.

The global lithium market will be watching closely. If electric vehicle sales accelerate in the second half of the decade as many analysts forecast, Covalent Lithium could be bringing new supply online just as demand outstrips current production capacity.

For now, SQM and Wesfarmers are placing a long-term wager that the energy transition remains on track.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Covalent Lithium joint venture?

Covalent Lithium is a 50/50 partnership between Chilean miner SQM and Australia’s Wesfarmers, a diversified industrial conglomerate with retail, chemical, and mining interests. The venture operates the Mt Holland mine and processing assets in Western Australia, producing spodumene concentrate for the global battery supply chain.

Why are SQM and Wesfarmers expanding during low lithium prices?

The expansion is designed to lower unit operating costs by spreading fixed expenses over a larger production base. This improves profitability even if prices remain subdued, and it positions the venture to capture significant cash flow quickly when electric vehicle demand pushes lithium prices higher.

How much lithium will the expanded Mt Holland project produce?

Once the second concentrator is online around 2030, the mine will produce 760,000 tonnes of spodumene concentrate per year, double its current capacity of 380,000 tonnes. The new ore-sorting facility will also recover an additional 3 million tonnes of material over the life of the mine from stockpiles previously considered waste.

World.title: Belmopan and La Libertad Sur strengthen ties through Sister-City Partnership
World.content:
Belmopan and La Libertad Sur strengthen ties through Sister-City Partnership

By Zoila Palma: On July 17, 2026, Mayor Pablo Cawich of Belmopan, and Mayor Henry Flores of La Libertad Sur, El Salvador, officially signed a Sister-City Memorandum of Understanding, marking a new chapter of friendship and cooperation between our municipalities.

The Belmopan City Council noted that this partnership will promote collaboration in key areas including technology and smart-city initiatives, public safety, tourism, culture, sports, youth development, women’s empowerment, and the exchange of municipal knowledge and best practices.

Mayor Cawich was joined on the official visit by Deputy Mayor Christopher Enriquez, Councilor Florita Botes, and members of the Council’s management team.

“Through partnerships like these, we exchange ideas, build stronger institutions, and create new opportunities for our people,” the council said.

World.title: Why the world turned on Messi, and what his fall teaches every Belizean
World.content:
Why the world turned on Messi, and what his fall teaches every Belizean

By Horace Palacio: Three days ago in New York, Lionel Messi walked off a football pitch in tears, beaten by Spain in the World Cup final. And across the planet, something remarkable happened.

Half the world celebrated. Not Spain’s victory. His defeat.

Sit with that. The most beloved footballer of our lifetime, the little genius whose 2022 triumph made grown men cry from Rosario to Belize City, finished this tournament as its villain. In five short weeks, the darling of the sport became the man millions wanted to see lose.

Today I want to examine how that happened, honestly, in full, because the answer is only partly about Messi. Most of it is about us, the crowd. And the crowd, my friends, lives in Belize too.

First, the honest ledger, because some of this anger was earned.

The resentment started building early. Argentina’s escape against Egypt, storming back from two goals down amid officiating so contested that Egypt filed a formal complaint to FIFA, planted a suspicion that followed the champions through every round. Whether or not the favoritism was real, the perception hardened.

Then Messi himself poured fuel on it. After Argentina eliminated England in the semifinal, he was asked about the accusations. His answer, in essence, was defiance. Argentina are the best in the world, he said, whether people like it or not, and nobody handed them anything. From an underdog, that sounds like heart. From a reigning champion accused of being favored, it landed as arrogance.

And then came the final, and the moment that will follow him. Argentina down a man after Enzo Fernandez’s red card, the match hanging in the balance, and there was the greatest player of all time, not conjuring magic, but pleading with the referee to send off Spain’s Cucurella on a technicality, the tournament’s new rule about covering your mouth. The genius of a generation, begging for a red card. Fans called it desperate, and worse. And by multiple accounts, Argentina’s conduct at Spain’s medal ceremony was the final stain, champions unable to lose with grace.

So yes, criticism was earned. Write it down plainly. How you lose is remembered longer than how you win, and after twenty years of glory, Messi’s last World Cup image is a man lawyering the referee and a team sulking through another nation’s finest hour. Endings weigh more than beginnings. Guard your endings.

But now the deeper truth, because the earned criticism explains the disapproval. It does not explain the hate. For that, we must look at the crowd, and at three ancient reflexes of the human heart.

Reflex one. We love the climb, never the summit. Cast your mind back to 2022. The entire planet, Belize loudly included, prayed for Messi to win that final. The story was irresistible, the genius denied his crown, one last chance, destiny on the line. He won, we wept, the story ended. But the man kept playing, and kept winning, and the same crowd that carried him began, almost immediately, to root for whoever stood across from him. Three weeks ago it was us. When tiny Cabo Verde pushed Argentina to the edge in Miami, who was this column cheering for? Not Messi. Nothing about the man had changed. The story changed. He stopped being the struggler and became the summit, and crowds do not love summits. They love climbers. The moment you finish climbing, they go looking for the next one, and you become the mountain to be conquered.

Reflex two. The world grows tired of hearing greatness praised. I wrote recently about Aristides of Athens, banished by a citizen who admitted he had done nothing wrong, the man was simply sick of hearing him called the Just. Twenty years of Messi is the best, Messi the greatest ever, Messi, Messi, Messi. The crowd’s ear wearied. Envy needs no crime. Excellence, sustained long enough, becomes the offense itself.

Reflex three. The lens changes, not the man. Here is the uncomfortable part. Messi has argued with referees his whole career. He has always played the dark arts, the insults, the pressure on officials, the gamesmanship. When we loved him, we called it passion, fire, the will of a winner. Now the identical behavior is called disgraceful. The acts did not change. Our lens did. And age sharpened the effect cruelly, because at 39 the dribble no longer blinds us, so the tricks that were always there are suddenly all we see. When the magic fades, the machinery shows.

So the honest verdict holds two truths at once, and a mature public should be able to hold both. Messi earned real criticism this month, the appeal, the defiance, the graceless ending. And Messi is also drinking from the oldest cup humanity serves its heroes, the one we fill with worship on the way up and poison at the top. Both are true. Grown-ups keep two columns in the ledger.

Now, why does this matter to a Belizean who may never watch him play again? Because the crowd that turned on Messi is the same crowd that lives on our timelines and in our districts, and its lessons are for all of us.

If you achieve anything in this life, understand the loan you are living on. The same public that celebrates your rise is pre-writing your fall, and they will publish it the first chance you give them. So never bank your worth in the crowd’s vault. That was the emperor’s whisper I wrote about, and it was Messi’s missing counselor this month. A man anchored in his own standards survives the turning. A man anchored in applause turns with it.

Give the crowd no chapter to end you with. Twenty years of genius, and the mob’s memory will replay one appeal to one referee. Unfair? Deeply. Also reality. Your conduct in your worst hour is the photograph that outlives the highlight reel. Lose clean, always.

And when you find yourself in the crowd, as we all do, catch the reflex in your own chest. Ask yourself honestly why you wanted him to lose. If the answer is his behavior, that is judgment, and judgment is healthy. If the answer is simply that he has won too much, that is the claw, the same bad mind I wrote about weeks ago, wearing a football jersey. The crab bucket has a global edition, and this month we all held tickets.

The boy from Rosario gave this world twenty years of joy no one can confiscate, and this month he gave us one final gift he never intended, a masterclass in how crowds love, tire, and turn.

Learn it well, Belize. Then go build your life on rock.

Applause is rented. It always was.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: International News: OpenAI says AI system went rogue and launched cyberattack
World.content:
International News: OpenAI says AI system went rogue and launched cyberattack

By Zoila Palma: OpenAI has disclosed that one of its advanced artificial intelligence agents escaped the boundaries of a controlled security test and carried out an unauthorized cyberattack against Hugging Face, a major platform for sharing AI models.

The company said the AI system, designed to operate autonomously after receiving human instructions, identified weaknesses in the testing environment and exploited them to bypass restrictions before gaining access to some of Hugging Face’s internal systems, BBC reports.

OpenAI described the incident as “unprecedented” and said it is investigating the breach in cooperation with Hugging Face.

The platform’s chief executive, Clement Delangue, said it was “mind-blowing” that the events unfolded autonomously. Hugging Face said it has since closed the vulnerabilities involved and rebuilt affected systems, while continuing to assess whether customer or partner data was compromised.

Cybersecurity experts warned that the incident highlights growing concerns over the ability of increasingly powerful AI systems to operate independently and potentially exploit security weaknesses.

World.title: International News: Spain battles to contain one of its largest-ever wildfires
World.content:
International News: Spain battles to contain one of its largest-ever wildfires

By Zoila Palma: Spanish firefighters are battling one of the country’s largest wildfires in recent history, with a blaze in Guadalajara province having burned approximately 32,000 hectares of land over nearly a week.

The fire, located northeast of Madrid, has prompted a major emergency response as authorities work to contain the flames before stronger winds forecast for Thursday potentially worsen conditions.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano García-Page met with emergency commanders on Wednesday to assess the firefighting operation. García-Page later expressed “cautious optimism,” saying progress on the ground offered hope that the situation could be stabilized in the coming days.

Improving conditions have allowed residents of five previously evacuated communities to return home, while authorities said people from La Mierla, where the fire began about 70 kilometres northeast of Madrid, could also be permitted to return soon.

Since the blaze erupted last Thursday, 34 communities have been evacuated and around 1,200 people moved to safety.

World.title: International News: Spain’s World Cup champions receive Royal welcome ahead of victory parade
World.content:
International News: Spain’s World Cup champions receive Royal welcome ahead of victory parade

By Zoila Palma: Spain’s World Cup-winning football team received a royal welcome Monday after returning home from their historic triumph in the United States.

King Felipe VI hosted the squad at Madrid’s Royal Palace, praising the players for what he described as an “epic” victory and calling them a “legendary and historic team.”

The king congratulated the players and urged them to enjoy the celebrations following their demanding tournament.

King Felipe described Spain’s World Cup campaign as a true “odyssey” and thanked the team on behalf of the nation, highlighting the country’s achievement of holding both the men’s and women’s World Cup titles.

Following the palace reception, captain Rodri and his teammates were scheduled to meet Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez before taking part in an open-top bus parade through central Madrid.

World.title: Saunders Food Truck Festival takes over Cahal Pech Village Resort today
World.content:
Saunders Food Truck Festival takes over Cahal Pech Village Resort today

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Foodies in the west, today belongs to you. The Saunders Food Truck Festival 2026 is happening today at the Cahal Pech Village Resort parking lot in San Ignacio, bringing together more than a dozen vendors and food trucks for one flavorful day on the hilltop.

The vendor lineup covers just about every craving. Flora’s Kitchen brings its famous plates, little place, big taste, while Jairo’s Pizza handles the slices and delivers too. Pana Churros is frying up sweetness, Pastry Box arrives with freshly baked happiness, and Love You a Latte covers the coffee fix. For the bold palates, Spicy Blessings and Chamoyadas Tropicanas are serving heat and tang, with Sweet Heart offering jewelry and chamoyadas in one stop.

The browsing is just as good as the eating. La Ixtabi, Escobar’s, Cutie Pie Accessories, Islandgirl Vibes, Finger Bites BZ, Sweet-n-vibes and Kreativ By Kay round out a lineup that mixes local food, treats and small business shopping in one location.

The festival runs today from midday into the evening at the Cahal Pech Village Resort parking lot, an easy stop with one of the best views in San Ignacio. Come hungry, bring the family, and support local vendors doing what they do best.

World.title: International News: Death toll rises to 53 in Guyana ferry disaster
World.content:
International News: Death toll rises to 53 in Guyana ferry disaster

By Zoila Palma: The death toll from a ferry disaster off the coast of Guyana has risen to 53, with hopes fading of finding more survivors after the passenger vessel capsized Saturday night.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips said that by Tuesday night, 76 people had been rescued alive, while dozens remained missing.

Officials said 179 people were believed to have been aboard the ferry, significantly more than the 133 passengers and crew listed on its manifest.

Authorities have launched an investigation into what caused the 87-year-old vessel, the MV Barima, to overturn, BBC reports.

The ferry had departed Georgetown on Saturday afternoon for Port Kaituma in northern Guyana.

The captain and another crew member were taken into custody after testing positive for cannabis, prompting officials to warn that anyone found responsible for negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing would face the full force of the law.

World.title: 1,320 pounds of ribs a year, and the BDF chief never tasted one
World.content:
1,320 pounds of ribs a year, and the BDF chief never tasted one

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): According to purchase records for fiscal year 2023-2024, as reported by 7News, the Belize Defence Force was purchasing 1,320 pounds of baby back ribs annually. Yet the man at the top of the BDF, Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez, told the station he has never eaten BDF baby back ribs in his 32 years in the army.

Pressed by 7News on where all those ribs went, the Commander offered his explanation. “I said I’ve never eaten baby back ribs, which is true. I’ve never had, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not purchased, right?” Velasquez said. “We tell the Ministry of Defense, this is what we want. And we want baby back ribs and conchs and shrimp and lobster for special events. One special event we had was last week, Wednesday, when we had the recruit passing out and the change of responsibility.”

The general said leftovers do not go to waste. “After these events are over, we stock some of them as well, and then whatever remains in stock, we give to the soldiers, so we send it to the battalions, the units in P.G. and Belizario,” he explained, while conceding the circle of beneficiaries is limited. “Few soldiers get to enjoy these because the ones on camp get to enjoy it, not the ones being deployed. So it’s a small number of soldiers that actually get to enjoy these things.”

He added that surplus supplies feature in training for new military cooks, who prepare what he called a culinary delight that everyone at Price Barracks is invited to sample.

The most striking exchange came when 7News’ Jaleeza Roberts asked whether the Commander had personally seen anyone around him enjoying the ribs. “I have never seen. Yes, I have heard,” Velasquez replied. “I have spoken to some other commanders, and they have received, the unit commanders, the battalion commanders, they have received the baby back ribs and the conchs and everything else, and they have given it to their soldiers.”

The ribs question forms one thread of the broader examination of defence ministry procurement, matters currently the subject of a government-ordered audit, with no findings made to date. The Commander’s account stands as the BDF’s explanation of purchases he says the force itself requested for special occasions.

Whether that explanation satisfies a public now reading the ministry’s grocery lists line by line is another matter. What is certain is that in 32 years of service, through every rank to the very top, the man who commands the Belize Defence Force says the baby back ribs never once reached his plate.

What do you make of the general’s explanation, Belize? Comment below.

World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Stacious savours emotional return to Sumfest
World.content:
Stacious is all the rage on the Sumfest stage last weekend. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Stacious stepped onto the Reggae Sumfest stage on Saturday night as a surprise guest during Mavado’s set it was more than a welcome return for the dancehall artiste; it was an opportunity to be part of a moment that will be remembered as one of the festival’s most significant.

The entertainer joined Mavado during his historic showcase with fellow headliner Vybz Kartel, a performance that celebrated unity over division and marked a new chapter in one of dancehall’s most defining rivalries.

For Stacious, whose catalogue includes one of the most notable collaborations with Mavado in dancehall history, the occasion carried both personal and cultural significance.

“I can’t remember the last time I did Sumfest,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the performance. “I know I’ve done the show three times in the past, but I can’t remember when was the last time. It’s a good feeling being back.”

Her return came after years away from the festival’s stage, making the appearance all the more meaningful.

“I’m here tonight not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall because Gully/Gaza did a run road, and now both deejays will come together in unity on one stage. It’s an honour to be a part of it,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

The sentiment echoed what many fans experienced inside Plantation Cove in St Ann as thousands watched two of dancehall’s biggest icons perform together, putting years of division behind them in favour of celebration.

For Stacious, the night also marked a long-awaited reunion with the man who helped produce, Come Into My Room, one of her most memorable collaborations.

“Mavado also hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while and I’m here to witness the return of the Gully Gad, so it’s a great night,” she said. “Mavado and I haven’t performed together in maybe over 10 years, so it’s been a long time. The awesome thing is that it’s always good when we connect, and we enjoyed ourselves, which was most important.”

Stacious was among the female voices who helped shape dancehall during the late 2000s and early 2010s. Her surprise appearance on Saturday served as a reminder of that era while signalling that she still has plenty left to offer.

Away from the nostalgia, the deejay says she is focused on new music and reconnecting with supporters. She is currently promoting two singles, Tears and Velvet Sweetheart, the latter of which recently received the visual treatment and is now available for streaming across digital platforms.

Stacious is encouraging fans to subscribe to her YouTube channel and follow her social media pages to stay updated on upcoming releases, performances, and other career developments.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: US$18-m fuel shield
World.content:
STATE-OWNED refinery Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising fuel costs to shield consumers from steeper price increases, with Chairman Metry Seaga saying the Government will eventually reimburse the company.

Seaga disclosed the figure during a panel discussion following Tuesday’s release of the second-quarter JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices, while responding to questions about measures being taken to contain energy costs.

“To date, Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising the cost of fuel,” Seaga said.

While acknowledging that the refinery has not done a good job of explaining how fuel prices are determined because of the complexity of the process, Seaga explained that Petrojam has been using a long-standing fuel price “smoothing mechanism” to cushion consumers from sharp swings in global oil prices. The mechanism was introduced to reduce volatility in fuel prices and lessen the inflationary impact of sudden increases in international oil prices.

According to Seaga, since the Middle East war began, domestic fuel-price increase reached as much as $40 per litre, leaving Petrojam to absorb significant costs rather than allowing domestic fuel price increases to immediately reflect international price movements which he said would have been “extremely inflationary”.

Under Petrojam’s pricing mechanism, weekly fuel price increases were initially capped at $4.50 per litre, before Cabinet approved an increase to $12.50. Petrojam calculates its prices using a US reference price and then applies costs within its control. When the calculated increase exceeds the cap, the refinery absorbs the difference rather than passing it on to consumers.

“The increase that the consumer saw last week of $12.50 is not a real number; the real number is significantly higher than that, but Petrojam has taken up any losses that are incurred,” he said. “Petrojam is doing everything it can, and the government by extension has to give us back that money, because the money has to come from somewhere.”

The JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices found that rising energy costs continue to influence the behaviour of both businesses and households. Among businesses surveyed, 36 per cent said rising electricity costs were significantly affecting their operations, while another 29 per cent described the impact as moderate. In response, businesses said they were reducing energy consumption, investing in renewable energy solutions, increasing prices charged to customers, cutting operating expenses elsewhere, investing in energy-efficient equipment and delaying investment or expansion plans.

Seaga acknowledged not all businesses can pass higher energy costs on to customers. Pointing to Jamaica’s geography, and dependence on imported energy, he said businesses must accept that the country will remain exposed to global price shocks.

“We have to recognise from the get-go we are subject to price increases worldwide, and these are things businesses must plan for, including natural disasters,” he said. “What we have to do is know they are coming and be more efficient.”

Beyond businesses, consumers are also changing their behaviour in response to higher energy bills. The survey found that 51 per cent of respondents had reduced their electricity usage, while others said they were using fewer appliances or purchasing more energy-efficient appliances and light bulbs. Respondents also called for measures to reduce energy costs, with 56 per cent saying the government should lower electricity rates. Other recommendations included more stable fuel prices, lower taxes and duties on energy-efficient appliances, and easier financing for residential solar systems.

However, Seaga argued that households have viable alternatives to reduce their electricity bills.

“Majority of the people I know are telling me about their light bills being $12 and $15, so there’s no good reason that people should not be putting solar into their homes,” he said, noting that financing options are available.

Seaga also disclosed that Petrojam is exploring diversification into LNG, solar and potentially nuclear energy. He also hinted at the possibility of participating in oil development should commercially viable reserves be discovered in Jamaica, extending its involvement from production to the sale of fuel. However, Seaga noted that such plans would require significant investment.

World.title: Mission in Mexico
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

Jamaica’s national men’s team haven’t qualified for a FIFA Under-20 World Cup in 25 years but Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president Michael Ricketts is confident that the current squad can end the drought after significant investment in the qualification campaign.

The under-20 Reggae Boyz will leave the island on Friday for the 2026 Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, where they will look to secure one of four spots to next year’s World Cup in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Rodolph Austin, who recently led Portmore United to their first Jamaica Premier League title since 2019, will lead the team along with Molynes United head coach Jermaine Thomas.

The pair oversaw Jamaica’s sweep through the qualifying tournament in Curaçao in February, with the team winning all five matches to reach the Under-20 Championship. They now face Honduras, Panama and Canada in Group C, with the top two advancing to the quarter-finals. A quarter-final victory would seal qualification for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup.

The team has been in a training camp at the Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence at the UWI, Mona campus and have played friendlies against Jamaica Premier League clubs Cavalier, Mount Pleasant FC and Arnett Gardens in the past two weeks.

Since their historic berth in 2001 tournament in Argentina, Jamaica have missed out on the last 11 World Cups and have only advanced to the knockout stages of the Concacaf final round twice in nine attempts.

However, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the JFF has made it a priority to give the team every opportunity to qualify, investing heavily ahead of the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in a bid to end the country’s drought.

“This year has been very busy for us and very expensive as well because of course the under-17s, under-20s on either side of the gender and of course the senior men’s and senior women’s have all been vying for a place in the World Cup tournaments,” he said.

“A structure has been put in place and it’s just now for us to execute. We really want to do well. I think we have a good set of young players and we are also hoping that they will make a transition and give some strength and support to our senior men’s team, but we would have given a lot more in terms of preparation.”

Ricketts says the JFF’s greater focus on its youth programmes over the past three years, along with improvements to its coaching structure, has given the federation greater confidence in qualifying for more World Cup tournaments.

“We are just very proud of our young coaches. Coach Austin and his deputy coach [Jermaine] Thomas have done an excellent job. We have a coaching programme that is probably second to none in the Caribbean and our coaches have done very well,” he said.

“Our TDS (Talent Development Scheme) programme is a huge success and it has evolved so much that our under-14 team won the Caribbean Challenge Series convincingly. Then a year after we stepped up in class, as they would say in racing terminology, and we went to Concacaf and we won that tournament as well and then afterwards we qualified for the U-17 World Cup.”

He added, “So it’s work in progress. Hopefully, all of this will translate into some success at the Under-20 level and, like I’ve said, the coaches have done well, the management structure has been at a premium and so we are optimistic and we are really expecting to qualify for the World Cup.”

Coach Austin named his 21-man squad last week with Cavalier standout Kimarly Scott, Mount Pleasant Football Academy star Jabarie Howell and Manchester United defender Dante Plunkett among the highlights of the squad. Che Gardner, son of Reggae Boyz legend Ricardo “Bibi” Gardner, has also been called up for the first time, having impressed for Stockport United in England’s third division.

The young Reggae Boyz take on Honduras in their opening game on Sunday before battling Panama next Wednesday and Canada next Saturday. All games are set for the Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico.
