World.title: Child’s body found in Trelawny; two injured by irate residents in mob attack
World.content:
TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Police are now on a scene where the body of a child was found with her throat slashed in Tyre district near Troy in south Trelawny, residents say.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that about 6:00 pm, the child’s body was found in bushes and an alarm was raised.

Residents say the child was raped before her death.

“A farmer went to look for his cow when he stumbled on the little girl’s body,” a resident who requested anonymity said.

Another resident said following the gruesome discovery there was a mob attack on a man who citizens accused of killing the child. His father was also wounded in the attack.

The men were reportedly taken to hospital. Their condition is not known at this time.

Efforts to get a comment from the police late Tuesday were unsuccessful.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Greece derails EU’s Russia sanctions plan
World.content:
Ambassadors will hold an extra round of negotiations on Thursday morning in a bid to save the package, an EU diplomat confirmed.

Ireland, which holds the rotating Presidency of the Council of the EU, on Wednesday proposed allowing European gas tankers to export Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) to third countries until January 2029. The proposal, seen by POLITICO, capped Russian exports and also banned new contracts.

But the Greek government has so far refused the compromise and instead wants an indefinite exception, said three EU diplomats involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to talk about the sensitive negotiations. Greece’s Dynagas shipping company is one of the few that operates ice-ready ships that can reach Russia’s LNG terminal on the Arctic Ocean. If the EU would ban its companies from exporting Russian gas, the Greek government argues the ships will simply register elsewhere, reducing EU oversight.

Greece's merchant shipping fleet of more than 5,000 vessels carries around a fifth of the world's cargo by weight, more than any other country. It has the world's largest LNG fleet by capacity.

The delay also means the ceiling the EU maintains on Russian oil purchases will need to be extended again for a short period of time. Moscow’s crude is only allowed to be sold at a fraction of the market rate, but rising energy prices as a result of the war in the Middle East would see the $44.10-per-barrel limit recalculated and the Kremlin receive a windfall profit.

Because sanctions require unanimity among the EU’s 27 capitals, national governments can put a price on their consent by seeking other concessions. Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, for example, was a notorious blocker of such support for Ukraine, although EU leaders hope Budapest will prove less obstructive under his successor, Péter Magyar.

The initial proposal for the sanctions package — the 21st since Russia launched its full scale invasion of Ukraine — included restrictions on travel for former fighters of the Russian armed forces, sanctioning dozens more banks and preventing another 250 individuals from entering the bloc.

The delay pushes discussions down to the wire and past the anticipated cut-off for legislative business, with Wednesday having originally been the final ambassadors meeting until after the August summer holidays. The evening session also saw envoys attend a farewell dinner for colleagues changing posts before they reconvene in September following the break.

World.title: NATO seals €27B overhaul of Cold War-era fuel network
World.content:
The military alliance also agreed to raise its common funding budget to “up to EUR 6.5 billion” for next year, and signed off on its investment priorities for the next five years. For 2026, allies had agreed on a budget of €5.3 billion.

Countries have held negotiations for months on the revamp of the alliance’s 10,000-kilometer Cold War-era pipeline network, which is designed to connect NATO’s existing system in Western Europe to newer alliance member countries in the east and north.

The project, touted as NATO’s largest-ever and most expensive commonly funded scheme, could take up to 30 years to complete and covers dozens of projects, ranging from pipeline upgrades to energy storage sites.

“A stronger NATO is in the pipeline,” said one of the diplomats.

NATO countries had previously disagreed over the high costs of the agreement, while some fretted that it would lock in fuel projects for decades, although they later dropped their objections.

At this month’s leaders’ gathering in Ankara, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte praised the political deal reached by allies on the revamp. The “historic step” on the revamp “will modernize our existing fuel storage and distribution infrastructure,” he told reporters.

World.title: EU sieht sich von Trumps neuen Generika-Zöllen nicht betroffen
World.content:
Im Rahmen der gemeinsamen Erklärung „haben sich die Vereinigten Staaten verpflichtet, Generika von den 15-prozentigen Zöllen auszunehmen; daher gilt weiterhin die Meistbegünstigungsklausel (MFN), was einem Zollsatz von 0 Prozent entspricht“, erklärte der stellvertretende Chefsprecher der Europäischen Kommission, Olof Gill. Er fügte hinzu, dass innovative Arzneimittel aus der EU weiterhin einem Zollsatz von 15 Prozent unterliegen.

„Dies zeigt deutlich, dass die gemeinsame Erklärung der EU und der USA ihre Wirkung entfaltet, indem sie Stabilität und Vorhersehbarkeit gewährleistet und einen wichtigen strategischen Sektor vor Störungen und Zollerhöhungen schützt“, betonte Gill. Die Vereinbarung an sich ist zwar nicht rechtsverbindlich, doch jeder Verstoß gegen ihre Bestimmungen würde wahrscheinlich eine Welle gegenseitiger Zollvergeltungsmaßnahmen auslösen.

Trumps jüngste Drohung kommt zu einem Zeitpunkt, an dem seine Regierung nach einem rechtlichen Rückschlag zu Beginn dieses Jahres eilig versucht, ihre Zollmauer wieder aufzubauen, da die vorübergehenden Zölle in Höhe von 10 Prozent am Freitag auslaufen sollen. Obwohl Washington beteuerte, dass die neuen Untersuchungen die im transatlantischen Abkommen festgelegte 15-Prozent-Schwelle nicht überschreiten würden, bereitet sich die EU dennoch auf weitere Untersuchungen vor, die sich auf Zwangsarbeit, Überkapazitäten im verarbeitenden Gewerbe und möglicherweise auch die Steuer auf digitale Dienstleistungen beziehen.

Risiken durch Arzneimittelknappheit

Die EU-Generika-Lobby „Medicines for Europe“ erklärte, die Maßnahmen könnten „erhebliche Arzneimittelengpässe in den gesamten Vereinigten Staaten“ auslösen. Patentfreie Arzneimittel aus Europa „sollten gemäß dem Turnberry-Abkommen unter allen Umständen von Zöllen ausgenommen bleiben“, so der Branchenverband.

Der Schweizer Generikahersteller Sandoz erklärte am Mittwochmorgen, es sei „noch zu früh, um die möglichen Auswirkungen einzuschätzen, da noch weitere Einzelheiten zur Umsetzung und zum Umfang der Maßnahme erforderlich sind“. Ein Sprecher von Sandoz fügte hinzu, das Unternehmen werde den Dialog mit den politischen Entscheidungsträgern darüber fortsetzen, wie die Erschwinglichkeit und der Zugang zu Medikamenten in den USA verbessert werden können.

Die Bedrohung für Generika erhöht den Druck auf die Pharmabranche, nachdem die Trump-Regierung Deutschland wegen seiner Preisgestaltung bei Arzneimitteln mit neuen Abgaben gedroht hatte.

World.title: Offener Widerstand gegen Weidel
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Im größten AfD-Landesverband Nordrhein-Westfalen tobt ein offener Machtkampf, der der Bundesspitze zunehmend entgleitet. Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren im Detail, wie das radikale Helferich-Lager die Listenwahl sabotieren wollte. Sie besprechen, warum Landeschef Martin Vincentz sich juristisch gegen Alice Weidel wehren wollte und wie das Tabu des Widerstands gebrochen ist.

Zudem diskutieren die beiden die fehlenden Berührungsängste der AfD-Spitze zur rechtsextremen Szene. Schindler und von Pezold beleuchten, wie Spitzenpolitiker wie Ulrich Siegmund dem verurteilten Neonazi Sebastian Schmidtke freundschaftliche Interviews geben. Dabei gehen sie der Frage nach, warum die Unvereinbarkeitsliste der Partei in der Praxis offensichtlich ignoriert wird.

Nach dem Rücktritt von Jens Spahn geht es zudem um die gezielte Instrumentalisierung der Debatte um Leihmutterschaft. AfD-Funktionäre nutzen die ethische Diskussion als Deckmantel benutzen, um homosexuellen Paaren grundsätzlich die Eignung zur Erziehung von Kindern abzusprechen.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: EU says Trump’s new generic drug tariffs won’t hit its exports
World.content:
Under the joint statement, “the United States committed to exempting generic medicines from the 15% tariffs; therefore MFN [most-favored-nation] treatment continues to apply, corresponding to a 0% tariff rate,” said the European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill. He added that EU innovative drugs continue to be subject to a 15 percent tariff.

“This clearly shows that the EU–U.S. Joint Statement is delivering by preserving stability and predictability, and protecting a key strategic sector from disruption and tariff increases,” Gill stressed. The deal as such is not legally binding, but any breach of its terms would likely unleash tit-for-tat tariff retaliation.

Trump’s latest threat comes as his administration is scrambling to rebuild its tariff wall after a legal setback earlier this year, with its temporary 10 percent tariffs due to lapse Friday. Although Washington insisted that the new probes would not breach the 15 percent threshold enshrined by the transatlantic deal, the EU is still bracing for more investigations, targeting forced labor, excess capacity in the manufacturing sector and possibly also digital services tax.

Drug shortage risks

The EU generics lobby, Medicines for Europe, said the measures risked triggering “significant medicine shortages across the United States”. Off-patent drugs from Europe “should remain exempt from tariffs under all circumstances” under the Turnberry agreement, the trade group said.

Swiss generics manufacturer Sandoz said Wednesday morning it was “too early to assess the potential implications, as further details on the implementation and scope of the measure are still required.” A Sandoz spokesperson added the company would continue dialogue with policymakers on how to improve affordability and access to medicines in the U.S.

Threats to generic medicines increase pressure on the pharmaceutical sector, after the Trump administration threatened new levies on Germany over its drug pricing policies.

Washington alleges that Berlin’s laws result in the U.S. paying a disproportionate share of research and development costs for innovative drugs. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week that he was also in talks with France over its pricing practices.

“The pharmaceutical sector is critically important on both sides of the Atlantic, with highly integrated supply chains, strong investment and research ties, and broadly balanced trade flows. Preserving these links is essential both for patient access and for sustaining innovation,” added Gill, the Commission spokesperson.

World.title: Macron convinces environment minister to stay on
World.content:
Tensions between Monique Barbut and the government came to a head over an agriculture bill. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

Monique Barbut had resigned earlier this week claiming the “forces opposing” her green transition agenda had become “too powerful.”

PARIS — French President Emmanuel Macron asked his Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut to stay in her role after she resigned on Wednesday morning.

"The French president refused her resignation," government spokesperson Maud Bregeon announced at a press conference. "They agreed on three fundamental pillars that will guide her action: forests, water and environmental health … on which she agreed to remain fully invested."

Barbut's office told French news agency AFP that she had agreed to remain in her post "at the request" of the president, citing "the urgent need to take action against the consequences of climate change."

World.title: Britain’s new defense chief Streeting says Israel has ‘fallen short’ in Gaza
World.content:
The defense secretary has previously said — in WhatsApp messages to former U.S. ambassador Peter Mandelson before Streeting took up his current job — that “Israel is committing war crimes before our eyes,” and is committing “rogue state behaviour” in the West Bank.

Asked about these messages Wednesday, Streeting refused to repeat them. But he said: “I’m not going to pretend I didn’t make those comments.”

His remarks highlight the continued ripple effects on the left of British politics over Israel’s protracted campaign in the Gaza Strip, which followed the deadly Oct. 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas. The new defense secretary nearly lost his parliamentary seat of Ilford North at the last general election after a large turnout among pro-Palestinian constituents, and has been projected to lose it by some pollsters.

Streeting also refused to say whether he believes Britain should continue to buy Israeli weapons as those are “not my decisions alone.”

“I’ve expressed very clearly my concerns about Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank,” he said, adding that he believes “very strongly in Israel's right to defend itself, to defend its values, its freedom, and its democracy, just as we do every single day.”

Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has tried to make a break with his predecessor, Keir Starmer, who was condemned by some in his own party for his staunch support for Israel in the immediate aftermath of October 7 – including a broadcast interview in which he appeared to say that Israel had the "right" to cut off water and energy to Gaza.

World.title: Marine microplastic pollution: How scientists detect it | Euronews Tech Talks
World.content:
The sea holds many secrets that are invisible to the naked eye when viewed from the shore: rare species, complex ecosystems and, sadly, loads of litter.

 

According to the United Nations, each year 52 million tonnes of plastic waste enter the ocean, resulting in an estimated 24 trillion microplastic particles.

Microplastics, tiny fragments of plastics less than 5 millimetres in diameter, can be found both in the depths and on the surface of the water, disrupting ecosystems in ways scientists are still trying to understand.

But how do microplastics get into the sea? What technologies can be used to identify them? And what impact do they have on marine species?

To answer these and more questions, Euronews Tech Talks visited the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in Ostend, on the Belgian coast. Here, a research group led by senior researcher Ana Catarino investigates marine microplastics, collecting data directly from the North Sea.

Marine microplastics pollution, climate change and risks

Plastics can enter the ocean in multiple ways: pieces of fishing nets that accidentally detach, litter coming from malfunctioning waste management systems, and so on.

Specifically, microplastics polluting the ocean can be divided into two categories: primary microplastics and secondary microplastics.

The former category comprises elements like nurdles, tiny plastic fragments designed for industrial purposes; while the latter involves particles stemming from the degradation of macro litter due to waves, wind and exposure to sunlight.

The extent of microplastic pollution is, therefore, tied to climate change.

“So if we have more sunny days and higher UV radiation exposure and heat waves and changes of temperature that might, for example, impact the degradation of plastics that are stranded,” Catarino said.

The impact of microplastics on marine species is also closely linked to climate change. On their own, the microplastics ingested by a species may not pose a significant risk.

But if that species is already under stress due to rising sea temperatures, the consequences can be different. “These combined effects, they can be cumulative in the organism,” Catarino explained.

Methods to identify microplastics

Marine microplastics are difficult to identify and quantify due to their small dimensions, irregular shape, and, sometimes, different colours.

Despite these challenges, recognising microplastics is possible, and VLIZ’s postdoctoral researcher Nelle Meyers has worked on a semi-automated method to identify them.

This technique involves collecting a sample from the sea using a net, cleaning the sample of organic materials, and staining it with Nile Red before placing it under a microscope. A fluorescence colouration analysis is then run and its results are passed through two automated programmes that can identify whether a particle is a microplastic or not and what type of microplastic it is.

“We wanted to automate to speed up the whole process,” Meyers said. “We wrote a code so when you upload the picture, the image analysis is done automatically,” she continued.

Thanks to this semi-automated step and the use of a fluorescence microscope, which is relatively common in laboratories, Meyers claimed the technique is cost- and time-effective.

However, the method also presents some limitations, as it lacks information about the chemical composition of the particles and can determine only certain types of polymers.

Microplastics’ impact on marine species

Just as larger plastic debris is ingested by marine species, tiny plastic particles can also be consumed by smaller organisms, like plankton.

“They [microplastics] can also get their stomach, their gut clogged. And then they [small organisms] don't eat their nutrients, they don't eat their own food,” Catarino explained.

“And this is worrying because then it brings other issues because these organisms are not able to reproduce and their population will not strive, so it will be affected,” she said.

The specific effects of microplastics depend on multiple factors, including the marine species involved, the type of microplastics, and other stressors to which the species is exposed, such as changes in sea temperature, ocean acidification, and more.

“Sometimes it’s not just one issue or another, it’s the accumulation of all these effects that may be harmful to the organisms,” Catarino told Euronews Next.

World.title: Could Gianni Infantino really become UN Secretary General if Trump puts him forward?
World.content:
Gianni Infantino would not have a clear path to become the next Secretary General of the United Nations, even with Donald Trump’s backing.

 

According to a report from The New York Post, the US President sees FIFA’s boss as a "respected" potential candidate, with a "special ability to bring people together" demonstrated by the success of the 2026 World Cup.

But in any event, his endorsement alone would not be enough to push to the world's most powerful diplomatic job a person who is not even a career diplomat.

Neither Trump nor Infantino have confirmed a candidacy, which, if submitted, would put him into a challenging and politically fraught selection process.

Infantino would need the support of many countries to win the post, and he could not afford to alienate Russia, China, France and the United Kingdom, each of which could stop him thanks to their permanent positions on the Security Council.

How the UN chooses its Secretary General

The UN Secretary General is appointed by the 193-member General Assembly following a recommendation from the Security Council.

This means the candidate is actually selected by a restricted group of 15 countries, including ten rotating members and five permanent ones, in a closed-door negotiation.

All the candidates have to be nominated by one or more UN member states and present their vision in public hearings, answering questions from ambassadors and civil society.

The Council then conducts a series of confidential straw polls before agreeing on a single candidate to recommend. Any of the five permanent members – the US, China, Russia, France or the UK – can kill a candidacy with a veto, making geopolitical acceptability as important - and even more - than diplomatic credentials.

The following approval of the General Assembly is regarded as a largely procedural step. The Assembly could, in theory, vote against the recommended candidate, but this has never happened so far in the UN's history.

With António Guterres leaving office at the end of this year after two terms, the race is in full swing and Council is expected to start considering candidates at the end of July. A debate entitled “UN Town Hall: The Next Secretary-General”, will take place on Thursday afternoon in New York, with all the current candidates.

However, there is no binding deadline to present a candidate, and the US or any other country could submit Infantino’s nomination while the process is ongoing.

Six candidates for the top job so far

Seven names have been put forward so far to be the next UN Secretary General, and one has already dropped out: Virginia Gamba, former UN special representative for the protection of children in armed conflict, was initially proposed by the Maldives, but her candidacy was later withdrawn.

One of the best-known candidates is Michelle Bachelet, the left-wing former Chilean president and ex-UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. She is a distinguished politician with decades of diplomatic experience, but could nonetheless prove divisive thanks to her outspoken criticism of authoritarian governments.

Chile's conservative new government, led by José Antonio Kast, withdrew its support for her, but Bachelet remains in the race, as her candidacy is still backed by the like-minded leaders of Mexico and Brazil.

Also among the more famous candidates is the current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Mariano Grossi, nominated by his home country Argentina, mainly thanks to his diplomatic role in the talks to ensure the safety of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant amid the war in Ukraine.

Other candidates are the former Senegalese president Macky Sall, nominated by Burundi; Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis, the boss of the UN Trade and Development department, nominated by his home country Costa Rica; and former foreign ministers of Ecuador (María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés) and Guyana (Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett), both nominated by their respective governments.

A difficult race for Infantino

According to an informal tradition of geographical rotation, the position of UN secretary-general is assigned to representatives from different continents – meaning that as a European, the Swiss-Italian Infantino would have few chances to succeed Portuguese Guterres.

Many governments are also arguing that a woman should hold the post for the first time, since the ten UN Secretary Generals to date have all been men.

Despite the UN Charter not requiring the UN leader to have diplomatic experience, Infantino also could face accusations of being unfit for the role, with his history of governance controversies at FIFA and his close relationship with Trump both major strikes against him.

His critics have repeatedly accused him of centralising power at the football association and overlooking human rights concerns linked to World Cup tournaments in Russia and Qatar.

Any supporters might argue that he has expanded football's global reach and managed one of the world's largest international organisations, with even more members than the UN.

A formal nomination by the US would kick off for him a difficult, but still open, contest.

The United Nations, FIFA and the European Commission refused to comment on the issue.

World.title: Trump threatens to bomb Tehran back for every Iranian attack in Hormuz
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday pledged that the US would bomb Iranian civil infrastructure every time Tehran fires at ships in the strategic Strait of Hormuz.

 

"From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by missile, rocket, drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy one bridge or power plant," Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump said this included Iranian facilities "located next to, or in, the capital city of Tehran."

Trump's threat came shortly before he headed to an airbase for the return of the remains of three US troops killed in Iranian attacks on US military facilities in the Gulf.

The US president said he was going to "honour our heroes and they're indeed great heroes."

"All of them said, very strongly, that we can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon, so we're going to honour them... For me it's one of the hardest things to do as president but it has to be done," he added.

Trump rejected polls that show the Iran war is unpopular with US voters ahead of midterm elections in November, with rising oil prices fueling a spike in the cost of living.

The war has already cost Washington $37.5 billion (€32.8bn).

"Americans don't want high gasoline prices but they're not against the war, that just came out loud and clear," Trump said.

Attacks shake Iran and Jordan

Washington has stepped up strikes against Iran since a preliminary ceasefire deal collapsed amid fighting over the strait, carrying out 11 straight days of attacks on the Islamic republic.

Iran has retaliated by firing at US military facilities in the Gulf.

Jordan’s military said it intercepted four Iranian missiles over Aqaba on Wednesday, while two others fell in “uninhabited areas”.

Plumes of smoke could be seen overhead in videos filmed by people in the nearby Israeli city of Eilat. Jordan said it also intercepted four Iranian drones.

Iran has avoided striking Israel since hostilities resumed last month, apparently hoping to keep it from reentering the war.

But the attack on Aqaba, within sight of Israel’s Eilat, raised concerns over a further widening of the conflict after an agreement to halt hostilities collapsed.

Another missile alert sounded in Bahrain, and Saudi Arabia warned residents of the Persian Gulf city of Dammam to seek shelter. Saudi authorities later said the danger had passed, without elaborating.

Iran's state-run IRNA news agency reported explosions across several provinces. Iran's Health Ministry says US strikes over the past 11 days have killed 53 people, including six women and three children, and wounded nearly 600 people.

Iran's IRGC insisted its retaliatory attacks would continue.

The US military said Wednesday's dignified transfer service at Dover Air Base in Delaware was for two service members killed in an Iranian attack on a base in Jordan and a service member killed during a controlled detonation of a drone in Iraq.

A third service member remains missing from the Jordan attack.

Trump has vowed to avenge the deaths of all US troops "many times over" and stepped up threats to target civilian infrastructure. The total number of US deaths since the start of the war is 18.

The US president also repeated threats on Tuesday to strike what he said was a secret Iranian nuclear complex called Pickaxe Mountain. Iran denies the existence of any facility at the site, which it calls Kolang mountain.

World.title: Trial date set in US drug trafficking case against Nicolas Maduro
World.content:
A US judge on Wednesday set a 1 June 2027 trial date for Venezuela's ousted president Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on drug trafficking charges.

 

Neither Maduro nor his wife spoke during Wednesday's 15-minute hearing.

Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein set the trial date at the request of lawyers for both sides. Under the agreed timetable, defence lawyers will begin filing motions in early September challenging the indictment.

During the hearing, Maduro’s lawyer, Barry Pollack, said he would first challenge the indictment on sovereign immunity grounds. Pollack, has previously said he expects to contest the legality of Maduro’s “military abduction.”

The lawyers have said there are complex legal defences that the court must address before a trial can begin.

Meanwhile, outside the court, demonstrators held signs in support of the ousted president and his wife.

People protest in support of former Venezuela President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores outside of Manhattan federal court, Wednesday, 22 July, 2026, in New York. AP Photo

Maduro and Flores have been held in a Brooklyn jail since a US military operation in January, awaiting trial on drug trafficking, firearms and other charges.

The couple was captured by US forces in a nighttime raid in January. Both have pleaded not guilty and face possible life sentences if convicted of conspiring to traffic cocaine into the United States.

“I am not guilty. I am a decent man, the constitutional president of my country,” Maduro said at his arraignment in January.

US President Donald Trump's administration has described the raid as a “surgical law enforcement operation” in a criminal case first brought six years ago. Maduro, however, has described himself as a “prisoner of war” and his capture as a kidnapping.

Prosecutors allege that Maduro conspired to traffic thousands of tonnes of cocaine into the United States by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement officials to assist drug kingpins.

Maduro and Flores have not asked to be released on bail.

World.title: Hungary's prosecutor resigns under pressure in political win for Magyar
World.content:
Hungary's Prosecutor General has resigned, bowing to pressure from Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who is seeking to remove key officials appointed under Viktor Orbán.

 

In a statement, Gábor Bálint Nagy said he was stepping down to safeguard the integrity and independence of the prosecutor office, condemning what he described as political pressure placed upon it.

"The prosecution service must not become an instrument in the struggles of political actors, nor can it be a stage for day-to-day political interests or power games," Nagy said, adding that he no longer wished to be part of a conflict "built on false premises and serving political ends."

Magyar welcomed the resignation, saying: "With this, the country has freed itself from another Orbán puppet."

Since his landslide election victory in April, Magyar has called for the removal of senior officials appointed during Orbán's time in office. Over the weekend, President Tamás Sulyok also signed a constitutional amendment ending his own mandate.

Nagy had also come under criticism from lawyers representing a group of Ukrainian cash couriers, who accused him of acting on political orders.

In early March, two vans carrying large quantities of cash and gold bound for Oschadbank's headquarters in Kyiv left Vienna before being stopped near Budapest. The crew were detained, questioned and expelled from Hungary, while the cash and gold were confiscated.

Lóránt Horváth, the lawyer representing Oschadbank and the seven detained Ukrainians, told Euronews that those responsible for the operation should themselves have faced prosecution.

"The chief prosecutor supervising and directing this investigation was appointed by the previous government, so it is also possible that he is providing political support, or a safety net, to his former bosses in some way," Horváth said.

The Prosecutor's Office has denied any political motive behind the operation. Nagy had led the office since last year.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: Hungary: Ex-PM Orban pledges resistance to Magyar 'tyranny'
World.content:
Hungary's former prime minister alleges that his successor has "dismantled the rule of law and eliminated checks and balances." Peter Magyar has pursued Viktor Orban and his allies since winning April's elections.

Hungary's former Prime Minsiter Viktor Orban accused prosecutors and the new government of sham investigations into his Fidesz party on Wednesday, a day after investigators seized equipment from the party HQ in Budapest as part of a corruption probe.

Hungary's longstanding leader, Orban lost April's general elections in a landslide to conservative rival Peter Magyar, himself a former Fidesz member, in a result hailed by much of Europe but not by the Trump White House.

Since coming to power, Magyar has moved to dismantle what he alleges to be systemic corruption of the Orban and Fidesz era, making a host of sweeping changes. Orban, however, on Wednesday, called these measures signs of "tyranny" and said that he and his opposition party would offer "resistance" by all peaceful means.

Orban chose to appear outside Fidesz's HQ a day after the buidling featured in domestic headlines for other reasons Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

What did Orban say?

Orban's online statement late on Tuesday night, followed by his press conference outside the Fidesz HQ on Wednesday, constituted two of his strongest political statements since returning to a role as leader of the opposition in early May after 16 years in power.

On Facebook, he first issued what he called a "statement of resistance" soon after his party announced that prosecutors had searched the party's HQ and seized computer servers and other materials. This is part of a corruption probe into the country's National Culture Fund, which is alleged to have been a state-run payment center for Orban's inner circle and a shadow election campaign fund.

"The National Culture Fund issue was just a pretext for this [search of the party headquarters]," Orban alleged, denying that there had been any wrongdoing.

He said Hungary had "ceased to be a democratic state" after the new center-right government used its parliamentary supermajority to pass a constitutional amendment ending the mandates of the president and the head of the Constitutional Court — both deemed to be Orban allies. He said he and his party would "employ all peaceful means" to oppose an "illegitimate" political system.

On Wednesday, outside Fidesz's base of operations, Orban said he believed Magyar was trying to hobble his party once and for all.

"By yesterday, I had come to realize what this was all about," he told reporters. "What happened was that this served as a pretext to seize Fidesz's servers ... This is a politically motivated legal proceeding designed to render Fidesz — which has clearly survived even this heavy political defeat and is growing stronger — legally unviable."

New laws on term limits mean Orban will not be eligible to stand in Hungary's next elections, assuming they hold Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance

How and when did Magyar win power?

Peter Magyar's new party, Tisza, comfortably won general elections on April 12, claiming more than 55% of the vote against Fidesz's tally of almost 37%.

Because of Hungary's first-past-the-post electoral system, Magyar now enjoys the same supermajority that Orban often did in his pomp, holding 141 of 199 seats despite having only won 55% of the votes. Fidesz holds just 52 seats.

In Hungary, a two-thirds vote in parliament is needed to amend the constitution.

The new prime minister, who had broken away from Fidesz in 2024, lamenting double standards and institutional corruption, took office on May 9. He had pledged rapid reforms if victorious, but the speed and scope of his actions even took some of his supporters by surprise.

Can the 'dancing minister' fix Hungary's healthcare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What has Magyar done since taking office to Orban and Fidesz's detriment?

As well as taking steps in foreign policy like trying to mend ties with Brussels and free up assistance for Ukraine since taking office, Magyar has moved quickly against alleged Orban-era corruption and misdeeds. Magyar often refers to this as targeting Orban's "mafia."

Magyar opened up former government facilities to the public to showcase some of the opulence he says indicates systemic corruption.

The national public broadcaster M1, which Tisza and others in opposition said had morphed into Fidesz's mouthpiece, was briefly taken off air this month and broadcast a black full-screen apology to launch a reform process.

Several political appointees have been removed from their roles — most notably President Tamas Sulyok via a constitutional amendment and Constitutional Court president Peter Polt. Magyar this week suggested chess star Judith Polgar for the largely ceremonial role as president, only for her to indicate that she was flattered but not interested.

On Tuesday, Prosecutor General Gabor Balint Nagy, appointed only last year, agreed to step down after being called Orban's "puppet" by Magyar.

Tisza has also introduced term limits of 12 years for all lawmakers, including the prime minister and government ministers. Orban says this means most of the veterans in his party, himself included, will be excluded from the next elections.

He told reporters in Budapest on Wednesday that this harkened back to the late 1980s and the latter days of Communist dictatorship "when there was no democracy in Hungary, there was no rule of law."

Corruption investigations, including but not limited to the investigation into the National Culture Fund, have also struck Orban and his allies.

Some other senior Fidesz members have voluntarily stepped out of the political limelight. Last week, parliamentary caucus leader Gergely Gulyas stepped down, while Orban's longstanding former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto left to take up an executive position with Chinese electric carmaker BYD.

Surveys suggest that Orban's party has suffered even more in its first few months in opposition, with one poll by Median this week showing 60% support for Tisza and only 18% for Fidesz.

World.title: Louvre's Apollo Gallery reopens, 9 months after heist
World.content:
The 17th-century Apollo Gallery reopened to the public without precious jewels or other objects previously on display.

Paris' Louvre Museum reopened its Apollo Gallery to the public on Wednesday, marking the first time visitors were allowed in since Ocotber 2025, when robbers stole €88 million ($102 million) worth of crown jewels in a dramatic daytime heist.

The Louvre is world's most visited museum, with guest numbers of up to 9 million a year.

It was originally a royal palace, which was opened to the public during the French Revolution. The museum houses the Mona Lisa, one of the world's most famous pieces of art.

The October 2025 heist shocked the world as the thieves used a crane mounted on a truck to enter the museum through a window at 9:30 a.m., when the museum was still opening.

The group broke in through the window, equipped with power tools like a disc cutter, and stole French crown jewels.

Thieves intended to take a crown, but they dropped it Image: Thomas Clot/MUSEE DU LOUVRE/AFP

Precious jewels relocated

On their way out, the thieves dropped a 170-year-old crown commissioned by Napoleon III as part of a pair of crowns for him and his wife, Empress Eugenie.

The crown was left "badly deformed," the Louvre said, but it was nevertheless "nearly intact" and could be restored. The crown was among other objects that were not taken from the gallery.

Museum operators said the Apollo Gallery will return to its 17th-century original ceremonial purpose, without any of the precious jewels or other objects on display.

The public will be able to tour the majestic room and view its gilded ceilings and Greek frescoes.

The Louvre's director, Christophe Leribault, said the former exhibits have been relocated elsewhere in the museum.

"It's also an opportunity to rediscover the splendid architecture and decor of this gallery," Leribault said.

The Apollo Gallery is considered one of the most marvelous areas of the Louvre, with ceilings designed by Charles Le Brun and later added to by, among others, French painter Eugene Delacroix.

A 'trauma for the entire world'

Leribault took over from former director Laurence des Cars, who resigned in the aftermath of the heist, which highlighted a string of security failures within the museum.

French Culture Minister Catherine Pegard referred to the heist as a "sinister day," adding that it cannot be forgotten.

"It was a trauma for the entire world, which, for several days, expressed its shock and sadness in every language. It was a trauma for us, discovering the fragility of a place we thought unshakeable, and which, like so many others, proved vulnerable," Pegard said.

Authorities have boosted security at the museum, having added new surveillance cameras and anti-intrusion systems.

Security improvements are part of the museum's decade-long modernization plan, estimated to cost up to €800 million.

World.title: Who could be the next UN Secretary-General?
World.content:
For the first time in a decade, the United Nations will soon choose a new Secretary-General. DW takes a look at the six candidates, what they stand for and the challenges they and the UN will face.

After a decade in power, Antonio Guterres, will end his second term as UN Secretary-General on December 31. There are currently six candidates lining up to replace him. Whoever emerges victorious has a tough task, with the relevance, power and financial capability of the UN under an increasingly harsh spotlight.

The UN Secretary-General is "equal parts diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO," according to the organization itself. The holder of the position oversees several vital UN organs, including the Security Council, charged with maintaining peace and security.

The 80-year-old UN is struggling for relevance — here's why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The winning candidate will be selected by the UN's General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council (whose permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States), making the path to victory narrow and fraught.

Here's what you need to know about each candidate ahead of a debate between them on Thursday (July 23) at the UN's General Assembly Hall in New York.

Michelle Bachelet

Michelle Bachelet is looking to add another first to her CV Image: Valentin Flauraud/Keystone/picture alliance

The first female president of Chile (from 2006 to 2010 and then 2014 to 2018) is vying to become the first female UN Secretary-General, after several women lost out to Guterres in 2016. "If I am polite, I would say the world was not prepared for it. Is it prepared now? I hope so," Bachelet, 74, said earlier this year. "It will be a very good signal," she said, adding that it would provide hope for many people.

Bachelet also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights between 2018 and 2022, a position which saw her involved in many of the key geopolitical issues she would face if elected. While she has admitted she has no "magic formula" to resolve the issues on the Security Council, Bachelet has sought to talk up her experience as a key asset.

Rafael Mariano Grossi

Rafael Grossi is looking to his experience in the nuclear energy sector to boost his bid Image: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

The Argentine diplomat has spent most of his career in the nuclear and atomic energy sectors, culminating in his 2019 appointment as director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), an autonomous organization within the UN.

Given the geopolitical landscape, with nuclear war perceived as an increasing threat, Grossi sees his background as "clearly an advantage. You have to understand the world you live in," he told Swiss outlet Geneva Solutions.

Grossi supports the UN's current attempt at reform known as UN80 and says there is "no need to reinvent the wheel" but wants to streamline the organization with mergers of UN entities and reductions in "duplications, triplications, even quadruplications or quintuplications of structures," which add significant costs to members.

Maria Fernanda Espinosa

Maria Fernanda Espinosa has enjoyed a varied career to date Image: Cyril Zingaro/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

The Spanish-born Ecuadorian has packed plenty into her 61 years. As well as a stint as Ecuador's foreign minister, Espinosa is a poet, essayist and an expert on sustainable development and climate change, particularly in the Amazon region, where she worked with indigenous communities at the beginning of her career.

Espinosa acknowledged the UN's budget difficulties in an interview with UK newspaper The Observer. "The biggest challenge right now is the financial challenge," said Espinosa, who was also president of the UN General Assembly. As a result, she says, the UN must "reform, transform or die."

To achieve such reform, Espinosa wants to work more collaboratively with regional organizations, and lean on Europe, both in financial terms and as a "bridge-builder" between states with conflicting interests and desires.

Rebeca Grynspan

Rebeca Grynspan wants to see the UN be stronger in its approach to problems Image: Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Vice President of her native Costa Rica between 1994 and 1998, Grynspan is currently Secretary-General of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which advocates for developing countries in trade deals. Her work on negotiating a deal between the warring parties for the continued export of Ukrainian grain after the Russian invasion in 2022 has been widely praised.

Grynspan wants the UN to be bolder. "Bureaucracies are very risk-averse by nature, and you cannot have a good idea or take risk," she said at a recent event hosted by think tank Chatham House in London. She has also called for wider representation on the Security Council, particularly from Africa or Latin America.

Macky Sall

A recent return to Senegal seems to have helped Macky Sall get the government behind his candidacy Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

While other candidates have held prominent political positions, Sall's experience is the most recent. The 64-year-old was president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024, having previously served as the country's prime minister.

During his presidential tenure, Senegal saw significant infrastructure improvements. But Sall's popularity took a downward turn in 2021, during his second term, after protests against the imprisonment of opposition leader, Ousmane Sonko. Sall's unsuccessful attempt to postpone the 2024 presidential election, which triggered further deadly protests, has left him a divisive figure in his homeland.

Senegal's current government did not initially support Sarr's candidacy for the UN role but u-turned last month to back his bid.

Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett

Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett has the backing of her native Guyana Image: Bianca Otero/ZUMA/picture alliance

The final candidate to throw their hat in the ring, Rodrigues Birkett entered the race in mid-June. She is the permanent representative of Guyana to the United Nations and has previously undertaken roles in both the UN and as Guyana's foreign minister, Rodrigues Birkett is an Amerindian (the Indigenous peoples of the Americas) and has also held governmental roles related to that community.

Guyana's president Irfaan Ali recently spelt out her UN ambitions.

"Ambassador Rodrigues Burkett's vision for the United Nations centers on strengthening multilateralism, enhancing effectiveness and responsiveness of the organization, promoting inclusive global governance and ensuring the United Nations remains capable of addressing contemporary challenges," he said.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: How Russia is luring foreign nationals to fight in Ukraine
World.content:
More and more, Russia is recruiting men from the world’s poorest countries to send them to the front in the Ukraine war. Why are people joining up?

Charles Mutoka, a 72-year-old Kenyanis in mourning for his son, Oscar Khagola Mutoka, a former soldier who traveled to Russia in the summer of 2025 to look for work.

His father said that he had tried in vain to talk him out of it. Oscar did not tell him and the rest of his family exactly where he was going but a week after leaving he sent a picture of himself in uniform and never got back in touch again.

His family found out that he had died some time later but, despite appeals to the Kenyan authorities, they were not able to recover the body.

In May 2026, the family held a symbolic memorial service and set up a makeshift burial site for Oscar, in order to at least have a place where they could pray. "The worst part is that I don't know if and where he was actually buried, or if his body was simply dumped in a forest in Russia," Charles Mutoka said.

Charles Mutoka, father of Oscar Khagola Mutoka, a former Kenyan soldier who died fighting in the Ukraine war Image: DW

Oscar Mutoka is one of an estimated 27,000 or more foreign nationals recruited by Russia for its war in Ukraine,according to the Defense Intelligence ofUkraine (HUR). A joint study conducted by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), the Truth Houndshuman rights organization and the Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law (KIBHR) provides evidence that Russia has set up a global network for recruiting foreign nationals.

"This recruitment targets people in economically, socially and legally precarious life situations. The methods employed range from enticing offers to deception and even coercion," Ilya Nusov, one of the authors of the study, told DW.

'I don't want to starve to death in Cuba'

For many people living in the world's poorest regions, the wages offered by the Russian army is a huge incentive as it means a chance to escape poverty and support their families. That's exactly why Yoan Viondi Mendoza, a Cuban national, decided to work in Russia. He was promised $2,000 (€1,750) per month, an enormous sum by Cuban standards, where the average wage is $20 (€17,50).

DW found out about Yoan Mendoza's story from his brother Michael Duro, who lives in the US. Yoan had wanted to emigrate to the US and be reunited with his brother, but this turned out to be impossible, because of financial and bureaucratic hurdles.

Then he came across a job offer in Russia, his brother said. "Yoan called and said he'd found a way out. He told me about a 'project' in Russia," said Duro, who told DW that he had tried in vain to change his brother's mind.

In September 2023, the Reuters news agency filmed young Cubans who wanted to go to Russia, including Yoan Mendoza who was 23 at the time. He told journalists that he knew exactly where he was going and that he did not want to starve to death in Cuba. He also showed a document that was purportedly a contract with the Russian army, which would also give him Russian citizenship.

Yoan Viondi Mendoza, a Cuban soldier who went to fight for Russia in Ukraine Image: Privat

Duro said that his brother was sent to the front in Ukraine and then tried to escape. "He pleaded, 'I made a mistake. Forgive me. Please get me out of here quickly,'" Diro said, adding that afterwards there was no contact. Yoan's name later surfaced on the lists of foreign nationals killed in action that were published by Ukraine.

'They used us as human shields'

Though Mendoza and Oscar Mutoka probably knew that they were going to Russia to fight in the Ukraine war, many other foreign nationals are being deceived to the front after being promised jobs in construction, security, logistics or agriculture.

That's what happened to Arman Mondol from Bangladesh. He wanted to work abroad to lift his family out of poverty. His father, a farmer, sold some property and took out a loan to pay a recruiter. Mondol was told that he would be working as a packer in a warehouse. Equipped with a tourist visa, he traveled via Saudi Arabia to Russia, where he was then forced to sign a contract in Russian, which he could not read.

Mondol said that he and other foreign nationals had been treated badly in the Russian army. "When we were on a mission, they always sent us ahead while they remained behind us. They used us as human shields and pushed us into the thick of the fighting," he told DW.

Arman Mondol, a Bangladeshi national who was forced into fighting in Russia's war in Ukraine but survived and came home Image: DW

During one of those missions, his vehicle hit a landmine. He was one of only two survivors and was taken to a military hospital, from where he managed to escape. In the end , the Bangladeshi embassy in Moscow helped him to return home, but the war continues to haunt him.

"I still have these images in my mind — dying people, their eyes, their disfigured faces. How they get blown up by landmines. How there was one drone attack after the next. How people's limbs were torn off. It was horrible," Mondol, who still has shrapnel in one leg and has a heavy limp, recalled. Back in his village, he has not found work.

Mercenaries or human trafficking?

Foreign nationals fighting for Russia in Ukraine are often called mercenaries. However, Ilya Nusov explained that, strictly speaking, this isn't what they are according to international law, since often people adopt Russian citizenship before joining the army.

While others had no intention of fighting in the first place. They could be considered the victims of human trafficking, if they are recruited on false premises and coerced. This violates the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, and the Palermo Protocol, which bans human trafficking and has been ratified by most countries in the world, including Russia.

Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia has insisted that all foreign nationals partaking in the "special military operation," as it calls its war in Ukraine, are involved on a voluntary basis. In March, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov claimed during a press conference with his Kenyan counterpart that "no one is being hired, just as no one is being recruited in the case of the special military operation. Volunteers get there in full compliance with Russian legislation."

DW asked the Russian Foreign Ministry for a statement but had not received a response by the time of publication.

Increasing number of recruited foreign nationals

The involvement of foreign nationals in the war is receiving increased attention, with their families protesting from Nepal to Peru. Some politicians, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, have even brought up the subject in meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to media reports, Russia restricted the recruitment of citizens from various "friendly" countries in February 2026. A list of those countries has not been published.

"In some cases, this has contributed to reducing or even stopping the influx of fighters from certain countries at least temporarily," said Nusov. "But we believe that Russia also has ways to circumvent this by reducing recruitment in one place and focusing on a different country." According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, Russia could recruit up to 18,500 foreign nationals in 2026.

Benjamin Alvarez Gruber, Nahid Anjuman, Felix Maringa contributed to this article, which was originally published in Russian.

World.title: Zelenskyy talks with Trump envoys amid attacks on Russia
World.content:
Ukraine's president said he discussed reinvigorating diplomacy with US envoys Witkoff and Kushner. The talk followed strikes by Ukraine's military on warehouses belonging to Wildberries — known as "Russia's Amazon."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he spoke with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Wednesday in an attempt to revive the prospects of a diplomatic end to Russia's invasion.

"I just spoke with President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," Zelenskyy said on X. "It was a good, important conversation on how to reinvigorate diplomacy and bring peace closer. Peace is needed — peace with dignity, and Ukraine has long been ready for it."

The discussion came after Ukrainian attacks on Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer. The company said Wednesday that several people were injured in Ukrainian attacks on the company's warehouses.

Vladimir Kondratyev, the governor of southern Krasnodar said one person was killed in Wednesday's Ukraine strikes, but did not clarify whether that was the strikes at Wildberries or elsewhere.

What do we know about the latest Ukrainian attack on Wildberries?

Wildberries co-founder and CEO Tatyana Kim said facilities in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk were targeted in Wednesday's attacks.

Social media footage showed smoke billowing above the Krasnodar logistics site, which Kim said had been evacuated along with a facility in Nevinnomyssk.

Ukraine has targeted Wildberries facilities twice within a matter of days Image: REUTERS

Zelenskyy addressed the attacks on X, without naming Wildberries.

"Today, Ukraine's long-range sanctions successfully struck important targets in Russia's Krasnodar and Stavropol regions – logistics hubs involved in supplying the Russian army with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear – as well as another oil depot," Zelenskyy wrote.

Wednesday's attacks follow the deaths of eight employees in strikes that destroyed Wildberries facilities on Saturday.

"There are no ⁠words ​to describe all the feelings and emotions caused by ​the attacks on ordinary people, on our employees, on all of us who are simply doing our ​jobs," Kim said in a ‌post on the Telegram messaging app.

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine expands defense to target Russia's civilian economy

Wildberries, often called the Amazon of Russia, is a key component of the country's civilian economy. Kyiv also accuses it of providing military logistics and shipping for the country's military.

Online sales in Russia totaled 11.5 trillion Rubles ($147 billion, €129 billion) in 2025 according to the country's Association of Internet Trade Companies, a 28% increase over 2024.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said sales of goods and services on digital platforms equated to around 8.5% of GDP.

Wednesday's strikes represent a widening trend of Ukrainian attacks deep within Russia as Moscow continues to target civilian infrastructure in the invasion it launched against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

Beyond its expanded attacks on Russia's civilian economy, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces announced that Kyiv's military had also struck 13 Russian vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov over the past 48 hours.
