World.title: New Danube railway bridge approved in Budapest as Hungary launches EUR 85 million upgrade
World.content:
The Hungarian government has approved the construction of a new railway bridge over the Danube in Budapest, launching a HUF 31 billion (EUR 85 million) project to replace the ageing Gubacsi railway bridge.

The investment is part of the government’s recently announced Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan and is intended to remove one of the country’s most significant bottlenecks for freight transport. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy announced the decision on Facebook following Wednesday’s cabinet meeting.

Bridge has been limited to walking speed for more than a decade

According to Vitézy, trains have been restricted to just 5 km/h when crossing the Gubacsi railway bridge since 2014 because of its deteriorating condition.

The minister noted that despite the severe speed restriction, the bridge remains one of Hungary’s most important freight rail links, carrying an estimated 10–15% of the country’s total rail freight traffic.

Several months ago, fellow minister and local MP Vilmos Kátai-Németh even filmed himself outrunning a freight train crossing the bridge to highlight the scale of the problem.

“Today we can finally talk about the solution,” Vitézy wrote.

New bridge to eliminate major rail bottleneck

Construction of the new railway bridge is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026, with completion expected by the end of 2029.

Once finished, the project is expected to:

remove one of Hungary’s most important railway bottlenecks;

improve access to the Freeport of Csepel and nearby container terminals;

enable more freight to shift from road to rail; and

reduce heavy road traffic in the surrounding area.

The government also plans to begin preparing the modernisation of the road section of the Gubacsi bridge, along with improvements to the nearby Corvin junction.

Government considering future road bridge upgrade

Vitézy said the railway bridge already has completed construction plans and a valid building permit, but the project had previously been halted under the former government.

He added that the government will also examine whether the existing railway bridge structure could be converted and refurbished for heavy road traffic once rail services move onto the new bridge. If that proves technically impossible, a completely new road bridge may also be required in the future.

Part of a larger railway revival

The minister described the Gubacsi bridge project as more than simply replacing ageing infrastructure. According to Vitézy, it symbolises an entire shift in transport policy after what he described as years of neglect, marking the beginning of a new period of long-term railway investment across Hungary.

The bridge replacement is one of the first major infrastructure projects announced under the government’s 10-year, HUF 3,550 billion railway modernisation programme, which also includes new rolling stock, station renovations, suburban rail improvements and preparations for an airport rail link.

World.title: Sziget Festival 2026 wristband holders offered discounts across Budapest!
World.content:
Sziget Festival 2026 is expanding beyond Budapest’s Óbuda Island with the launch of Sziget City, a new initiative connecting festivalgoers with some of the Hungarian capital’s best-known cultural venues, clubs and community spaces. Wristband holders will also receive exclusive discounts at participating locations between 7 and 16 August.

The project is intended to build a closer, year-round relationship between the Sziget community and Budapest’s cultural scene. Rather than treating the capital merely as the backdrop to one of Europe’s largest festivals, Sziget City aims to present the city itself as an essential part of the visitor experience.

An interactive map available through the official Sziget mobile application will help users locate participating venues and browse their programmes, recommendations and special offers. The festival’s official website describes the initiative as a way for visitors to explore both popular locations and lesser-known Budapest destinations while navigating the city “like a local”.

Sziget City connects the festival with Budapest nightlife

Several dozen venues had already joined Sziget City by the time of its launch. The initial partners include Szimpla, Dugattyús, Arzenál, Turbina, Heavy, Atno, Palazzo Permanens, Pontoon, Szatyor and Trafó.

The list represents several different sides of Budapest’s cultural life. Szimpla is one of the city’s best-known ruin bars, a type of nightlife venue that emerged in previously abandoned buildings and courtyards in the historic Jewish Quarter.

Trafó is an important centre for contemporary theatre, dance and visual arts, while venues such as Turbina and Arzenál are associated with Budapest’s club and electronic music scene.

“Sziget and Budapest are inseparable,” said Ábel Zsendovits, head of Szimpla. According to Zsendovits, the festival and the capital have grown together over more than three decades, helping place Hungary on the international festival and nightlife map.

Márk Drahovszky, head of Palazzo Permanens, said the programme creates common ground for valuable cultural venues in Budapest. He described Sziget City as a community-building initiative based on the recognition that the participating organisations support and depend on one another.

During the Sziget Festival 2026 period, visitors will be able to present their festival wristbands at participating venues to access discounts created specifically for the Sziget community. The offers will be available from 7 to 16 August, covering the days immediately before, during and after the main festival.

Major international performers coming to Sziget Festival 2026

The main five-day edition of Sziget Festival 2026 will take place on Óbuda Island from 11 to 15 August. The official programme includes internationally recognised artists such as Florence + The Machine, Twenty One Pilots, Lewis Capaldi, Bring Me The Horizon and Zara Larsson.

Other announced performers include Ashnikko, Biffy Clyro, Parcels, Underworld, Wolf Alice, Richie Hawtin, Dom Dolla, Sara Landry and Hungarian rapper Beton.Hofi. Organisers say the complete festival will feature more than 600 music, theatre, circus, dance, workshop and sporting programmes.

A special Day Zero will also be held on 10 August, reviving a feature familiar from earlier editions of Sziget. Faithless, Morcheeba and Goran Bregović and his Wedding and Funeral Orchestra will return to evoke some of the festival’s most memorable previous decades.

Festival returns to Hungarian ownership

The introduction of Sziget City comes as the festival begins a new chapter under Hungarian ownership.

Sziget was first organised in 1993 as Diáksziget, or Student Island, before developing into a major international music and cultural event. In 2017, a 70% stake was acquired by the Providence-backed international festival group Superstruct Entertainment.

In November 2025, the festival left Superstruct and returned to the hands of its founder, Károly Gerendai, and the existing management team. Gerendai rejoined Sziget after an eight-year absence, while chief executive Tamás Kádár remained in his position.

The new owners have placed renewed emphasis on Sziget’s relationship with Budapest, its cultural diversity and its identity as an independent festival. Sziget City is one of the clearest signs of that strategy: an attempt to ensure that international visitors discover not only the stages of the Island of Freedom, but also the neighbourhoods, clubs and cultural communities that shape Budapest throughout the year.

World.title: Mayor: Budapest’s busiest M3 metro to be extended after EU funding secured!
World.content:
Budapest’s busiest metro line is set to be extended after the Hungarian government confirmed funding for the long-awaited northern expansion of the M3 metro.

The announcement was made on Wednesday by Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy during the presentation of the government’s new Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan. The project will be financed through European Union funds.

The extension will take the M3 metro line beyond its current northern terminus at Újpest-központ to Rákospalota-Újpest railway station, creating a new interchange with suburban rail services.

Mayor welcomes ‘historic day’

Reacting to the announcement on Facebook, Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony described the decision as a “historic day” for public transport in Hungary. He said the capital had long argued that no seven-year EU budget cycle should pass without a major metro investment in Budapest.

Karácsony also criticised the previous Orbán government, saying its policies had cost the country valuable time and funding, but added that the new government had managed to “save what can still be saved” by securing EU financing for transport projects.

Plans already prepared for further extension

According to the mayor, detailed plans have already been completed for extending the M3 metro line all the way to Káposztásmegyer, one of Budapest’s largest residential districts. However, he said that, given current financial and time constraints, only the first phase as far as Rákospalota-Újpest can be delivered for now.

Karácsony nevertheless described the project as a major step forward because it can be coordinated with planned suburban railway developments, improving connections for both Budapest residents and commuters travelling into the capital from surrounding towns.

Part of wider rail modernisation programme

The metro extension forms part of the government’s newly announced 10-year railway investment programme, worth approximately HUF 3,550 billion (EUR 9.7 billion). Read more about it here!

Alongside the M3 metro line extension, the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan includes new InterCity trains, a replacement fleet for Budapest’s HÉV suburban railway, station modernisation projects, preparations for an airport rail link and upgrades to major railway corridors across Hungary.

The government says the programme is intended to modernise Hungary’s rail network and strengthen cooperation between national and Budapest transport developments.

World.title: Orbán declares “We’re fine” as Fidesz launches ‘resistance’ campaign against Hungary’s new government
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán insisted that “we’re fine” as Fidesz sought to regroup after its heavy election defeat, unveiling a new strategy that frames the party as the leader of a nationwide “resistance” against what it calls Hungary’s new “authoritarian” political system.

Speaking outside Fidesz headquarters alongside the party’s newly elected parliamentary group leader János Bóka, Orbán accused the new government of dismantling the rule of law through constitutional amendments and pledged that Fidesz would fight back using “every peaceful means” available.

Fidesz forced outside after server seizure

The press conference was held outside the party’s headquarters after prosecutors reportedly seized Fidesz’s servers as part of the ongoing investigation into the National Cultural Fund (NKA) case. Orbán claimed the seizure left the party without internet access and unable to operate its internal systems.

“We did not expect to be holding this press conference under these circumstances,” he said.

He described the investigation as politically motivated, arguing that authorities had effectively paralysed the party by confiscating its communications infrastructure and membership database.

Orbán: Hungary is no longer a democracy

The former prime minister said Hungary had entered a fundamentally new political era following the latest constitutional amendment, comparing the situation to the final years of Hungary’s communist Kádár era. According to Orbán, the amendment unlawfully restricted who can stand in parliamentary elections, depriving voters of their democratic choice.

He also argued that the removal of former President Tamás Sulyok marked the collapse of constitutional checks and balances. Orbán claimed the current political system is “illegitimate” and declared that Sulyok was “the last legitimate President of the Republic”, quotes 24.hu. He added that Fidesz would not recognise public office holders appointed under the new constitutional framework.

Fidesz launches “resistance” campaign

Orbán said the party’s newly adopted “Declaration of Resistance” commits Fidesz to restoring Hungary’s democratic rule of law. While he declined to explain exactly how the party intends to organise its campaign, saying he would reveal more details during his upcoming speech at Tusványos, he stressed that all action would remain peaceful.

According to Orbán, Fidesz will continue participating in parliamentary work rather than boycotting the legislature. He also said the party does not intend to dictate the pace of opposition activity, describing Fidesz instead as a “service centre” supporting all Hungarians who oppose what he called political authoritarianism.

“We’re fine”

One of the most striking moments came when Orbán was asked whether Fidesz had been weakened following last week’s political setbacks and poor polling. His response quickly became the headline of the press conference.

“We did not support the creation of this system. We’re fine.”

Orbán argued that the real question is how long former Tisza Party voters will tolerate what he described as an increasingly authoritarian government. He predicted that resistance would gradually become a broad national movement rather than one based on party politics or ideology.

Stay up-to-date: Fidesz’s parliamentary group elected new leader after previous one stepping down

Szijjártó’s new job praised

Orbán also defended former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó, who recently left Parliament to take up a senior position at Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD. He said he had fully supported Szijjártó’s decision.

“A very important role still awaits him in Hungarian public life. That won’t be tomorrow, but the day after tomorrow. It is also important that he is working in a place that holds enormous value and opportunities for Hungary.”

Bóka added that outstanding personnel issues within the parliamentary group would be settled before Parliament’s autumn session begins.

More on Orbán and Fidesz: Former prime minister says from now on, their mission is “to restore the democratic rule of law”

Private US trip

Responding to questions about his recent visit to the United States during the FIFA World Cup, Orbán insisted he had travelled privately and paid for the trip himself. He confirmed that he had held unofficial, non-public meetings while in the US but declined to reveal any details.

Joking about the cost of attending the tournament, Orbán remarked that he was glad the World Cup only takes place every four years because he could not afford it annually.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary’s Public Prosecutor resigns
World.content:
Hungary’s Public Prosecutor, Gábor Bálint Nagy, submitted his resignation on Wednesday, according to a statement published on the Prosecutor General’s Office website.

‘The prosecution service must not become a political tool’

In a statement also sent to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI), Nagy said safeguarding the independence and authority of the justice system, including the prosecution service, is one of the cornerstones of a democratic institutional framework.

He stressed that the prosecution service “must not become an instrument in the struggles of political actors” and should not serve as an arena for day-to-day political interests or power battles.

“To make this unequivocally clear, today I submitted my resignation through the acting President of the Republic in a declaration addressed to the Deputy Speaker exercising the powers of the Speaker of the National Assembly, initiating the termination of my mandate with effect from 25 August 2026,” Nagy said.

His resignation is set to take effect on 25 August 2026, subject to the relevant constitutional procedures.

PM Magyar reacts

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar reacted on Facebook:

“The Public Prosecutor has just resigned. With this, the country has rid itself of another Orbán puppet who was obstructing the democratic transition. Gentlemen, who will be next?”

World.title: Four Hungarian paramedics beat intoxicated patient unconscious three times
World.content:
Four paramedics in southern Hungary have been charged with repeatedly assaulting an intoxicated patient inside a hospital detoxification unit, allegedly beating him until he lost consciousness three times.

According to the Baranya County Prosecutor’s Office, the incident took place in November 2025 at the Emergency Clinic of the University of Pécs Clinical Centre. Prosecutors have requested suspended prison sentences and a ban preventing all four defendants from working in healthcare, the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) reported.

Patient allegedly assaulted after trying to leave detox unit

According to the indictment, the man had been taken to the emergency department after suffering a head injury in the street. Because he was intoxicated, he was placed in a detoxification room.

Prosecutors say the patient did not want to remain there. He reportedly shouted and repeatedly punched the door while attempting to leave.

The indictment alleges that the four healthcare workers, who were employed as paramedics and registered nurses, entered the room on several occasions and assaulted the man, sometimes together and sometimes individually.

Allegations include punches, kicks and spitting

According to prosecutors, the patient was punched and slapped in the head and face, kicked in the head and legs, had his coat pulled over his head, and was spat on by one of the defendants.

The prosecution alleges that the assaults caused the man to lose consciousness on three separate occasions.

The charges relate to repeated assault committed in a group by persons performing a public duty, along with other offences.

Trial to determine criminal responsibility

The case will now be heard by the Pécs District Court, where the defendants will have the opportunity to respond to the allegations.

The prosecutor’s office is seeking suspended custodial sentences rather than immediate imprisonment, while also requesting that the four defendants be prohibited from practising healthcare professions if convicted.

The charges have been filed, but no verdict has yet been reached.

World.title: Hungary unveils EUR 10 billion railway modernisation: New trains, airport rail link and faster journeys promised!
World.content:
The Hungarian government has unveiled what it describes as one of the largest railway development programmes in the country’s history, committing around HUF 3,550 billion (EUR 9.8 billion) to modernising the national rail network by 2035.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy presented the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station in Budapest on Wednesday.

According to the government, the programme is intended to reverse decades of underinvestment, improve reliability, modernise rolling stock and make rail a more competitive alternative to driving.

Dávid Vitézy and Péter Magyar at the press briefing. Photo: MTI

Railway seen as a national strategic priority

Speaking at the launch, Magyar said railway development was not simply a transport policy but a matter of national strategy, affecting economic competitiveness, regional development, labour mobility and Hungary’s international connections.

He argued that rail investment should become a long-term national project extending beyond individual government terms, noting that many European countries are increasingly prioritising rail transport because of its environmental and economic benefits.

The prime minister also criticised the previous government’s approach, saying Hungary must catch up after years of neglect.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy and Prime Minister Péter Magyar. Photo: Facebook/Vitézy Dávid

Six priorities for Hungary’s rail network

The Baross Gábor plan is built around six main objectives:

faster, more reliable rail links to every county seat;

preserving and modernising regional railway lines;

expanding suburban rail services around Budapest and major provincial cities;

strengthening cooperation with Budapest on transport projects;

increasing rail freight capacity to reduce road traffic; and

improving international rail connections.

Among the longer-term ambitions are preparations for a rail link to Budapest Airport, further studies into high-speed rail, and closer cooperation with neighbouring countries, including the proposed Visegrád high-speed railway network.

New InterCity trains, HÉV fleet and station upgrades

One of the centrepieces of the programme is the renewal of Hungary’s ageing rolling stock.

The government plans to purchase at least 35 new InterCity trainsets and 42 new HÉV suburban railway trains, while preparations will begin immediately for the comprehensive renovation of Hungary’s ten busiest railway stations.

The programme also aims to eliminate many permanent speed restrictions, expand rail capacity, improve digital passenger services and better integrate train and bus timetables.

According to official figures presented at the event:

the average age of Hungary’s railway vehicles is 43 years;

almost half of all railway seats lack air conditioning;

around 40% of the rail network is subject to speed restrictions; and

approximately one-quarter of the Hungarian State Railway’s (MÁV) rolling stock is currently out of service.

The government’s target is to significantly reduce the average age of trains, improve reliability and eventually achieve an average station-to-station speed of at least 100 km/h on main railway lines.

Projects already taking shape

While the government presented the plan as a new long-term strategy, many of the proposed projects have previously been discussed by Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy.

Expected developments include:

new tram-train routes around Miskolc and Debrecen;

modernisation of the Budapest–Szeged, Budapest–Miskolc and Budapest–Lajosmizse railway lines;

upgrading the Szabadbattyán–Lepsény section towards Lake Balaton;

improvements to the Budapest–Vienna corridor;

further planning for the proposed Warsaw–Prague–Bratislava–Budapest high-speed railway; and

replacement of ageing HÉV trains serving Szentendre, Ráckeve and Csepel.

Several previously suspended railway projects around Budapest are also expected to resume under the programme.

Funding from EU sources and international financing

According to Vitézy, the programme’s HUF 3,550 billion budget would come from several sources. The current funding plan includes:

HUF 1,100 billion from EU Cohesion Funds;

from EU Cohesion Funds; HUF 700 billion from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF);

from the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF); HUF 400 billion in loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB);

in loans from the European Investment Bank (EIB); HUF 400 billion through concession-based investments; and

through concession-based investments; and HUF 950 billion earmarked for projects in the EU’s 2028–2034 funding cycle.

The government says the programme aims not simply to deliver individual infrastructure projects, but to create a faster, more reliable and passenger-focused railway system capable of competing with road transport by 2035.

World.title: Survey: Doctors enjoy highest degree of trust in Romania, but half of respondents question vaccines
World.content:
Around 54% of Romanians have a lot or very much trust in doctors. At the same time, half of Romanians disagree or are hesitant when it comes to the safety of vaccines, according to a new Poll/Int Romania Barometer conducted by the Political Rating Agency (ARP)

According to the survey, 72.1% of Romanians believe that Romania is heading in the wrong direction, while only 16.9% believe that the country is moving in a good direction. Another 11% did not express an opinion.

Compared with April, the public perception has changed very little, indicating that dissatisfaction with the country's direction remains at a high level. The authors of the report emphasized that the lack of trust is not limited to the political class, but affects several areas of society, as cited by Digi24.

Asked who they trust the most, Romanians first indicated doctors. More than half of respondents (54.1%) say they have a lot or very much trust in this professional category.

Teachers rank second, with 48.9%. Far behind are private companies (27.5%), banks (27.4%), town halls (27.3%) and foreign investors (24.9%). The press is trusted by only 16.2% of respondents, while influencers and social media content creators rank last, with only 7.7%.

The report also showed important differences between population groups. For example, young people have less trust in the press and more trust in influencers, while people over the age of 60 show the opposite tendency. In addition, people aged between 40 and 60 have a lower level of trust in doctors and teachers compared with other age groups.

The barometer showed that only 56.7% of respondents believed that vaccines are generally safe. The rest either disagreed or hesitated to provide a clear answer, which, according to the authors, indicates a significant erosion of trust in vaccination.

Regarding children's immunization, the level of support is higher. Almost two-thirds of respondents (64.9%) believe that it is important for children to receive vaccines recommended by doctors. Even so, more than one-third of survey participants do not express firm agreement with this statement. Trust in vaccines was lower in rural areas, among people with lower levels of education, and among AUR voters or undecided voters.

The survey also revealed a high level of distrust regarding the quality of products sold in Romania. Around 52.8% of respondents said that international products sold in Romanian stores are of lower quality than those sold in Western countries.

Only 20.3% believed they are at the same level, and 6.5% said that products in Romania are actually of better quality than those in Western countries.

According to the report's conclusions, the population's level of trust is closely linked to electoral preferences.

The survey was conducted between June 30 and July 3, 2026, on a representative sample of 1,774 adults, through telephone and online interviews. The maximum margin of error is ±2.8%.

(Photo source: Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Nearly half of Romanians would accept authoritarian regime that ensured order, stability
World.content:
Around 46.3% of Romanians would accept an authoritarian regime if it provided more order and stability, according to the latest INSCOP survey.

On the other hand, 47.2% of survey participants believe that democracy is preferable, even if it sometimes involves more conflicts and political debates. The rest chose not to answer.

Those who declared that they prefered democracy in a significantly higher proportion than the average were Liberal (PNL) and USR voters, men, young people under 30, people with higher education, and residents of large urban areas.

AUR voters, people aged between 45 and 59, those with primary education, and rural residents prefered a less democratic regime because it provides more order and stability, in a higher proportion than the rest of the population.

Split down party lines, 59% of AUR voters said they would prefer a less democratic regime. Around 45% of Social Democrat (PSD) voters said the same, and so did 27% of PNL voters and 14% of USR voters.

There is, however, a pro-democracy majority. Roughly 60.6% of respondents said that it is more important for power to be democratically controlled, even if decisions are made more slowly. At the opposite end, 29.5% believe that it is more important for decisions to be made quickly, even if power is controlled democratically to a lesser extent. The share of non-responses is 9.8%.

Those who stated that it is more important for power to be democratically controlled, in a higher proportion than the average, were PNL and USR voters, people aged between 45 and 59, those with higher education, residents of Bucharest and large urban areas.

Those who believe that it is more important for decisions to be made quickly, in a significantly higher proportion than the rest of the population, were AUR voters, people aged between 30 and 44, those with primary education, and rural residents.

“The majority continues to support democratic control of power even at the cost of a slower decision-making process, which shows that democratic principles still maintain an important basis of legitimacy. The tension between these two attitudes reflects the existence of a vulnerable democratic culture, in which a significant part of society is willing to relativize democratic norms when it perceives that they no longer provide order, efficiency and stability,” said Remus Ștefureac, director of INSCOP Research.

The Informat.ro – INSCOP Research BAROMETER is a monthly opinion poll conducted by INSCOP Research at the request of the Informat.ro news platform, in partnership with the Strategic Thinking Group think tank. Data were collected using the CATI method (telephone interviews), with a simple random sample size of 1,100 people, representative of significant socio-demographic categories (gender, age, occupation) for Romania's non-institutionalized population, aged 18 and over. The maximum accepted margin of error of the data is ±2.95%.

(Photo source: C Studio|Dreamstime.com)

World.title: Romanian prime minister Ilie Bolojan congratulates new Moldovan PM Vasile Tofan
World.content:
Romania’s acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan sent congratulations to Vasile Tofan, who was confirmed as the Republic of Moldova’s new prime minister on Tuesday, July 21.

"I assure him of the full support and cooperation of the government of Romania. It is important that we continue to move forward with the projects on our bilateral agenda, from transportation and energy interconnection projects to those in the fields of culture and education," acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan wrote on X.

He also praised "Chișinău's progress in the EU accession process: As I have said on other occasions, Romania remains its most active and dedicated supporter."

Vasile Tofan’s cabinet was approved by the Moldovan Parliament on July 21, receiving the votes of the 53 deputies of the governing PAS party out of 101.

Asked where he would like to make his first foreign trip during an interview, Vasile Tofan indicated Romania, mentioning the strategic partnership linking the two countries. "We have not yet agreed on the first visit. I believe we have a strategic partnership with Romania. I would like it to be Romania," replied the new prime minister.

"Now I understand that the political situation in Romania is a little more complicated than ours, but if you ask me where I would like to go on my first visit, I would like to go to Romania," Vasile Tofan added during the program "În PROfunzime" on ProTV Chișinău, in reference to Romania’s ongoing political crisis.

He also said that a second important destination would be Brussels. As PM-designate, Tofan said he would accelerate Moldova’s accession to the EU.

In the same interview, Tofan said he has two citizenships, "like all well-intentioned Moldovans" (with dual citizenship), those of the Republic of Moldova and Romania. He added that around a third of all Moldovans are in the same situation.

Tofan, 44, studied at Erasmus University Rotterdam and Harvard Business School, and speaks fluent English, French, Dutch, Ukrainian, and Russian.

He worked as an investor through Horizon Capital, a fund with approximately USD 1.6 billion in assets under management, focused on Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova. He led investments in the companies Purcari, Glass Container Company, and Maib. He was a member of the boards of directors of AmCham Moldova, Startup Moldova, and Media Alternativa (TV8/1TV).

Earlier this month, the previous Moldovan PM, Alexandru Munteanu, announced his resignation amid an investigation by Ziarul de Gardă into the state-owned enterprise MoldATSA, the body charged with air traffic safety in the Republic of Moldova.

(Photo source: Vasile Tofan on Facebook and Gov.ro)

World.title: Romania’s weather agency issues red alert for Tulcea county amid widespread storm warnings
World.content:
The National Meteorological Administration (ANM) issued a red weather warning for Tulcea county as heavy rain, strong winds, and severe thunderstorms are expected to affect parts of Romania through Thursday morning, July 23. Yellow and orange alerts have also been issued for several other regions, with forecasters warning of torrential rain, hail, and damaging wind gusts.

The red alert for Tulcea is in effect from 6:00 p.m. on Wednesday until 6:00 a.m. on Thursday. Forecasters expect exceptionally severe weather, including torrential rainfall, frequent lightning, wind gusts exceeding 80-90 km/h, and storms. Rainfall totals are forecast to reach 90-110 liters per square meter, with isolated areas receiving more than 120 l/sqm.

An orange warning covering the same period has been issued for Galați, Brăila, and Constanța counties, as well as the eastern parts of Ialomița and Călărași counties. These areas are expected to experience heavy downpours, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h, with rainfall amounts of 30-50 l/sqm and isolated totals of up to 90 l/sqm.

A yellow alert is in place overnight for eastern Muntenia, southwestern Moldova, and parts of the Eastern Carpathians, where thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, and wind gusts of 50-70 km/h are forecast.

Earlier on Wednesday, ANM issued yellow and orange warnings for large parts of the country, including Oltenia, Muntenia, Dobrogea, southern Moldova, southern Transylvania, and mountain areas, as storms moved eastward during the day.

After the red warning expires, Tulcea county will remain under an orange alert from 6:00 a.m. until noon on Thursday, with additional heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and wind gusts of 70-90 km/h expected.

ANM said it will update its forecasts depending on the evolution and intensity of the weather system.

World.title: Four Romanian female tennis players included in 2026 US Open main draw
World.content:
Four Romanian players have been accepted directly into the women's singles main draw of the 2026 US Open, according to the entry lists published on Wednesday, July 22, by the United States Tennis Association (USTA).

Sorana Cîrstea, ranked 17th in the WTA rankings, is the highest-ranked Romanian representative on the US Open entry list. She is followed by Jaqueline Cristian (WTA No. 41), Elena-Gabriela Ruse (WTA No. 73), and Irina-Camelia Begu, who will compete using a protected ranking, reserved for players who have been absent from the tour for an extended period due to injuries, according to Mediafax.

The 2026 US Open will take place from August 23 to September 13, with the main draw singles matches beginning on August 30.

The entry lists were compiled based on the ATP and WTA rankings of July 20. The last woman accepted directly into the main draw is Anastasia Zakharova, ranked world No. 102, while in the men's draw the last direct entrant is Filip Misolic, who entered using a protected ranking.

In the women's competition, world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka will attempt to win her third consecutive US Open title. Other leading favorites include Elena Rybakina, this year's Australian Open champion, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff, Mirra Andreeva, and Iga Swiatek.

In the men's competition, world No. 1 Jannik Sinner will attempt to reclaim the trophy he lost last year to Carlos Alcaraz. The former recently defeated Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final to win his fifth Grand Slam title. Alcaraz, who missed the last two major tournaments due to a wrist injury, is on the entry list and hopes to return to the tour during the North American hard-court season.

The US Open initial field includes 17 former Grand Slam singles champions (11 women, six men), including 10 former US Open champions.

Among the countries represented at the US Grand Slam, the United States has the largest delegation, with 28 players accepted directly into the main draws, 14 women and 14 men.

The 128 places in each main draw will be completed by players receiving wild cards from the organizers and by athletes who qualify through the preliminary tournaments scheduled during the week preceding the start of the main draws.

(Photo source: Sorana Cirstea on Facebook)

World.title: Air traffic at Bucharest airports reaches record 8.45 mln in first half of 2026
World.content:
Bucharest’s two airports, the Henri Coandă International Airport and the Băneasa "Aurel Vlaicu" International Airport, welcomed 8.45 million passengers in the first half of 2026, according to the National Company Bucharest Airports.

Traffic data for the first six months of this year indicate a significant 5.08% growth from the same period in 2025.

Air traffic growth was also reflected in the number of aircraft movements. During the first half of the year, 68,367 landings and take-offs were recorded, 3.37% more than in the January–June 2025 period.

"The results we have achieved are the effects of the new management strategy, focused on attracting new airlines, expanding the number of routes operated from Bucharest, increasing operating frequencies on existing routes, and, last but not least, optimizing the quality and safety of airport infrastructure," said Bogdan Mîndrescu, General Director of the National Company Bucharest Airports, cited by Economedia.

Henri Coandă Airport exceeded the threshold of 7.7 million passengers, but the absolute record belongs to Băneasa Airport, which reached 745,674 passengers in the first half of the year, 50,956 more than the total number of passengers recorded at this airport throughout the entire year of 2025.

"The National Company Bucharest Airports recorded solid and sustainable growth, with the priority of CNAB's management being to ensure optimal conditions for this development, with major concern for maintaining the strictest standards of safety and security for passengers and air operations at the Capital's airports," Bogdan Mîndrescu said.

Last year, the Social Democratic-led Ministry of Transport blocked a key procedural step required for the listing of Bucharest Airports Company on the Stock Exchange (BVB), then valued at around EUR 1 billion. The ministry owns roughly 80% of the company’s stocks.

World.title: CoE Commissioner for Human Rights expresses concern over illegal care homes case in Romania
World.content:
The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, addressed an open letter to Romanian acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan on Tuesday, July 21, expressing concern over the issue of the unauthorized care homes operating in Bihor County, western Romania.

The letter follows a visit to Romania that O’Flaherty conducted in May of this year, during which he gained “deep insights into the human rights situation of older persons in residential care.” The CoE official noted that Romania achieved progress in reforming social services in recent years.

“I was encouraged by the commitment demonstrated by many of those working in care homes,” he said.

The visit also revealed problems. “Older people and others in care institutions continue to be regarded as beneficiaries of services rather than fully-fledged rights holders, a perspective that warrants reconsideration across the social care system. The ongoing shortage of care services makes access difficult, particularly as Romania’s population ages and care needs are growing,” the official noted in the letter.

Similarly, some of the most vulnerable, including those living in poverty or with disabilities or mental health issues, struggle to obtain proper care.

Bihor illegal care homes

The letter, however, centered on the issue of unlicensed care homes operating illegally in various forms in Romania, particularly the ones in Bihor County, where Ilie Bolojan served as mayor of Oradea and then County Council president.

“For many years, this institution operated unlawfully, reportedly hosting thousands of vulnerable people under abusive conditions, with over a thousand deaths recorded. I welcome the recent intervention of the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism and the transfer of residents to hospitals and licensed care facilities. However, I am concerned by how long this situation persisted, despite repeated alerts from civil society and journalists,” the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights said.

The CoE official argued it would be useful to review and adopt legal provisions to combat the operation of illegal care homes and to strengthen independent monitoring mechanisms. He said Romania should establish clear procedures for reporting and investigating deaths occurring in homes for elderly people.

Michael O'Flaherty also said that care home residents should have access to mechanisms through which they can report problems and request their resolution. At the same time, the role of non-governmental organizations in promoting respect for human rights and the dignity of residents should be recognized and supported.

Care homes owner’s response

The owner of the illegal care homes in Bihor, Viorel Paşca, responded to O’Flaherty’s letter, rejecting his criticism. Paşca disputed the CoE official’s information and said that his establishment, Dumbrava, never operated as a center or a care home.

“All the locations were actually residential homes where Romanian citizens lived and had their official residence. None of them lived there illegally, were held against their will, abused, or tortured, as was claimed in the media,” he said in a post on Facebook.

Finally, Viorel Paşca criticized O’Flaherty’s appreciation for DIICOT prosecutors and the way they acted in the Dumbrava case.

The Bihor illegal care homes case broke at the end of last month, uncovering similarities with another, more serious case from 2023. Prosecutors claim that hundreds of elderly individuals, people with severe mental disabilities, and homeless people were turned into simple “sources of income” under the guise of charitable activity. According to DIICOT, over 2,200 vulnerable persons passed through centers controlled by the group in the last 6 years.

Unlike the 2023 case, however, the situation of the care homes in Bihor is not as clear, leading many to argue that Viorel Pașca and his association were doing their best with the available resources, taking care of patients who had been abandoned by state institutions.

(Photo source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights on Facebook)

World.title: German company DEHN starts production at first Romanian factory in Pitești
World.content:
German electrical technology company DEHN has started production at its first manufacturing facility in Romania, located in Pitești. The new plant will supply surge protection devices for European markets and is expected to employ up to 150 people.

The facility, which began operations in July, is part of DEHN's global manufacturing network and complements the company's existing production sites in Neumarkt and Mühlhausen, Germany. While the German factories focus on high-volume, highly automated production, the Romanian site specializes in smaller production runs that require a higher degree of manual assembly, the company said.

The 9,500 sqm built-to-suit factory was developed by industrial real estate company CTP at CTPark Pitești and marks DEHN's first manufacturing investment in Romania.

“We are proud to have partnered with DEHN on its first manufacturing investment in Romania and to contribute to strengthening the country’s position as a destination for high-value industrial production. This project also reflects the growing demand we see from international manufacturers looking for flexible, future-ready facilities in strategically located industrial parks,” said Tatiana Axinte, CTP Romania Business Developer.

According to the company, Romania was selected after evaluating several locations across Europe, with factors including transport infrastructure, access to skilled workers, and proximity to technical universities contributing to the decision.

In addition to manufacturing and logistics, the Pitești site will also host support functions such as human resources, IT, marketing, and other shared services.

The factory is part of DEHN's broader strategy to expand production capacity closer to key markets. The German family-owned company, which specializes in lightning protection, surge protection, and electrical safety equipment, also opened a manufacturing facility in Mooresville, North Carolina, last year to serve customers in the United States.

Located near the A1 motorway, CTPark Pitești now comprises around 80,000 sqm of industrial space and provides direct road connections to Bucharest, Western Europe, and the Port of Constanța.

(Photo source: the company)

World.title: Romanian City Holds Out Against Authorising LGBTQ+ Pride March
World.content:
Oradea’s unauthorised Pride March in 2025. Photo: Photo: Ovi D. Pop/Oradea Pride.

Just over 250 kilometres separate Romania’s western city of Oradea from Budapest in Hungary, but until recently the two cities shared another distinction: both had refused to allow Pride marches.

Hungary’s capital hosted a Pride event this year despite government opposition. Oradea is now the only major city in the European Union where local authorities continue to deny permission for a Pride march, after refusing to authorise the 2026 event on Wednesday.

“The City Hall has decided not to approve the event. All 115 possible routes proposed by the organisers are concentrated in the city’s central area … These routes are unavailable because they overlap with other authorised events, or are affected by major public infrastructure works,” municipal spokesperson Octavian Haragoș said, as quoted by the local news outlet ebihoreanul.ro.

The municipality did not explain why alternative routes outside the city centre could not be considered. The decision followed weeks of delays by the city council in ruling on the organisers’ request, where conservative councillors and religious groups dominated the debate.

Human rights groups condemned the decision, arguing that it violates the constitutional right to peaceful assembly.

“We consider this decision completely unacceptable because it effectively blocks people’s constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” Victor Ciobotaru, director of ACCEPT, Romania’s leading LGBTQ+ rights organisation, told BIRN.

“Under Romanian law, local authorities cannot ban a public march. Their role is to identify practical solutions to ensure that such events can take place safely and under appropriate conditions, not to prevent them altogether,” Ciobotaru added.

Citing the same legal argument, ARK Oradea, the organisation behind the city’s Pride Parade, said the march would go ahead on July 25 despite the municipality’s refusal to authorise it.

“Our march will take place … As a sign of solidarity and concern for the situation in Oradea, representatives of nine diplomatic missions accredited to Romania, as well as representatives of the Ombudsman Institution, will be present in Oradea to monitor the unfolding of events,” ARK said, adding that the presence of diplomats reflects growing international concern over restrictions on freedom of assembly and LGBTQ+ rights in Romania.

This marks the fourth consecutive year that Oradea’s authorities have refused to authorise the Pride Parade.

Last year, however, an unauthorised march was still held through the city centre, attended by several hundred mostly young people. There were brief scuffles between some participants and the police but the situation did not escalate.

Authorities later imposed fines totalling 19,800 lei (about 3,900 euros) on organisers and participants in the unauthorised march

Romania has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights since joining the European Union in 2007 but continues to rank among the bloc’s weakest performers in terms of legal protections and social acceptance.

Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 2001, but same-sex marriage and civil partnerships are not recognised, despite a 2023 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights requiring Romania to provide legal recognition and protection for same-sex couples.

Public attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people remain largely conservative, particularly outside major cities. Pride marches have been held annually in Bucharest for two decades, however, and in several other cities, generally under police protection and without major incidents.

Human rights organisations have urged Romania to strengthen anti-discrimination protections and fully implement European human rights standards, arguing that it is lagging behind in terms of the country’s commitments as an EU member.

World.title: EU, OSCE Missions Criticise Kosovo’s Demolition of Serb-Owned Villas
World.content:
Demolition of villas near Ujman/Gazivoda lake in north Kosovo on July 21, 2026. Photo: BIRN

International missions in Kosovo expressed concern on Wednesday over the police’s demolition of 11 villas belonging to local Serbs near Lake Ujman/Gazivoda in the Serb-majority north of the country.

Kosovo authorities said the houses were built illegally on land owned by the public water management company Iber-Lepenc, near the Ujman/Gazivode Lake. The operation began on June 26.

The European Union Office in Kosovo said that it regretted Tuesday’s demolitions, noting that, “the affected residents had already initiated court proceedings within the 15-day deadline provided in notices issued by the public enterprise Iber-Lepenc to vacate the land”.

The EU called for an “immediate halt to any further demolitions, forced removals or takeovers until concerns relating to due process, proportionality, property rights, human rights and effective remedies are adequately addressed.

“Irreversible enforcement measures in the context of pending proceedings and contested property claims raise serious rule-of-law concerns,” the statement added.

The OSCE Mission in Kosovo said that, “any action affecting property rights, including the demolition of illegally constructed buildings, must be carried out strictly within the applicable legal framework, with full respect for due process”.

The mission said affected individuals should be informed promptly and adequately of the legal basis for actions taken against their property. “The rule of law, transparency, and due process must be applied consistently and without distinction to all illegally constructed buildings across Kosovo,” it said.

It added that enforcement measures against unauthorised construction should follow the same legal standards and procedural safeguards for all communities. “Selective or uneven application of the law, whether real or perceived, risks undermining public confidence and negatively affect inter-community relations and trust,” it said.

Faruk Mujka, Chief Executive of the state- owned hydro- economic company Iber- Lepenci, wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that “11 illegally constructed villas had been removed during Tuesday’s operation”.

Mujka said the action was carried out by the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure with assistance from the police following a request from Iber-Lepenc to return the property to the company’s management.

Ujman/Gazivoda Lake is considered strategic infrastructure for Kosovo. It supplies drinking water to several cities, supports electricity generation and provides water for irrigation.

Fitore Pacolli, acting minister of the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure, noted at the start of demolition work in June that the operation was being conducted to return illegally occupied property in northern Kosovo to the administration of Iber-Lepenc.

“The protection of our water resources remains our highest priority. For this reason, we will continue to protect them, manage them responsibly, and develop them as a vital asset for Kosovo,” Pacolli wrote.

But the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo condemned the operation as a “violent demolition” undertaken “without any court verdict”.

“The owners of the villas found out about the demolition of their property, which they had acquired for years, from the notices that were attached to their buildings, and when they asked for court decisions today, they did not receive them,” it said.

“All this indicates that these demolitions were not carried out with the aim of implementing some kind of law, but for a political reason,” it added.

Note: The article was updated on July 22 to reflect Faruk Mujka’s exact position.

World.title: Serbia Indicts Six for Drug Trafficking Linked to North Macedonia
World.content:
Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime filed an indictment on Tuesday accusing six alleged members of an organised crime group of producing and trafficking drugs within Serbia and North Macedonia during 2025 until January 29, 2026.

The prosecution on Wednesday said the indictment was filed against Aleksandar Mijajlovic as the organiser, Ivan Dragnic as the co-organiser, and Nebojsa Spasojevic, Rade Spasojevic, Uros Mladenovski and Robert Zivkovic as members of the same crime group.

“The evidence collected … indicates that the organisers devised the group’s operational structure, established its hierarchy, assigned roles among its members in advance, and secured the financial resources necessary to carry out the criminal plan,” the prosecution said in a press release.

The group is suspected of transporting nearly five tonnes of marijuana from North Macedonia to Serbia and storing it in residential and commercial premises used by Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic in the village of Konjuh, near Krusevac, central Serbia, where the drugs were repackaged and prepared for distribution to end-buyers.

Spasojevic was a local official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the time of the bust. Serbian Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, himself from Krusevac, denied the party was involved and repeated that it was clear that there are “no protected individuals” in Serbia because they had arrested Spasojevic.

The suspects are charged with using the company Alfapharm Group, based in Skopje, as a legitimate business entity to cover the narcotics production.

The company held permits issued by the authorities in North Macedonia to cultivate and produce cannabis extracts for medical purposes.

“The company was misused to conceal the organisation of the procurement, storage, repackaging, and transportation of large quantities of the narcotic drug marijuana,” the press release said.

According to the prosecution, in November 2025, the group organised the procurement of 8,832 kilograms of dried cannabis flower from the supplier CBD Med Plant from Strumica, North Macedonia.

The drugs were stored at the premises of Alfapharm Group, weighed, repackaged and prepared for transportation. The group used documentation relating to the export of textile goods for this during international transport.

The indictment added that Robert Zivkovic is charged with managing storage of the drugs, supervising the packaging process, organising their transportation, and overseeing their unloading and storage in Serbia. Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic are alleged to have been responsible for receiving, storing, repackaging, and arranging the further transport of the drugs.

Serbian police arrested Uros Mladenovski at the end of January in Belgrade, when he collected around a hundred kilograms of marijuana from Spasojevic’s premises and transported it to the capital.

During searches of the residential and business premises used by the Spasojevic family, police discovered various arms, such as automatic firearms, ammunition, and a “Zolja” hand-held anti-tank rocket launcher.

Dragnic, Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic and Mladenovski are in detention.

Zivkovic is a fugitive. A detention order has been issued for him, and both domestic and international arrest warrants have been sought.

Aleksandar Mihailovic was arrested in Austria on July 1 and a Serbian request for his extradition is pending.

The prosecution added that proceedings are being conducted before the North Macedonian authorities as well, and that both countries “continue to cooperate and exchange information within the framework of international legal assistance”.

Serbia’s authorities on January 29 seized five tons of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, which the Serbian prosecution then suggested may have originated from North Macedonia. A week later, North Macedonia police seized more than 40 tons of drugs.

The record-breaking seizures in both countries fuelled questions about whether North Macedonia’s legalisation of marijuana grown for medicinal purposes in 2016 has encouraged illegal production and smuggling.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Access-to-Information Agency Accused of Hindering Appeals
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information. Photo: BIRN.

Legal experts and transparency advocates have criticised North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information after it began requiring electronic signatures on email appeals, arguing that this unlawfully restricts access to public information.

The Agency is the only institution responsible for deciding appeals when public bodies refuse or fail to provide information requested under the country’s freedom of information law.

Until recently, appeals could be submitted by email without additional formalities. However, the Agency has started rejecting emailed appeals unless they are certified with an electronic signature, which costs 2,000 to 4,000 denars (30 to 65 euros) annually.

Critics say the changes create an unnecessary financial and administrative obstacle to exercising a constitutionally guaranteed right.

“I believe they obstruct free access to public information in this country,” German Filkov, one of the authors of the Law on Free Access to Public Information and president of the Centre for Civil Communications, an anti-corruption and transparency watchdog, told BIRN.

Instead of creating new barriers, Filkov said, the Agency should focus on the growing number of state institutions that fail to respond to freedom of information requests.

The Agency has defended the new requirement by citing the 2015 Law on General Administrative Procedure, which it says obliges anyone communicating electronically with state institutions to use an electronic signature.

However, the State Administrative Inspectorate, which the Agency initially cited as the source of the guidance, told BIRN it had issued no written decision or instruction requiring such a practice.

One of the authors of the Law on General Administrative Procedure, which the Agency cites as the legal basis for its new practice, Skopje university law professor Borce Davitkovski, also questioned the Agency’s interpretation.

“They are not allowed to reject an appeal because it lacks an electronic signature,” Davitkovski told BIRN, noting that the law was designed to protect citizens rather than burden them with unnecessary bureaucracy.

Konstantin Bitrakov, an assistant professor at Skopje’s State Faculty of Law, argued that the Agency was misapplying the legislation and “setting a negative example for public institutions that hold information, whose decisions it is supposed to review on appeal”.

He said the legal provisions on electronic signatures apply to officials issuing administrative decisions, not to citizens filing appeals.

Lawyers told BIRN that citizens and organisations whose appeals have been rejected for lacking an electronic signature should challenge the Agency before the Administrative Court within 30 days.

The dispute comes amid concerns over access to public information.

A BIRN analysis found that the number of appeals filed with the Agency over administrative silence or incomplete responses had doubled last year, from over 300 filed in 2024 to over 600 in 2025.

The European Commission’s latest Rule of Law Report warned that some public institutions continue to reject information requests on arbitrary grounds or with significant delays.

In April, the new head of the Agency, Petar Gajdov, told BIRN in an interview: “As institutions, we are service-oriented towards citizens.”

World.title: Who Really Benefits from ‘Strategic Investor’ Status in Albania?
World.content:
A company granted a stretch of Albania’s Adriatic coastline lists its official address as the 12th floor of the European Trade Centre in Tirana, where, according to a BIRN investigation, “there was no company sign, and building staff said they were unaware of any company by that name”.

A public asset belonging to all citizens is now registered under the name of a company that cannot even be found at its own listed address – because its ownership has been ‘constructed’ as a chain of corporate shells, one nested inside another, with the final shell empty. In that vacuum is where the problem begins.

Attempts to frame the public debate over luxury tourist developments in Zvernec, on the Albanian coast, and nearby Sazan island as a choice between environmental protection and economic development are, at best, unhelpful. At worst, they are misleading.

World.title: EU’s Failure to Address Balkan Disputes Undermines Its Credibility
World.content:
It also underlines the consequences of the EU’s failure to put forward an overall strategy to address the many bilateral disputes in the Western Balkans.

North Macedonia’s current centre-right government led by Hristijan Mickovski, elected in 2024, has insisted that before it amends the constitution, Bulgaria should guarantee it will make no new demands that could further block negotiations down the road.

The background to this request relates to the long list of obstacles placed on the country’s aspirations to join the European Union ever since it applied for membership in 2004, and successive governments’ efforts to address them with varying degrees of success.

In her response, however, Commissioner Kos underlined that “EU enlargement is not built on guarantees given in advance. It is built on trust, commitments, dedication in fulfilling these commitments and hard work”.

A week later, she repeated the same call on the government to build trust with all the EU member states.

In doing so, she seemed to forget the number of times North Macedonia’s citizens were let down by promises made by the EU which were not kept. She should acknowledge that trust can only succeed if it exists on both sides and is based on solid foundations.

Under the so-called Prespa Agreement, signed with Greece in June 2018, the country agreed to replace its constitutional name with “Republic of North Macedonia”, to be applied erga omnes. The agreement also included recognition of the Macedonian language.

In return the EU assured the country that this agreement would open the door to EU and NATO membership, only to be confronted with a French government veto in 2019, calling for a pause on EU enlargement.

This was resolved the following year with the adoption of a revised methodology for accession negotiations, and the European Council recommendation that negotiations should start with both Albania and North Macedonia.

However, Bulgaria then decided to impose its own veto against the latter, which was transformed into an EU veto in 2022, with the adoption of the French proposal. Under this proposal, formal negotiations with both countries were launched in July 2022. But until parliament in North Macedonia adopts the constitutional amendment, its accession negotiations remain blocked.

Renewed momentum flawed by unanimity rule

World.title: ‘Nobody Mentions Us’: Silence Surrounds Wartime Rape of Kosovo’s Ethnic Minorities
World.content:
Those who fled and never returned often have no means of applying for recognition as survivors of wartime sexual violence.

That includes a fourth woman interviewed by BIRN, who was 29 years old when she was raped twice by uniformed men in the police headquarters in Gjakova/Djakovica in March and April 1999. A cleaner in the building, she fled when the war ended out of fear of being targeted for revenge as a former employee of the Serbian state.

The woman now lives in the Montenegrin capital, Podgorica, but does not possess Kosovo documents.

“Living in a refugee camp for a long time, we didn’t have food, let alone a psychologist,” she told BIRN. “Sometimes I bought sedatives when I had a few dinars.”

When the war ended, ethnic minorities were targeted for revenge by Kosovo Albanian guerrillas and civilians.

Speaking to BIRN, an Egyptian woman from a village near Peja/Pec recalled five armed men entering her house on July 27, 1999, one of them in a T-shirt featuring the symbol of the guerrilla Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA. Her husband was beaten and she was dragged into the woods. “One of them raped me, and my husband was unable to help.”

The men later went next door, where they raped the woman’s neighbour.

Three days later, the family left Kosovo. Her case was documented in a 1999 report by the Belgrade-based Humanitarian Law Centre. In the report, she says: “When they came, they asked me to find two other women and go with them. I told them I could not find any and begged them to let me go because I was a mother with small children. One of them threatened to kill my husband if I did not comply. Crying, I went there. They left me there, crying and dishonoured.”

However, Kosovo’s Law on the Status and Rights of Martyrs, Invalids, Veterans, Civilian Victims, and Victims of Sexual Violence only provides for recognition of survivors of wartime sexual violence between February 1998 and June 20, 1999, i.e. roughly a week after Serbian forces pulled out of Kosovo and the war ended.

The woman said she doesn’t “need” recognition. “But I am frustrated that nobody mentions us,” she said. “Egyptian Roma women have also been raped here.”

Agushi, the Roma rights activist, said rape survivors from minority communities barely feature in public discourse surrounding the war and wartime sexual violence; those raped after the official cessation of hostilities are doubly discriminated against.

“They are even more marginalised, and those who were victims of sexual violence after June 20, 1999, are particularly discriminated against because they are not legally recognised and remain in the shadows.”

Campaign of terror

World.title: Land Registry Cyberattack Exposes Holes in Romania’s Digital Defences
World.content:
Photo illustration: EPA/SASCHA STEINBACH

This summer was supposed to mark an important milestone for Stefania Guga. By the end of July, the 32-year-old had hoped to buy a two-room apartment in a newly built complex on the outskirts of Bucharest, fulfilling her ambition of becoming a homeowner, Guga told BIRN.

“I wanted to finalise the transaction before August 1 to avoid paying the higher VAT rate. But for more than a week now, everything has been at a standstill, and I still don’t know whether I’ll make the deadline. It’s no longer up to me – the problem lies with Romanian state institutions,” she said.

Guga’s plans have been disrupted by a cyberattack on July 14 targeting the IT infrastructure of Romania’s National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration, ANCPI, effectively freezing property registration services and real estate transactions.

For Guga, the timing could hardly be worse. Under the government’s latest fiscal package, the VAT rate for newly built homes will rise from 9 to 21 per cent on August 1.

If she misses the deadline, it will significantly raise the overall cost of her apartment, adding thousands of euros to the price.

The ANCPI has described the cyberattack as “the most serious technical incident in the institution’s history”.

It crippled the agency’s digital systems, disrupting online land registry services, official email communications and apps used daily by notaries, lawyers, cadastral surveyors and ANCPI staff.

Authorities were left unable to register new property transactions, process pending requests, or issue essential land registry documents, bringing much of Romania’s real estate market to a standstill.

Just one day after the agency’s systems were compromised, some of the stolen data appeared for sale on a well-known hacking forum.

The leaked files included employee login credentials, internal documents and technical information about the agency’s IT infrastructure, raising concerns that the attackers had gained deep access to critical systems.

Experts say that, although the attack did not look particularly sophisticated from a technical standpoint, its consequences are serious.

“This is arguably the most severe cybersecurity incident in Romania’s relatively short history of the digitalisation of public administration,” said cybersecurity expert Andrei Avadanei.

“It affects data belonging to infrastructure classified as critical national infrastructure, including records covering every property in the country.

“It has disrupted essential public services and directly affects hundreds of thousands of citizens whose property transactions and administrative procedures are now vulnerable,” he added.

Avadanei also said the incident could likely have been prevented if the ANCPI had invested more consistently in cybersecurity and implemented stronger preventive measures.

The agency’s spending priorities appear to reinforce that criticism.

According to media reports, ANCPI has invested around 710 million lei, or about 135 million euros, in digitalisation over the past two decades. But only about 0.2 per cent of that, roughly 305,000 euros, was allocated to cybersecurity.

Experts say that figure is woefully inadequate given the sensitivity of the data the agency manages and its role in operating one of the country’s most critical public databases.

Officials have sought to reassure the public and limit the fallout from the cyberattack. In a statement, ANCPI said the incident “did not compromise the agency’s technical or legal databases” and stressed that core land registry records were neither altered nor destroyed.

The agency also said it has begun migrating its applications to the Romanian Government Cloud, a process expected to be completed on Wednesday. Once the migration is finished, specialists will carry out comprehensive integrity checks before services are gradually restored.

At the same time, the incident has exposed the fragility of Romania’s public digital infrastructure at a time when the country is facing a sustained wave of cyber threats linked to the broader security environment created by Russia’s invasion of neighbouring Ukraine.

Romanian authorities and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly warned that government institutions, critical infrastructure and public databases have become attractive targets for hostile cyber actors.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire public administration,” interim Digitalisation Minister Irineu Darau said in a televised interview.

Darau acknowledged that the digitalisation of Romania’s public institutions has been carried out in a fragmented way, without a coherent national strategy or common security standards.

“It is time to make digital transformation and cybersecurity genuine national priorities,” he said.

“That also means offering better salaries to cybersecurity professionals working in the public sector so that state institutions can attract and retain the expertise needed to protect critical systems,” he concluded.

World.title: Dinamo Draw at the Start of Champions League Qualifying
World.content:
Dinamo Zagreb played out a 1-1 draw against Thun in Switzerland in the first leg of the Champions League second qualifying round. The hosts took the lead through a Brighton Labeau goal in the 20th minute, before Miha Zajc set the final score in the 86th minute. The tie will be decided in the return leg in Zagreb in a week.

Thun are the first of three potential opponents Dinamo must overcome to secure a place in the Champions League group stage. The second round is followed by the third round and then the play-off. Dinamo’s possible third-round opponent will be the winner of the tie between KÍ Klaksvík of the Faroe Islands and Lithuania’s Kauno Žalgiris. Should they fall to Thun, Dinamo would continue their European campaign in the Europa League third qualifying round against the loser of the tie between Hapoel Be’er Sheva and Vikingur.

After a quiet start, the Swiss side took the lead in the 20th minute. Fabio Fehr’s cross from the right caught goalkeeper Ivan Filipović out, and Brighton Labeau headed home to make it 1-0. Just a minute earlier, Filipović had misjudged a free-kick delivery but redeemed himself by saving two efforts from the home side.

Dinamo almost leveled quickly, but Dion Drena Beljo’s effort in the 22nd minute went straight into the hands of goalkeeper Niklas Steffen. The Thun keeper also did well to save a fine long-range attempt from Moris Valinčić in the 28th minute. Thun’s best chance to extend their lead came in the 30th minute, when Furkan Dursun found himself unmarked five metres out but headed wide of the post.

Dinamo created a few more openings before halftime, but efforts from Miha Zajc and Gabriel Vidović fell short, and Thun led 1-0.

Dinamo continued to press after the restart. In the 53rd minute, Beljo’s header from a corner was cleared off the line by a home defender, and in the 65th minute a Mislav Oršić effort was again blocked on its way towards goal. Thun threatened on the counter, coming closest in the 73rd minute when Valmir Matoshi’s shot went narrowly wide.

Dinamo’s persistence paid off in the 86th minute. Fran Topić, on since the 79th minute, supplied the assist from the right for Miha Zajc, and the Slovenian midfielder finished first-time from 17 meters to make it 1-1. The score remained unchanged until the final whistle, leaving the tie to be settled in Zagreb.

World.title: Will Smith Visits Rimac Campus Near Zagreb
World.content:
July the 22nd, 2026 – Hollywood star Will Smith paid a visit to Rimac Campus near Zagreb this week, where he was treated to something special indeed.

The well known actor was given a behind-the-scenes look at one of Croatia’s most celebrated technology companies, and judging by his reaction, he was thoroughly impressed! Poslovni reports that the Oscar-winning actor toured the state-of-the-art headquarters of Rimac Technology, meeting founder and CEO Mate Rimac while exploring the cutting-edge engineering and production facilities that have helped place Croatia firmly on the global automotive map.

During the visit, Smith experienced several of Rimac’s innovations firsthand, including the company’s world-renowned electric hypercars. Videos shared from the visit captured the actor reacting with visible excitement, laughing, shouting in amazement and expressing disbelief at the performance and technology on display. According to those present, Smith was particularly impressed by the speed, engineering and innovation that have become synonymous with the Rimac name.

putting croatian innovation on stage

Founded by Mate Rimac back in 2009, the company has grown from a small garage startup into one of the world’s leading developers of high-performance electric vehicle technology. Today, Rimac supplies advanced battery systems, electric powertrains and software to some of the biggest names in the automotive industry, while its Nevera hypercar has repeatedly broken global performance records. The Rimac Campus, located in Kerestinec on the outskirts of Zagreb, has become a symbol of Croatia’s growing reputation as a centre for advanced engineering and innovation.

Smith’s visit shines another international spotlight on one of Croatia’s biggest business success stories. Over the past few years, the company has welcomed politicians, investors, automotive executives and celebrities eager to see firsthand how a Croatian startup evolved into a global technology powerhouse. The visit also serves as another reminder that Croatia’s international reputation is increasingly being shaped not only by tourism, but also by world-class innovation and high-tech manufacturing.

more than just fast cars…

While Rimac’s electric hypercars often capture the headlines, the company has become equally important as a technology partner for the wider automotive industry. Its expertise in battery systems, electric drivetrains and vehicle software is helping shape the next generation of electric mobility, with technologies developed in Croatia finding their way into vehicles produced around the world. For Will Smith, the visit offered a glimpse into the future of transportation. For Croatia, it was another high-profile endorsement of a company that continues to demonstrate the country’s ability to compete at the highest possible levels of global technology.
