World.title: 'Grave concern' as Wagga Wagga's homeless threatened with $1,100 fines
World.content:
Homeless advocates are slamming the approach of a New South Wales council that has threatened to fine people sleeping rough.

Wagga Wagga City Council has warned homeless people living at a campground near the CBD they could face penalties of $1,100 or more if they do not leave the site by July 28.

Wagga Women's Health Centre president Vickie Burkinshaw said there should be a more humane approach to solving the crisis.

"Rather than treat it as a welfare issue, we're treating it as a compliance issue," she said.

The council says there will be penalties for those who don't leave the area before the deadline. (ABC Riverina)

The council's move comes two weeks after it issued compliance action notices for people at Wilks Park to move on.

That tactic was part of a NSW government-led response to the crisis following the death of an infant at a nearby camp.

Vickie Burksinshaw says the council is turning a welfare issue into a compliance issue. (ABC Riverina: Jess Scully)

But Ms Burkinshaw said the strategy failed "to understand the individual needs of the people they're claiming to support".

"Being moved on to another city without the wraparound supports, without the outreach, is setting people up for failure," she said.

Rachael Vorhauer, who has lived at the campground for more than three years, said the notices prompted her to leave Wagga Wagga and travel to Sydney in the hope of securing stable housing.

"I'm not in Wilks Park because I want to be," she said.

"It was a leap of faith to come to Sydney."

Rachael Vorhauer has been homeless for nine years, three of which she has spent living at Wilks Park. (ABC Riverina: Jess Scully)

The ABC understands Ms Vorhauer was offered accommodation in Wagga Wagga and Sydney.

She is now living in temporary accommodation in Sydney but her pathway to permanent housing is unclear.

Ms Vorhauer said she hoped there would be more support options in the city than in Wagga Wagga.

Homes NSW said there was no limit for how long someone could stay in temporary accommodation, as long as they were still engaging with their support plan.

NSW Housing and Homelessness Minister Rose Jackson previously told the ABC every homeless person camped in Wilks Park and Wagga Beach had been offered accommodation.

Homeless people living at a campground in Wagga Wagga have been warned they could face fines if they do not leave the site by the end of July. (ABC Riverina)

Fines could be an incentive, council says

Council general manager Peter Thompson said further enforcement action could be taken if people refused the support being offered.

"The knowledge that we will eventually exercise some form of regulatory power might incentivise them to take up the opportunities being provided to them," he said.

The council said in a statement that it sought extensive legal advice before issuing the notices, but could not provide any detail because the advice was subject to professional privilege.

Kira Levin acknowledges that councils are under pressure to act, but says punitive measures are not the answer. (Supplied: Homeless Persons’ Legal Service)

Homeless Persons' Legal Service principal solicitor Kira Levin said there were better ways to address homelessness.

"We have grave concerns about forcibly removing people," she said.

"We don't think fining people is going to result in anything positive. If anything, it will further marginalise people and move the problem."

Ms Levin said councils were under pressure, but argued individual support was more effective than "punitive measures".

She said temporary accommodation also failed to provide long-term certainty.

"If they do agree to leave and go into temporary accommodation, where do they go once their time is up?" Ms Levin said.

Ms Vorhauer hopes the move to Sydney will eventually lead to a stable home.

"I came down with a suitcase and, as it turns out, I'm still here," she said.

World.title: Inside CPAC London: Charlatans, conspiracy theories and loud snoring
World.content:
In 10 years at the ABC, I've had some strange experiences. I can now add last week's CPAC conference in London to the list, and it's going somewhere near the top.

After two-and-a-half days, I left with serious questions about where right-wing politics is heading, not just in Britain, but abroad too.

On the auditorium stage, current and former MPs decried the state of the United Kingdom. Between their speeches were sermons from conspiracy theorists and charlatans. Here's a taste: one panel on Saturday was titled The Truth About Covid. It was presented by a major anti-vax group.

Also at the conference, Australian senators Pauline Hanson and Bridget McKenzie both had their own speaking slots, but small audiences. Indeed, sparse attendances were a feature of the whole thing.

It got me thinking; who is this event actually for?

Pauline Hanson spoke to around 120 people at CPAC on Saturday. (ABC News: Riley Stuart)

The Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) was first held in the United States in the 1970s, and populist, MAGA diehards have towered over its latest iterations. While multiple foreign countries, including Australia, have hosted their own CPACs, this is the first time the UK has staged one.

There were early warning signs last Thursday when only a few dozen people were in the InterContinental Hotel's Arora Ballroom to hear Liz Truss open proceedings. The former British PM — CPAC's UK chair — strode out onto the stage to music and flashing lights to demand the civil service be dismantled (she sometimes calls this "the blob"), and complain her country had churned through too many leaders in the past decade.

The UK has had seven PMs since 2016, but had Truss forgotten she was the most short-lived of them all? Her tenure in office lasted just 49 chaotic days in 2022. A live-streamed lettuce with googly eyes stuck to it famously outlasted her.

Truss had become so unpopular by the last general election that she was booted out of her previously safe Conservative seat and sent into the political wilderness. Presumably, it's how she ended up at CPAC. As one journalist quipped to me: "Couldn't run the country, and can't run a conference."

CPAC chair Matt Schlapp and former UK prime minister Liz Truss take to the stage in London. (Instagram: @cpac_gb)

The event was held in North Greenwich. London is among the cultural capitals of the world, but this partly gentrified industrial area is so soulless, it would give Sydney Olympic Park or Melbourne's Docklands a run for their money.

The desolate environment was compounded by the lack of attendees. There were just so few people who turned up to CPAC this year, it all felt a bit deflating. One criticism I heard constantly was that the format had far too much American razzle dazzle to be palatable for a British audience.

When Truss asked the crowd on day one what they thought of Andy Burnham (the UK's new PM), it elicited a few limp "boos". Someone who was there later posted online about the lack of enthusiasm in the auditorium, saying they had seen more life in a supermarket clearance bin.

Things got worse. During a session on Friday, my colleague Latika Bourke noted a man behind her in the crowd had "fallen asleep and was snoring loudly".

Away from the main stage, an adjacent room where a handful of exhibitors had set up stalls seemed to be deserted every time I stuck my head in. The corridors and bars around the cavernous five-star complex were largely empty too.

Where was everyone? Perhaps the VIP area, which you had to pay 10,000 pounds ($19,100) to access. I'll never know.

Sea of empty seats for most speakers

Many of those at CPAC London seemed to have made their way there from the political fringes. They're the type of people you hear lament: "I didn't leave the Conservatives, the Conservatives left me."

There was more youth in the crowd than you might think. I spotted Lorcan Barker, a 19-year-old far-right activist who goes by the online alias Angloid, taking selfies. He advocates for mass deportations and spoke at a remigration summit in Portugal earlier this year. Last month, he posted a video on Instagram claiming the Daily Mail had falsely accused him of being a white supremacist.

After CPAC concluded, he took to social media to say the whole thing had been "terrible". "I got countless dirty looks," he wrote on X.

Full disclosure, I could not attend the Thursday sessions of CPAC, but watched a few online. My boss Mazoe Ford went to some in-person, though.

By the time I arrived at the venue on Friday, things had picked up a little. In the afternoon, a decent crowd was building for the most high-profile speaker at the conference, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart was spotted in the crowd last week. (ABC News: Daniel Pannet)

Ahead of his address, I watched Gina Rinehart sashay to a seat near the front. The Australian billionaire was hard to miss, donning bejewelled sandals and a pink cowboy hat (tell me you have just been holidaying in Sicily without telling me).

A little later, Hanson made her way into the venue with her chief-of-staff James Ashby. She looked annoyed as she strode through the doors. Then I noticed my colleague Elias Clure trailing her with a microphone. Ah, that explains it, I thought.

Farage is riding high in UK opinion polls. Whether you agree with his politics or not, he is a brilliant orator. In a searing 30-minute address, he seldom looked at notes and got a standing ovation, albeit from a very friendly crowd.

"I genuinely believe we are in a battle for the soul of our nation," he said, before going on to talk about immigration, the economy and how the party he founded, Reform UK, could win the next general election (not due to be held until 2029).

"I believe an historic upset is on the cards," he said.

On the way out of the auditorium, I overheard one man gushing to another: "How can you not love him?"

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage drew the biggest crowd of the conference. (X: @Nigel_Farage)

The fact the audience was packed out for Farage was an aberration. When Hanson spoke on Saturday morning, the room was less than a quarter full. By the time McKenzie took to the stage later that day, there were even fewer bums on seats.

The Nationals deputy leader went a little off-piste in her speech, telling those who were still in attendance that dishing out foreign aid was actually OK, so long as it was to prevent the Chinese having influence in the Pacific. She admitted those listening to her would probably be sceptical. No one clapped.

The discussions at CPAC were a mixed bag. A panel named The Problem With Central Banks featured two people from cryptocurrency groups. Consecutive sessions on Thursday were initially given titles complaining about "the blob", so one was changed to What About White Working-Class Boys?

American activist Jack Posobiec delivered a speech on the opening afternoon. You might remember him as being among the main pushers of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy theory (if you don't, I'll let you Google that one).

A few people at CPAC told me they felt the fringe nature of some sessions took away from what could have been, in several cases, constructive conversations.

For example, Ellie Reynolds, a survivor of child sexual abuse at the hands of Britain's so-called grooming gangs, was among those speaking on Saturday.

Topical political issues like the UK's cost-of-living crisis, levels of migration and the education system were key themes across the two-and-a-half days.

Loading YouTube content

After Hanson's speech, it was my job to wait outside the VIP room and ask her questions in case she emerged. After about an hour, I abandoned my post because I had to file a story (and, to use a favoured phrase of the One Nation leader's, I'd had a gutful). As it turned out, Hanson gave Australian journalists the slip and found a way to exit the conference undetected.

If I had been able to track her down, I would have asked her about her decision to participate in an interview with anti-immigration activist Tommy Robinson — something that has been widely criticised — while in the UK. Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is a convicted criminal, and did not speak at the conference.

I returned to the auditorium in time to catch some of The Truth About Covid session. It was what those in mainstream medicine would describe as absolute quackery.

The panel included Danish doctor Vibeke Manniche, who is not permitted to practice independently. She received a suspended prison sentence in 2024 for issuing invalid COVID test exemptions. She was joined, among others, by Maria Hubmer-Mogg, a charismatic Austrian physician and anti-COVID activist who was fired from a clinic in 2021 over her views.

Matt Schlapp takes the stage at the CPAC conference in the US earlier this year. (Reuters: Daniel Cole)

Globally, CPAC is chaired by US lobbyist Matt Schlapp, who loomed large over the event in London. Schlapp, 58, has faced allegations of sexual assault multiple times, but denies all and has never been charged with a crime. He settled a lawsuit with one male accuser in 2024 for $US480,000 ($684,000).

In the US, CPAC is huge. It has been staged in Australia multiple times. In fact, it has now been held in Poland, Brazil, Japan, the list goes on. There are plans to expand to Italy next year.

A blurb on CPAC's website said the London gathering would "unite common-sense politics". The conference is supposed to serve as a launch pad for conservative grassroots political advocacy and energise right-wingers. I'm not certain that happened last week.

Several conservative media outlets were critical of the event. "It was shallow, senseless and utterly detrimental to the conservative cause it claimed to champion," was The Spectator's review. "The name itself is lifted directly from its American counterpart, and the cheap imports only became more apparent from there," a story on the UK website Conservative Home read.

For the moderate-right, this CPAC was too radical. For hardliners, it was not extreme enough.

On Saturday, Schlapp said the inaugural UK event had laid a good foundation for future summits. I took that to mean: we know no one came this time, but we will hold it again next year.

I hope they do, I can't wait to go back. Although I'm not sure how many others will join me.

World.title: Data company urged to be 'good' after water plan slip reveals intentions
World.content:
A farmer has urged an artificial intelligence company to "be a good corporate citizen" after it accidentally revealed plans to use water earmarked for agriculture to cool a data centre.

Firmus Technologies, the company behind three data centres being progressed across northern Tasmania, "inadvertently" revealed the plan on its website.

The "internal" note outlining a plan to use water from the Tasmanian Irrigation scheme at its proposed Wesley Vale centre was published on its FAQ page and deleted after questions from the ABC.

The company says most of the water the Wesley Vale data centre needs for cooling will be rainwater captured and stored on site, and that anything outside of that was for "contingency and resilience planning".

In the past, Firmus has said its Wesley Vale centre would use about the same amount of water as a "restaurant" annually.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff visited one of Firmus' sites and met with co-CEOs Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

The Firmus Technologies site in St Leonards, Launceston and site for the proposed Southgate Project (empty grey area mid image). (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

'Not a lot of water' needed, but concerns remain

Tasmanian Irrigation (TI) is a state-owned company that has been developing water pipelines around the state to guarantee water supplies for farming since 2008.

Is Tasmania ready for the AI data centre boom? An artificial intelligence company wants to build three AI factories in Tasmania, but questions are being raised about the impacts and benefits for the state.

Farmer Nathan Richardson is chair of the Sassafras Wesley Vale portion of the irrigation scheme, and said he had been assured Firmus was seeking a "minimal" amount of water.

"In the scheme of farming, [it's] not a lot of water," he said.

But he said farmers across the region and Tasmania more broadly had agreed to the irrigation infrastructure being built on their land believing it was good for farming.

"Farmers have been very obliging by letting this pipeline go through, make a hell of a mess in their farms, for the betterment of agriculture and the district," he said.

" We didn't know about Firmus or the data centre when we sat down with TI years ago. "

Mr Richardson said it was up to TI and the government to approve Firmus' use of water from the scheme, but he expected them to do so in the best interests of other scheme users.

"I would expect TI and the government to negotiate very handsomely on the side of our district and our community," he said.

Similarly, he encouraged Firmus to act in the interests of the existing landholders in the region.

" Be a good corporate citizen, Firmus. "

Matt Ryan, another farmer in the area, said the amount of water Firmus expected to use was not problematic, but he had previously been aware of talk about opening the irrigation scheme to industrial users.

"If that makes the scheme viable, then that's worth considering," he said.

"If it's going to be a big user and it's going to fundamentally change the scope of the scheme or the impact on irrigators, then obviously that's another conversation."

Firmus, led by Tim Rosenfield (left) and Oliver Curtis, plans to build three data centres in Northern Tasmania. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Firmus claims rainwater will cool centre on hot days

Responding to questions from the ABC, Firmus said it intended to harvest and store rainwater onsite as the "primary water solution for the facility" at Wesley Vale.

On its website, the company claims a "very limited amount of water is used" to cool its data centres, as it is only required on "hot days" above 26 degrees Celsius.

"Discussions regarding any supplementary water sources are separate to that primary strategy and relate to resilience and contingency planning," the company said.

It said the centre will be able to store 1 million litres on site, 700,000 litres of which will be dedicated to cooling.

"Our modelling indicates the maximum water usage over a summer period, based on the 26 years of BOM data, is [608,000 litres]," they said.

And, though they had not yet made a formal request to TI, if a connection to the irrigation scheme is not available, they will truck water to the site.

AI factories contain data centre infrastructure, advanced cooling systems and graphics processing units that generate AI tokens — the currency of AI needed for tools such as ChatGPT. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

No proposal put forward yet, says government

In a statement, a TI spokesperson said "no undertaking" had been given to Firmus about providing water.

"Any application for water from industries outside of this would require consideration by the Tasmanian government and engagement with the community, including our customers," they said.

Minister Felix Ellis said the government would consider any proposal through its usual process, if and when it receives one.

"We haven't actually received any proposal along those lines," he said.

" I do note as well that Firmus more broadly speak about their reduced water usage, and their ability to capture a significant amount of water with their on-site facilities. "

Labor MP Jen Butler said the party was seeking more information about the proposal from the government.

World.title: Rock Posters proud to capture artists' 'blood and tears' in billboards
World.content:
Pop diva Kylie Minogue and British rockers The Rolling Stones might be miles apart on the musical spectrum, but their posters hang side by side among scores of other performers at a Melbourne factory that has helped enhance the city's gig and live music culture.

"It's interesting for people to see 40 years of history in the one place," said Marcus Seal, Rock Posters general manager.

"The posters tend to bring back memories of going to a show, or listening to an album for the first time."

Behind an unassuming factory facade in Thornbury, the steady whirr of printing presses thrums a base track for the creation of colourful concert billboards and s that still adorn buildings across the city, despite the advent of social media advertising and influencers.

Loading...

"We watch artists go and stand in front of their own billboard, and that's what they want to show to their mum … it's not the digital ad that you see on Meta," Mr Seal said.

"We've got tens of thousands of stories of Australian tours, record releases, art exhibitions, and we're still very vibrant and relevant today."

He added that ink and paper conjured a special nostalgia, given "it's been around for 3,000 years, and it might be around for a few thousand more".

Colourful posters adorn the walls of the Rock Posters printing factory in Thornbury. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The late legendary music promoter Michael Gudinski summed up the natural creative fit when he once quipped that "music without the art is like the rock without the roll".

Unsurprisingly, he was an early and steadfast supporter of the company when it first opened in 1986.

"I think a lot of Melburnians consider Melbourne as the music capital of Australia — Sydneysiders might disagree — but I like to think that Rock Posters probably could have only been started in Melbourne," Mr Seal said.

"A lot of blood, sweat and tears has gone into these tours and these artists who work really hard to get there, so this provides a bit of a snapshot … it's a great privilege to be around it every day."

Luke Stewart (left) has worked in the industry for nearly a decade. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Others will get their chance to reminisce when the factory opens its doors to the public for the first time this weekend, as part of the Open House Melbourne event.

Mr Seal hopes visitors will gain a finer appreciation of the street poster campaigns that have helped shape Melbourne's cultural life, and the creative vision behind them.

"You'd expect someone like Beyoncé to be very particular and for good reason. U2 and Sting were very particular too, and Kiss curate everything they do very well," he said.

Marcus Seal says posters help provide a snapshot of the hard work that goes into music tours. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"They're all very evocative, but the Midnight Oil sprint hand is quite iconic; there's a lot of ACDC, and from the original Sex Pistols to the most recent tour of the Sex Pistols is also interesting as well.

"It's wonderful to be amongst all this creativity".

Rock Posters art director Luke Stewart has worked at the intersection of design and gigs for 27 years and said technological advances meant they could produce "roughly about 10,000 standard posters per week", but he still counted traditional screen print art among his favourites.

The Rock Posters printing press in Thornbury. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"I really like a lot of stuff designed by Ben Brown, who is a famous Australian artist, like the Hoodoo Gurus poster: multiple colours, very bold and bright," he said.

"Most people only have a couple of seconds as they drive past, and you want to be as bold and artistic as possible to catch their eye so hopefully they go to the gig.

"It would be weird to drive around and not see any of this advertising for bands; it makes the cityscape something interesting to look at."

Australian artist Ben Brown designed the Hoodoo Gurus poster. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

And there are some colourful tales behind the creation of these rock star images.

"The Cold Chisel Last Stand poster, I have on very good authority that it wasn't actually taken during the show even though it looks as if Jimmy [Barnes] is sweating, but I think somebody's thrown a bucket of water over him," Mr Seal said.

"And that vodka bottle he's holding may not have vodka in it, not at nine o'clock in the morning, I don't think!

"It's a classic iconic poster that's survived since that great tour, that didn't actually end up being The Last Stand.

"But Jimmy would be able to tell you the truth."

World.title: Labor conference to debate gas, gambling and Gaza
World.content:
It was an appropriate curtain-raiser for the Labor Party's 50th National Conference kicking off today.

"Left Right Out", a pub-rock band made up of Labor MPs and staffers including Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on guitar, put on a show at a heritage-listed Adelaide hotel last night.

As the name suggests, the band involves the left and right factions coming together, sticking to a set playlist and staging a performance. It's exactly what critics say this party conference is all about.

At $100 a ticket for MPs and supporters, $50 for "staff and unwaged" and reportedly $1,000 for lobbyists, last night's gig also served as a handy Labor fundraiser, of which there will be several over the coming days.

To dismiss this Labor conference as being nothing but theatrics, however, isn't entirely fair.

The national Labor conference kicked off with a performance by "Federal Parliament's best (and only) rock band" Left Right Out. (Supplied)

Gas, gambling, Gaza

The fiery debates of years gone by may not be as public as they once were, but the triennial national conference still serves as a mechanism to give rank-and-file ALP members a say. Behind closed doors at least.

"It isn't just the Eye of Sauron turning on the Adelaide convention centre for the next three days, it's cabinet ministers all year fronting up to branch meetings and the National Policy Forum," noted one minister yesterday, referring to the body set up to involve branch members and unions in policy debates.

Others in Labor who yearn for more transparent debates on the conference floor see these closed forums as purely designed to stifle genuine policy arguments.

Gambling watchdog push revived Labor members and unions are gearing up for fights over gambling, gas and AI at the party's national conference later this week.

Late yesterday, Labor's factions were still working to settle a range of positions.

The prime minister's move last week to shift and sharpen his position on artificial intelligence was in part driven by the conference process. The pledge for new AI laws and safeguards has been broadly welcomed, even if some at the conference will push for more.

The three most contentious outstanding issues as the conference begins are gas, gambling and Gaza.

On gas, momentum to introduce a new export tax will be demonstrated on day one of the conference, even if it's not explicitly endorsed in the party platform. Supporters of a gas tax point to former leader Bill Shorten publicly backing the idea on 7:30 this week and note the treasurer has always left the door ajar (while defending current arrangements), including yesterday on Afternoon Briefing.

On day two, debate over gambling advertising is likely to see an impassioned plea for the Albanese government to go further than the reforms it has introduced to parliament.

The government privately accepts it may have to give some ground to win Coalition support in the Senate. It will likely involve only a modest change, extending bans on gambling ads before and after live sports broadcasts.

A messy day-three debate over Gaza now appears to have been avoided after the left and right factions last night agreed on a draft set of words that calls on Israel to "bring its illegal settlement activity" to an end, while also condemning terrorism and violent extremism "including as perpetrated by Hamas".

Not everything has been nailed down as this conference begins. Genuine debates are still being had, even if not all of them are happening publicly. The factions last night failed to resolve disagreements over increasing funding for local government and a push from the right faction and Transport Workers Union to establish a new national coordinator to set safety standards and "fair pay" across the aviation sector.

The day three debate over Gaza remains the "most unresolved" according to Labor sources. Plans to strengthen criticism of Israel is being met by demands for stronger language about Hamas. Neither side of this debate is likely to be entirely satisfied.

Loading

A plan worked out off-stage

Not everything has been nailed down as this conference begins. Genuine debates are still being had, even if not all of them are happening publicly.

At the midway point of his second term in office, the prime minister will use this conference to make some new policy announcements, including today's commitment to extend "Prac Payments" — a payment to ease the financial strain of unpaid student placements — to more frontline health workers.

The main aim, however, is to use the spotlight to sell what the government is doing more broadly on the practical concerns of voters, including those flirting with One Nation. For him, that means a strong focus on cost of living, not gambling or Gaza.

Anthony Albanese may have been a keen participant in robust conference debates in years gone by but is now using his authority to enforce a much more controlled process.

A few surprises are fine but stick to the plan worked out off-stage.

Like any good pub-rock band.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: How we got to Glasgow 2026 and what the Commonwealth Games will look like
World.content:
As we adjust our body clocks from the FIFA World Cup, you would do well to stay a little out of whack as the 2026 Commonwealth Games kicks off in Glasgow.

It's been an unusually rocky road for the sporting carnival, so here's what you need to know.

When are the Glasgow Commonwealth Games on?

The 2026 Commonwealth Games start on July 23 and run through until August 2 (the early hours of August 3 in Australia).

The first event of the Games takes place on Day Zero, with an extra session of bowls and para bowls added to the schedule (from 6:30pm AEST July 23 to 1:25am July 24) due to "unprecedented demand".

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

Later that day, the opening ceremony will be held from 5am AEST on July 24.

Track and field star Nina Kennedy will be Australia's flag bearer.

Most days, competition will start about 5:30pm AEST and wrap up the following morning after 7am, with swimming (July 24–30) and athletics (July 27 — August 2) finals in that morning slot.

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the Games.

Weren't they supposed to be in Victoria?

Oh boy, were they ever.

It was a rollercoaster year for then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews. (AAP: James Ross)

There was an initial campaign from regional centres in Victoria — Greater Shepparton, Wodonga, Bendigo, Ballarat, Warrnambool and Traralgon — to host the 2030 Games.

Then, in April 2022, it was confirmed that the Commonwealth Games would head to Victoria four years early, in 2026, centred in Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and Gippsland, with an opening ceremony in Melbourne.

Then-premier Daniel Andrews spruiked the jobs, infrastructure and income the Games would bring to the regions and promised "a Commonwealth Games like no other".

Daniel Andrews gleefully announced the success of the bid in Ballarat. (ABC Ballarat: Lexie Jeuniewic)

Turns out he was right, just not in the way he or we might have expected.

Over time, criticism of the decision mounted, adjustments were made to the plans, and costs blew out.

Then, in July 2023, just 15 months after winning the hosting rights, the Victorian government announced it was pulling out of hosting, much to the chagrin of Commonwealth Games Australia and the international organising body.

Andrews said the cost, initially slated to be $2.6 billion, was looking more like $6 billion and it was no longer tenable.

Loading...

Shortly after withdrawing, the then-government reached an agreement to pay $380 million in compensation to the Commonwealth Games Federation (now Commonwealth Sport), Commonwealth Games Federation Partnerships and Commonwealth Games Australia.

In September 2024, it was announced Glasgow would host again, 12 years after the 2014 Games in the Scottish capital, albeit with about $200 million from Victorian taxpayers.

As a result of the truncated planning time, a month later organisers announced the slate of sports would be cut way back.

So, what sports are being played at Glasgow 2026?

Glasgow hustled to put together these Games with just 10 sports, down from more than 20 (depending on how you count it) at the 2022 Games in Birmingham.

Hockey, diving, badminton, beach volleyball, cricket, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon and wrestling were all ditched, leaving us with:

3x3 basketball and 3x3 wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics and para athletics

Bowls and para bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming and para swimming

Track cycling and para track cycling

Where will the events be held?

The Hydro will host the netball and opening ceremony at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The events selected meant the slimmed-down Games could be hosted in existing venues in a 13-kilometre corridor along the River Clyde.

Swimming will be held at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre and Scotstoun Stadium will host the athletics.

Glasgow International Arena will pull double duty as the venue for track cycling (at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome) and artistic gymnastics.

The Scottish Event Campus includes three venues: The Hydro, which will host the opening ceremony and the netball; the Armadillo, for weightlifting and para powerlifting; and the SEC Centre, a series of exhibition halls where the basketball, bowls, boxing and judo will play out.

Who is competing for Australia?

Australia is sending 256 athletes to Glasgow, competing in every sport on the program.

The athletics team has 86 competitors, while the Dolphins are bringing 59 swimmers.

World.title: Lisa came to China for a better life, but was 'auctioned off' for marriage
World.content:
Lisa grew up in a small rural village in Tonga.

Her family are farmers, and the 23-year-old lived a simple life.

But she always dreamed of something bigger.

So when a Tongan woman living in China contacted her through a family member with an offer of a better life, she was intrigued.

"She told me there was an opportunity in China if I was willing to get married," she told the ABC.

"She sent me photos of two Chinese men. One worked in a restaurant, the other owned a car business. She told me [if] I married one of them, I wouldn't have to pay for anything, and I'd be able to send money home every month.

"I agreed because I believed it was an opportunity that would allow me to support my family and improve my own life."

Lisa with another young Tongan woman who was brought to China for marriage. (Supplied)

Lisa, who asked to be de-identified to protect her family, packed her bags.

She boarded a flight — her first time travelling alone and first time flying overseas — and arrived in China in October last year.

But things soon turned sour.

"The situation in China turned out to be completely different from what I had been told in Tonga.

"I felt as though I [was] something that had been bought and sold."

Little did she know she had inadvertently been drawn into an arranged marriage syndicate that has enticed multiple Tongan women to China — a syndicate now being investigated by Tongan police.

Women 'auctioned off'

When Lisa arrived in China, she was taken to Fujian province and introduced to the people who helped organise her trip.

Days later she was introduced to several different men — different to the photos she was originally shown — and was told to "marry" and then "show affection" to one of them.

'Give us a baby and we'll let you go': Girls sold as sex slaves to China Seng Moon was just 16 when she was abducted and sold off to a Chinese man who repeatedly raped her while keeping her locked in a room for two months.

Tapenisa Mahe, a Tongan woman studying in Fujian province who came to translate and support Lisa, was there when that happened.

She said it was like they were "auctioning her off".

"Different families came to look at her and decide whether they wanted her," she said.

"I began to feel very uneasy. I wondered whether this was somehow normal in China."

Tapenisa Mahe was worried about the transactional nature of what she saw. (Supplied)

Ms Mahe was told by the people who organised Lisa's trip — and who asked her to help translate — that she had come "to try to build a better life".

"I only agreed to help because I wanted to help another Tongan," she said.

But she said she quickly became "seriously concerned".

"The man's family started talking about money that had been paid to the matchmakers.

"That's when I realised something much bigger was happening."

'They wanted to come'

The ABC has confirmed Lisa's trip to China was organised by Maata Aso, a Tongan woman living in China, and a Chinese national called Auntie Shulan Fang, better known as "Auntie Julie".

Ms Aso, who has lived in China for more than a decade, rejected claims that women were mistreated after arriving in China.

Maata Aso rejected claims that the Tongan women were treated poorly. (Supplied)

She said there were many Tongan women happily married there.

"The reasons Tongan women come to China are different," she told the ABC.

" Some come to get married, some come because they're poor, and some come looking for a better life. "

She also rejected claims she was paid.

"The claims that people are making about money are false," she said.

"I've never told anyone that I receive money. They [the women] themselves told me they wanted to come."

Auntie Shulan Fang, better known as "Auntie Julie", organises the trips for Tongan women to China.

The ABC has seen WeChat conversations that discuss payments of about $20,000 linked to the marriages; however, it is unclear who receives money and what it is used for.

Ms Aso said the arrangement between the families in China was organised by "Auntie Julie"

"The agreement was that Auntie would cover the costs first, and the family would repay her later," Ms Aso said.

"I don't know whether they [Lisa's former husband in China] repaid her or not. All I know is that all the expenses were paid by Auntie".

The ABC has contacted Auntie Julie and Lisa's former husband in China for comment.

'They took my passport'

Lisa said despite communication difficulties, at first, her new husband and the family were supportive and kind.

Lisa says at first the family was supportive, but that all changed. (Supplied)

But she said that all changed when she pushed back on the family's pressure to "make a baby".

"They took my passport," she said. "The family then began pressuring me to work, but I refused because I didn't have a work visa".

Months later, with conditions worsening, Lisa asked her husband for a divorce.

"The family began neglecting me," she said. "I was moved into a separate room in the house.

"There were times when I became so hungry that I drank water from the bathroom just to stay alive.

"There were moments when I felt completely hopeless."

Lisa was excited at first to move to China. (ABC News: Supplied )

Tapenisa Mahe later provided a safe house for Lisa. She says she helped her escape and organised help to get her back to Tonga.

Last week, after nine months in China, Lisa returned home.

The promise of 'a better life'

The allegations about a human trafficking syndicate involving Tongan women in China began to spread on social media last month.

Facing a public backlash, the Chinese Embassy in Tonga released two public statements, describing the issue as a "transnational marriage dispute".

It said with "assistance from Chinese police, the Tongan Embassy and students in China" it helped Lisa and another woman return home from China.

"Transnational marriages face gaps in language, culture and lifestyle," it said.

Why some Pacific islanders want to make themselves whiter Skin bleaching and lightening products are widely sold in Tonga, which is part of a region with a long history of colourism.

Acting Tonga Police Commissioner Tevita Vailea said police quickly learned that more young women were preparing to leave Tonga in organised trips and advised the women to rethink their plans.

The ABC has spoken to one of them. The 20-year-old said she cancelled her trip to China, organised by Auntie Julie and Mataa Aso, after the allegations emerged on social media.

Like Lisa, she was told all expenses would be paid by her prospective husband and had been sold the idea of "a better life".

At the time of ABC's interview, Commissioner Vailea said two more women were due to return to Tonga from China, and police were prioritising their safety before continuing the investigation.

Tonga Police Commissioner Tevita Vailea said they have warned other women planning to travel to China. (ABC News: Marian Kupu)

He said they have not yet determined whether the case involved criminal human trafficking.

"We have seen some areas of interest to focus on," Mr Vailea said. "But it is still in the early stages of our investigation."

According to ʻOfa Likiliki from Tonga's Women and Children Crisis Centre, the situation is simple.

"Based on what the young women who have courageously sought our services have disclosed to us, we have identified indicators that are consistent with internationally recognised indicators of human trafficking," she said.

She said they have supported a number of other young women who have returned to Tonga after travelling to China.

"Our immediate focus has been making sure the young women are safe and protected."

Lisa has been back in Tonga for a week. (ABC News: Marian Kupu)

Lisa, now home with her family, decided to speak out to ensure other young Tongan women contemplating travelling to China were aware of what is going on.

She said it was an experience she never wanted to relive.

"I simply hope no one else goes through what I went through," she said.

"I believed I was travelling for a better future. Instead, I found myself in a situation I never expected."

World.title: How One Nation's winning over the bush
World.content:
As you drive from the coastal town of Yeppoon to Rockhampton in Central Queensland there's a huge billboard.

Pauline Hanson looms over the road in a checked shirt.

The sign reads: "$13 million Cooee Bay Pool delivered."

One Nation didn't pay for the pool, but its leader did lobby the federal government for funds.

Regional Queensland is where One Nation first found support as a fringe movement.

Thirty years on, Pauline Hanson's party is rolling out a well-funded, grassroots campaign across regional and rural communities the country over.

Loading...

Housing and jobs in Central Queensland

Messaging around migration is resonating with homelessness advocate Cheryl Dolan.

"We don't have the houses to fit the population now at the minute," she said.

"So let's slow down the population until we can get the housing crisis in order."

Cheryl Dolan says there's a housing crisis in Central Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Ms Dolan previously voted Labor but switched to One Nation at the last election, saying she had lost faith in the major parties.

"I have to agree with Pauline," she said.

" She's for putting Australians first. "

Housing, economic pressures and energy policy are the key issues drawing regional people to One Nation according to Rob Manwaring, an associate professor in business, law and government at Flinders University.

"Voters who think that the economic climate is more pessimistic, and are more downbeat, are far more likely to vote for a minor party, including One Nation," Dr Manwaring said.

James Ashby has lived in Central Queensland for roughly a decade. (ABC News: Jasmine Hines)

One Nation has long had a presence in central Queensland and the new billboard is a literal sign this area is once again in its sights.

Pauline Hanson's chief of staff, James Ashby, lives on the Capricorn Coast and ran unsuccessfully for the seat of Keppel in the 2024 state election.

In last year's federal election One Nation picked up 22.6 per cent of the vote in Capricornia on the three candidate preferred count.

And the party has confirmed it's now got approval to open a new office in the electorate.

Tanya Edwards would like to see less red tape for small businesses. (Supplied: Tanya Edwards)

Tanya Edwards owns a real estate company nearby and says she's worried about the economy.

She says Senator Hanson's "fish and chip shop credentials" have given her faith that the senator knows the needs of regional businesses.

"Everything just keeps going up, all our subscriptions, taxes, rents, electricity," she said.

" Everything just keeps getting more expensive and we've just got to keep paying more tax. "

How economy might look like under One Nation From interest rates to policy advice from billionaire buddy Gina Rinehart, here is how One Nation's economic platform could look.

Coal-mining country in One Nation's sight

More than 500 kilometres south of the Queensland border, energy is shaping up to be a key issue for One Nation voters in the coal mining heartland of Singleton, New South Wales.

It's the second-largest town in the seat of Hunter, long held by Labor, but where miner Stuart Bonds is one of Pauline's most recognisable federal candidates.

"No-one gave us a snowflake's chance in hell," Mr Bonds said.

"We've had a really strong presence in the Hunter Valley and it's not going anywhere."

Stuart Bonds came second after preferences in the federal seat of Hunter at the 2025 election. (ABC News: Bridget Murphy)

The mostly blue-collar electorate, inland of Newcastle, was retained by Labor's Dan Repacholi, who secured 59 per cent of the post-preference vote in last year's federal election.

But Stuart Bonds leapfrogged the Nationals and came in second after preferences at 41 per cent, with a six-point swing on first preferences.

Mr Bonds is a vocal proponent of One Nation's policy to expand coal and gas mining as well as scrapping net zero.

"What is going to stop and kill this industry is the government," he said.

"Government regulation and red tape and this ideological belief that we can change the weather here in Australia by digging out a bit less coal."

Rob Manwaring's research is in the areas of political science and public policy. (ABC News: Malcolm Sutton)

Dr Manwaring says One Nation is using "issue ownership" tactics on energy and climate to try to leverage an advantage.

"[It's] where a political party tries to capture a particular issue and claim it as their own," he said.

"The base of One Nation is particularly amongst tradies and those in blue-collar sectors, and particularly in the mining sector.

"These are messages that are going to resonate really well with that community."

Migration and the One Nation vote

Anti-migration sentiment has long been central to Pauline Hanson's politics, and it comes up in conversations about housing and the economy.

She recently attracted controversy for being interviewed on a podcast by Tommy Robinson, a far-right activist in the UK and a convicted criminal.

When asked about mass deportation on Channel Seven's Spotlight program, she said: "Oh, I love it."

She later said that she only wanted to target "the ones who are here illegally in this country".

Pauline Hanson appeared on Tommy Robinson's podcast during a trip to the UK. (YouTube)

But Dr Manwaring says migration isn't the number one issue for voters.

He believes anti-migration policies may only shore up One Nation's base and won't shift votes to the party.

"Some of the research and evidence we have suggests it's not the only issue, or perhaps one of a number of important issues," he said.

"It only ranks about third behind these economic kinds of questions."

Darumbal woman Aunty Sally Vea Vea is an Indigenous elder on the Capricorn Coast.

She says One Nation's messaging around multiculturalism is harmful.

"It's divisive politics," she said.

"Multiculturalism is what makes Australia a beautiful country of all the different nationalities and Indigenous people and all those who come to live on our country."

Darumbal elder Aunty Sally Vea Vea believes One Nation's politics will cause division. (ABC News: Jasmine Hines)

In a statement, a One Nation spokesperson said it was "on the record in our support for working holiday maker visas and the PALM scheme, which assist in meeting agricultural labour demand".

"We enjoy strong support from Australia's agricultural sector and do not significantly increase housing demand or constitute permanent immigration," it said.

Political outsider gets mainstream support

Pauline Hanson has attracted the support of Australia's richest person, Gina Rinehart.

Despite this, political historian Benjamin Jones says she has retained her status as a political outsider.

He says it's helped her build support in Central Queensland in particular.

Benjamin Jones says grievance politics have been successful for populist parties. (Supplied: Benjamin Jones)

"Queensland, perhaps more than any other state, is decentralised and already has a sense of us versus them," Dr Jones said.

"So there already is that sense of being an outsider. That marries nicely with the One Nation brand of being the outsiders."

Dr Manwaring says financial support like Gina Rinehart's is crucial to the party's growth in the regions.

"What this means is the party will have some significant resources to professionalise, set up local offices, and organise volunteers," he said.

Another factor Dr Manwaring says will help fill One Nation's coffers is election funding.

After its performance in the 2025 federal election, One Nation received more than $6 million in taxpayer funds out of a total of $90 million paid to political parties.

Gina Rinehart has gifted Pauline Hanson serious political donations and a toy bulldozer. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki )

The battle for the bush

One Nation has taken full advantage of the collapse in support of Coalition parties.

Major opinion polls reveal one in four Australians support the party, peaking at 31 per cent last month.

This week's Newspoll has One Nation back at 30 per cent.

Given support for the party is higher in the bush, Dr Manwaring believes it could pick up more than a third of Australia's bush seats in 2028.

"On the basis of some of the modelling I've seen, where there's a seat which would be down to a One Nation versus Labour two-party or two candidate preferred vote, then there are estimations that One Nation could pick up around about 30–35 of those regional seats," he said.

Pauline Hanson gave her first National Press Club address this year, pledging to "end multiculturalism". (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

But politics expert Jim Jose, an emeritus professor from the University of Newcastle, says between now and the next election, voters will want to see solutions to their grievances.

"Eventually people have to start thinking about and will start thinking about, 'Well, how do we solve this? Does One Nation have the answers that we're seeking?'" he said.

"Even in the regions, people recognise some of the things that One Nation stands for are going to be counterproductive."

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb Stan Choe July 23, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is drifting in mixed trading, while oil prices climb another 3 per cent as fighting continues in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 slipped less than 0.1 per cent, coming off its best day in three weeks, after swinging between modest losses and gains for much of the day. The Dow Jones was up 61 points, or 0.1 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street swung between gains and losses throughout the session. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures pointing to a gain of 75 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.99¢. The majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rose after more companies reported strong profits for the spring. Expectations are high for the reports, and companies will need to match them after their stock prices already neared records on anticipation for them.



Philip Morris International rose 2.4 per cent after the seller of Marlboro cigarettes reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Its shipments of smoke-free products rose 7.5 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AT&T climbed 2.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected. CEO John Stankey also said the telecom is accelerating plans to send roughly $US10 billion ($14.3 billion) to its shareholders this year through the buybacks of its stock. Super Micro Computer soared 21.1 per cent after the seller of AI servers said it expects to report stronger profit margins for the latest quarter than it had earlier forecast. It, though, also said that revenue will likely come in at the low end of its forecasted range of $US11 billion to $US12.5 billion. They helped offset a 7.9 per cent drop for GE Vernova, which reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Alphabet ticked 0.1 per cent higher ahead of its earnings report, which is scheduled to arrive after trading ends for the day. Anticipation is high, and not just because the parent company of Google is one of the largest stocks on Wall Street. It’s also one of the biggest spenders on artificial-intelligence technology. Investors are looking for signs that the deluge of dollars going into processors, computer memory and other building blocks of the AI boom are producing the kinds of productivity and profits that would make the investments worth it. If that isn’t the case, stocks of chip companies and other AI winners would look very expensive following their rushes higher. Such worries have kept AI stocks at the center of Wall Street’s swings for weeks. Micron Technology swung between a loss of 3.6 per cent and a gain of 0.8 per cent Wednesday. That’s after it jumped 14.4 per cent in the first two days of this week to reclaim nearly all its 13.3 per cent plunge from the week before. It’s still up roughly 241 per cent for the year so far. Stocks broadly also felt pressure from continuing climbs for oil prices, which raise costs for most businesses and erode their profits.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 3.3 per cent to $US94 after briefly topping $US95 in the morning to touch its highest price in nearly six weeks. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing It’s News Corp v the ‘byte burglars’: Murdochs fire up in AI content battle Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Rising oil prices are threatening a reacceleration of inflation. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.66 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Tuesday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. It’s already helped bring long-term US mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year. Oil prices have climbed as fighting across the Middle East keeps oil tankers from using the Strait of Hormuz to exit the Persian Gulf. Normally, a fifth of all oil and natural gas traded passes through the narrow strait.



The auto club AAA said Wednesday that the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the US jumped again overnight to $US4.06. That’s still below highs of around $US4.56 per gallon in May, but it had been below $US3 before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. In stock markets abroad, indexes climbed in Europe following a mixed session in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman Long before she started her eponymous fashion label or her more recent role as kikki.K creative director, the designer learnt a lesson that’s served her well in life. Jane Rocca July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I meet Lisa Gorman inside kikki.K’s new retail store in Fitzroy, in the heart of Melbourne’s cosmopolitan inner north. A vintage workshop bench greets you on arrival – it feels more co-working space than retail – and it’s where they’ll host masterclasses, the first being a sketch series inspired by a calligraphy book that Gorman’s father gave her when she was eight years old. A cash register anchors the lifestyle and stationery brand’s space in a nod to preserve the past, while a moss-green cork floor screams of her love of ’80s decor. There’s a lived-in, homely feel here: a space where Gorman invites you to linger longer. Oh, and the green racks are the same shade as her Laminex kitchen at home, while oranges and browns in the retail space also show her allegiance to bygone eras. Kikki.K’s Lisa Gorman: “Heading up the rejuvenation of a known and existing brand nowadays requires a very different approach than what was required to start a label in the ’90s.” Peter Tarasiuk You’ll find journals, pens, and mix-and-match covers on display, but garments also feature throughout: pops of lemon-coloured denim, shrub-green jeans and hard-yakka blue tones are curated alongside boxy knits, shirts and jackets that show us Gorman the fashion designer, version 2.0, is back. Gorman has been kikki.K’s creative director for three years now and setting up shop on Gertrude Street is the latest move under her watch. It’s a role she came to after leaving her eponymous brand in 2021, her signature bright prints having established her as one of Australia’s most popular fashion designers.



During her tenure, Gorman has doubled down on kikki.K’s distinctive stationery, developed its travel accessories and introduced some fashion into the mix. Now, she’s hoping to tap into the love of neighbourhood shopping with kikki.K’s first foray into the high street – a notable shift from shopping centres, where the brand’s outlets have long resided. Gorman outside kikki.K’s first “high street” shop. Peter Tarasiuk Gorman has been instrumental in shaping the look and feel of the new retail space. Fitzroy is familiar stomping ground for Gorman, who has lived in the neighbourhood for 20 years with her husband, Dean Angelucci – a mid-century furniture dealer who owns a store around the corner on Smith Street – and their two daughters, now aged 17 and 20. Wearing a cinnamon jumpsuit that she designed (it’ll be available in-store from August), Gorman says the decision to join the high street was not accidental timing; there have been many discussions around how to grow a brand and introduce new fans at a time when brand loyalty is dwindling. “The focus on community and localised shopping is what we’re about,” says Gorman. “While shopping centres are a really important part of retail in Australia, and have been for the best part of 30 to 40 years, there’s a shift happening in the way people shop. Gertrude Street felt like the spot to move into and give this a go.



“Fitzroy is where I live, work and have traded over the years, so I understand the area and enjoy the product mix in this street. This felt really homely for us. It’s popular with locals and tourists, it has a mix of independent designer labels, such as from my best friend Megan Park to Northside Records; it’s a nostalgia trip for me. It’s a textured street that made sense to be part of.” Gorman (at right) with a model at the 2006 Australian Fashion Week. AAP Fashion has quietly found its place in kikki.K under Gorman, but it’s less about high volume; it feels more like the Benetton era of the 1980 and 1990s. “We’re not about putting out a new collection every four weeks and being stuck in the fashion cycle,” Gorman says. “That’s not useful anymore; people are focusing on building a wardrobe that lasts longer. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns, such as the classic bandanna or a simple plaid. I am also bringing coloured denim back. This reminds me of growing up in the ’80s. There are barrel jean shapes, cropped oversized denim jackets and patching – it’s an ode to the time that reminds me of my childhood.” Lisa Gorman has added colourful apparel to kikki.K’s range. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns,” she says. @kikki.k/Instagram



That childhood was spent in the Victorian coastal town of Warrnambool. Gorman is the eldest of four daughters, and she went on to become a nurse before becoming a fashion designer. She followed in the footsteps of her late father, Brian, who went back to TAFE to study English when she was in high school. (English was one of the requirements needed for him to become a nurse.) He had left school at 14 to go to work to help support his mum and siblings. Gorman’s maternal relatives worked at Warrnambool’s Fletcher Jones: her grandfather was the company’s accountant while her mother, Jane, and aunts all worked on the department’s shop floor. Fabric swatches became a part-time obsession; the warp and weft would inspire her own solo exhibition, Fluorescence, held at Warrnambool Art Gallery three years ago. Related Article Fashion designers The women who walked away from fashion to find something more As a child, Gorman loved sewing clothes for her Barbie dolls with her sisters. They’d fill Tupperware bowls with hand-sewn rah-rah (ruffled, tiered) skirts and boob-tube tops for their imaginary poolside Barbie runway shows. She also spent hours at the kitchen table tracing calligraphy. “I am still quite analogue myself,” Gorman says. “I don’t use the Adobe suite. I still sketch, and it goes back to my time as a kid when I just loved that feeling of drawing.”



Gorman arrived in Melbourne in the 1990s to start work as a nurse at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. One day, strolling through the city after work, wearing her nursing whites and dreaming about fashion, she stumbled upon a sign in the window of the Mariana Hardwick bridal store on Bourke Street. “They were looking for two trainees,” she says. “What drew me in was the sheer scale and architecture of the [wedding] dresses, and the hours, thought and hand-finishing touches put into those sculptural pieces. I walked in, had a good chat with Mariana and got the job.” Gorman ultimately left nursing, but says her experiences at the time have stayed with her. “When I was 18, I was looking after a terminally ill girl of the same age who was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer,” Gorman says. “One day, she asked me to cut off her long hair and I remember sitting at the end of her bed and thinking, this woman is my age – it didn’t feel right. It was really eye-opening for me. ‘I’ve never been the type of person to let go of opportunities, so saying yes to this job felt right.’ Lisa Gorman “It was the first time I’d ever cared for someone my age that had a life that was about to be shortened. That moment gave me perspective like nothing else and that has always stuck with me. What I saw and experienced gave me such a level head when it came to the fashion industry. It kept everything in perspective and served me well in life.”



Gorman is adamant that letter-writing is not dead, and neither is keeping a journal – they’re both part of the increasing appreciation for slowing down and finding the analogue element in an age of digital fatigue. “People are returning to writing things down, so there’s still 100 per cent a place for paper in our society,” says Gorman. “But the value around paper is changing and we’d be fools not to realise that. Related Article Australian fashion What Gorman did next: the designer weaving new patterns “In this digital age, a quality notebook and pen are viewed almost as luxury items. It’s the time, thought and permanency that stationery can provide that I feel is the luxury in paper these days, and without it carrying a luxury price tag – at least not at kikki.K. The value is in what it provides to you, rather than what it costs you to buy.” Despite coming from the era of Australian fashion that gave us high-octane labels such as Sass & Bide and Zimmermann, Gorman has always been an advocate for applying a more measured pace to work and life. In her 20s, a two-week visit to New York turned into a stay that lasted a few years while she took on a number of jobs. Meanwhile, she says kikki.K’s DNA, which lies in its heritage of quality stationery, is firmly staying put. She’s well versed in running a business, having done so for 21 years, and has quietly found her feet at the helm of kikki.K, which is celebrating 25 years of operation after being bought out from voluntary administration in 2020.

World.title: There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder
World.content:
InspirationNew Zealand There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder Natasha Bazika July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anyone who has ever flown business class knows the real luxury isn’t the wider seat or the gourmet meals (though they’re definitely perks). It’s the curtain, a visual barrier that separates you from the frantic, elbow-to-elbow situation of the main cabin. RealNZ and Altitude Tours have essentially pulled that velvet curtain across the day trip from Queenstown to Milford Sound with their new premium tour, Milford Sound Business Class. Milford Sound on the MV Sinbad. The upgrade starts at 7.30am. Instead of the typical 50-seat coach, I’m in a 14-seat Mercedes Sprinter. A lambswool blanket is left on my seat and a ginger tonic waits in the pocket, a preemptive strike against the notoriously winding roads ahead. Our driver, Ash, handles the two-hour stretch to Te Anau with a running commentary of fast facts. My favourite is the Maori legend of Lake Wakatipu, New Zealand’s longest lake, said to have been formed by the burning body of a giant taniwha named Matau. “Some say you can still see his heart beating with the rise and fall of the lake level,” she says over the microphone. “It pulses around 12 centimetres every half hour.”



By our morning tea stop in Te Anau, I’m entirely sold on the road experience. But the weight of the $NZ699 ($575) a person ticket rests on the cruise and the five-course tasting menu. To deliver it, they’ve partnered with chef Tom Hishon from Auckland’s acclaimed seafood restaurant, kingi, to bring the sensibility of a high-end urban restaurant and set it afloat in the middle of Fiordland. 



I sit down for a course, spot a waterfall spilling down the cliffs, and run to the top deck. I come down for the next dish, paua served in-shell with black garlic, only for the captain to steer us beneath Stirling Falls moments later for what she calls a “glacial facial”. Another few bites arrive, Mount Cook Alpine caviar served on a potato rosti with sour cream and a Titi (muttonbird) croquette with a delightful citrus spin. The menu is by chef Tom Hishon of the acclaimed Auckland restaurant kingi. For the main, we scoop up Fiordland wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps, and swallow in one bite smoked eel under a slice of beetroot. The windows at each table frame the landscape, but on this unusually bright day, they mostly reflect glare and streaks of salt. Besides, no one comes to Milford Sound to stare at it through a window. Someone shouts “dolphins!” at the bow, and every passenger clears out. No one comes back in a hurry, prompting the staff to bring dessert up instead, a flat white-inspired dish served in a glass.



The food is well executed, exactly what you would expect from Hishon, but the portions are too light for a 12-hour day. That becomes most obvious during the optional wine pairing, where generous pours arrive, two at a time, alongside one-bite courses. Related Article Opinion

Adventure holidays I went on my first big hike in my 40s. It changed the way I see travel Bianca O'Neill Contributor Drinking like that on an empty stomach before a three-hour drive back to Queenstown is a tough sell. For a faster return, you can skip the road and fly back by plane ($NZ500) or helicopter ($NZ1000), but that doesn’t fix the issue. There just isn’t quite enough food for the day. A more substantial main would have made a real difference here. Those of us who skip the scenic flight back load onto the van and find a packet of chips and a chocolate bar waiting on our seats. The crinkle of packets being opened and finished fills the van before we’ve even passed the edge of the national park. THE DETAILS



CRUISE

RealNZ Milford Sound Business Class starts from $NZ699 a person and includes return transfers from selected Queenstown accommodation, morning tea and coffee in Te Anau, a five-course tasting menu, and a two-hour Milford Sound cruise. Guests can upgrade to a scenic fixed-wing flight back from around $NZ500, or a helicopter flight with optional alpine landing from around $NZ1000, weather permitting. The optional wine pairing is $NZ65 a person, payable on the day. See realnz.com STAY

QT Queenstown (qthotels.com) has rooms from around $NZ450 a night. In Te Anau, Tasman Holiday Parks (tasmanholidayparks.com) has self-contained cabins, apartments and powered sites; one-bedroom apartments from around $NZ275 a night. See tasmanholidayparks.com; qthotels.com/queenstown FLY

Air New Zealand, Qantas and Virgin Australia operate direct flights from Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne to Queenstown. HIRE CAR

Snap Rentals has a branch five minutes from Queenstown Airport with a free shuttle service. It’s also one of the few rental companies offering one-way hires, so you don’t need to return the car to Queenstown if you plan to drive elsewhere. See snaprentals.co.nz The writer travelled as a guest of Luxury New Zealand Collection. See luxurynewzealandcollection.com

World.title: Inside Queensland’s bid to claw back $66 million from Fortescue
World.content:
Queensland lost several economic opportunities, including the potential to foster an emerging export hydrogen industry worth $1.7 billion a year, the state government will argue as part of its $66 million claim against mining giant Fortescue. The government has now called in several experts, including major consulting firm KordaMentha, to prove its economic loss in its fight against Fortescue, owned by iron ore billionaire Andrew Forrest. Fortescue is fighting against claims it breached its funding agreement with the state for its green hydrogen facility in Gladstone, central Queensland. Fortescue boss Andrew Forrest in Gladstone alongside former premier Annastacia Palaszczuk and her then deputy, Steven Miles. The resources giant dumped the project at the same time it canned a similar one in Arizona in 2025, when US President Donald Trump slashed tax breaks for clean energy investments.



The Queensland site has previously been described as a “vanity project” and a “terrible deal” by Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie. Related Article Exclusive

Energy ‘Dud project’: How Andrew Forrest’s green dreams cost taxpayers $80m As part of Supreme Court documents filed in recent weeks and seen by this masthead, the state has indicated it will file an amended claim. An order made by the court late last month gave Fortescue until July 22 to apply to have the new claim struck out. The government has indicated it would argue for damages based on claims that it lost multiple economic opportunities, including the potential to foster an emerging hydrogen industry worth $1.7 billion in exports annually, according to recent submissions. If Fortescue had upheld its end of the deal, it would have meant the electrolyser manufacturing facility would have continued to operate until 2032, Queensland claims.



That facility would have enabled Queensland to potentially become a global leader in the production of green hydrogen for export. Queensland would also have been well placed to capture the opportunity of future increases in international demand for green hydrogen, according to the documents. A former government source familiar with Fortescue’s original pitch but not authorised to speak on the record told this masthead the mining giant said the project would support 48 ongoing high-end manufacturing roles. Andrew Forrest and former Labor leader Annastacia Palaszczuk in 2021. Queensland was also told the site at Aldoga, central Queensland, could potentially lead to the company securing various future projects, such as manufacturing for battery, wind turbines, cables and solar power systems. In the state government’s claim, it said the development of the industry in Queensland would have enabled it to capture emerging large-scale hydrogen markets in Asia, particularly in South Korea and Japan.



The state said it had become apparent following a first review hearing of the case that Fortescue had “misconstrued” the nature of the government’s case, which was that it would seek to prove the economic benefits flagged from helping to get the industry off the ground were reasonably expected. The funding agreement came after Fortescue sent a letter to the government in May 2021 regarding the project, to which the state responded that Fortescue’s plan aligned closely with Queensland’s policy priorities. The proposed manufacturing facility near Gladstone. The agreement came against a backdrop of the then Labor government, led by Annastacia Palaszczuk, implementing the Queensland Advanced Manufacturing 10-year road map and action plan. According to Supreme Court documents, the then premier said: “Now the world is looking to hydrogen, and we want them to get it from Queensland so we can create even more jobs in our regions.”



Palaszczuk also spoke of the emerging industry having enormous economic benefits for Australia, pointing to the $1.7 billion export figure. Fortescue claims, however, the government has no leg to stand on. It says the funding agreement did not refer to the Hydrogen Industry Strategy or the 10-year road map. In launching its defence, the company said the alleged loss and damage did not flow from the claimed breach of the funding agreement. Fortescue said the Hydrogen Industry Strategy was only expressed to apply between 2019 and 2024 and came to an end in 2024.



Related Article Investigation

Philanthropy ‘Next shiny thing’: Inside Twiggy Forrest’s $7 billion charity “The state would have, in any event, abandoned the Hydrogen Industry Strategy as it, in fact, did in or around October 2024, or alternatively February 2025, or alternatively October 2025,” documents filed on behalf of Fortescue state. Those dates coincided with the October 2024 state election, which resulted in a change of government. The new administration, under LNP leader David Crisafulli, removed the strategy from the government’s website. According to Fortescue, in February 2025, the state withdrew financial support for the Central Queensland Hydrogen Hub – the state’s flagship $12.4 billion green hydrogen project led by Stanwell Corporation. And in October 2025, the state released the Queensland Energy Roadmap, which made no mention of any hydrogen industry policies. “The state would have, in any event, abandoned the 10-year road map as it, in fact, did in or around September 2025,” the documents state.



Fortescue also pointed to how in September 2025, the state released the Transforming Queensland Manufacturing Strategy 2025-30, which made no reference to any hydrogen industry strategies and said the state had not suffered the alleged loss because it had obtained the benefit of at least $37,222,506 in site work costs from stage 1 of the project. The company’s legal team also questioned why another company would not take up the commercial opportunity at the site, and it pressed the state as to why it would not take up the opportunity, given that it had now exercised the buyback right. The industrial site in central Queensland remains abandoned and there are no current plans to either sell or contract a new company to work there, this masthead has confirmed. According to documents recently filed by the state, the government’s identified witnesses to be brought in would include an economic expert to analyse the financial benefits that were expected to flow to Queensland from the agreement. The state said it had already engaged Synergies Economic Consulting to provide an expert economic report, in addition to KordaMentha’s expert accounting context.



Other expected witnesses include a hydrogen industry expert to give evidence concerning the market and potential market for the electrolyser technology and for green hydrogen internationally, both at the time the agreement was entered into and the likely trajectory and future prospects of the market through to 2032 and beyond. The state’s documents say in the six months ending in December 2020, Fortescue had a net profit after tax of $US4.1 billion.
