World.title: I thought I was getting more open-minded as I got older. Until I saw this at the shops
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Opinion I thought I was getting more open-minded as I got older. Until I saw this at the shops Kerri Sackville Columnist and author July 23, 2026 — 5:00am

July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As I have edged past middle age and moved towards, well, later middle age, I have noticed myself becoming less judgmental. I don’t care about a person’s life choices, as long as they are nice human and do no harm to others. Just the other day, for example, I was listening to a podcast about polyamory as I was climbing the escalator at my local Westfield. Wouldn’t be my cup of tea, I thought, as a woman described her relationships with her three partners, but hey, good for her! As I congratulated myself on my open-mindedness, I spotted a man standing on the wrong side of the escalator, blocking my path. What a moron, I thought, as I stomped pointedly around him. How hard is it to stand to the left? Live and let live? Sure. Just don’t stand on the wrong side of the escalator. iStock I realised, at that moment, that I have found myself in a rather contradictory state of mind. As much as I wholeheartedly accept people from all walks of life, I will turn on them in an instant if they inconvenience me in any way.



I am both wonderfully compassionate and intensely intolerant. You breastfed your son until he was eight and you only eat white foods? My, how fascinating. You do you! You stand stock still on the wrong side of the escalator? I want to call the police and have you banned from the shops. Life is tough, so whatever brings you joy or fulfillment is fine, whether it is selling jewellery made from semen (it’s a thing!) or marrying a chatbot on your phone. KERRI SACKVILLE You identify as a Wiccan and changed your name to Goddess Spirit Love? Cool, sounds interesting, tell me about it. You ride an e-bike without a helmet with your mate on the back? I want to scream at you for your idiocy and smack you in the head. I truly do not care what lifestyle you adopt, as long as it does not impact negatively on others. Life is tough, so whatever brings you joy or fulfillment is fine, whether it is selling jewellery made from semen (it’s a thing!) or marrying a chatbot on your phone. But life is also short and people’s choices keep impacting negatively on me! And I don’t want to waste a minute of the (increasingly limited) time I have left on this planet being stuck behind some dude standing on the wrong side of the escalator, or veering out of the way of a cyclist who is riding without a bloody helmet in peak-hour traffic.



I don’t want to be so intolerant of other human beings. I want to be a good and serene person, particularly as I get older. I don’t want to be that grumpy old lady who mutters angrily at passers-by. I want to radiate love and acceptance for all. Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life The day I offered to cut my partner’s hair marked our first fight. It’s still going Kerri Sackville Columnist and author And I’d be able to, if the other people in the world weren’t so insanely irritating. Drivers who fail to let me into their lane. Customers who make interminable small talk with the cashier while I’m standing in a queue behind them. Acquaintances who post ridiculous conspiracy theories online, clogging up my Facebook feed with their nonsense. Patrons who get out their phones in the cinemas and distract me when I’m watching a movie. Groups of pedestrians hogging the footpath when I’m on my morning walk. Neighbours who put food scraps in the yellow recycle bin instead of the green. The list goes on. They all make me incensed. I know what the younger people would say because three of them are my children, and they say it to me. They’d say, “Hey, Boomer, don’t sweat the small stuff!” (And for the record, I’m not a Boomer, I’m Gen X, thank you very much.)



Thing is, though, the small stuff is all I can sweat. The big stuff is just too big. I have worked very hard in recent times not to dwell too much on massive, intractable problems. Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life How far would you go to retrieve a missing phone? As far as it takes, I learnt Kerri Sackville Columnist and author Perhaps my aggravation at minor inconveniences is just redirected anger at the state of the world. Perhaps the rage I feel at the woman who didn’t clean up her dog poop is actually sublimated rage at climate change and the evils of technology. Perhaps my urge to hunt down the call-centre operator who disconnected me after I’d been on hold for 23 minutes is simply displaced grief at global conflicts and injustices. Or perhaps I really am just a grumpy old lady, all out of patience after 57 years of life on this chaotic planet among this crazy species. Either way, be careful if you see me at the shops. I will honour your gender identity. I will respect your religious beliefs. I will not judge your sexual preferences or your parenting style or your appearance or your work. But if you push in front of me in a queue, or take too long to order your coffee, or let your silly dog lick my ankles, or block the supermarket aisle with your trolley, you’d better be prepared for the consequences.



I will roll my eyes at you. I will sigh. I will mutter. Watch out. I am going to be cross. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning. Sign up here for our free newsletter.

World.title: If you love Neil Diamond, you’ll love this show. Just try not to sing along
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a blustery Monday morning, and inside Opera Australia’s Southbank rehearsal studios, the cast and crew of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical are starting their second week of rehearsals. About a dozen young dancers in exercise gear are working with associate choreographer Yasmine Lee, traversing the space in exaggerated, slow-motion movements. In the rehearsal space next door, associate director Austin Regan is giving notes to the cast as they run scenes. The show opens with an elderly Diamond (Terence Crawford), talking to a psychologist about being depressed that his failing health – the singer was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2018 – has put an end to his touring career. As he muses that songwriting gave him a ticket out of the working-class Brooklyn neighbourhood of Flatbush, the music changes, with the background piano chords suddenly turning into the instantly recognisable opening of Diamond’s 1967 hit, Shilo. With the first preview about three weeks away, the cast members are fizzing with energy. Dancers during rehearsals for A Beautiful Noise. Justin McManus A Beautiful Noise would never have come about were it not for another musical biopic, Jersey Boys, the story of the Four Seasons – Frankie Valli, Tommy DeVito, Nick Massi and Bob Gaudio. When Gaudio, a friend of Diamond’s, left the Four Seasons, he became a record producer, producing some of Diamond’s biggest hits. A Beautiful Noise musical supervisor Sonny Paladino says: “Neil was a fan of Jersey Boys, and he saw it a bunch in New York. And one time he said to Bob afterwards, ‘Could I have one of these?’” Music supervisor Sonny Paladino watches rehearsals. Justin McManus The answer was yes. But with 38 top 40 singles and 33 studio albums, winnowing down Diamond’s back catalogue for the show was a daunting task. “What makes this musical work so well is that there’s nothing superfluous,” Paladino says. “If the song is in the show, it has to be part of the show and make the audience care about what’s happening.



“Even in act two, we do a sequence that we call stadium medley, where he’s basically touring the world as he did, and even those songs are part of the narrative. There’s a great song called Heartlight, which we tried to get in there, but it just didn’t work.” Plenty of songs did make the cut, though – there are 25 tracks on the soundtrack, and a few are medleys. The musical opened in Boston in 2022 and has been touring the US since. Audience members turn up in tour T-shirts, aware that this is the closest they will get to seeing the man himself perform. Will Swenson told his agent to be on the lookout for a Neil Diamond musical. Justin McManus “I think a lot of people are coming to see the show, particularly just to have like a Neil concert experience,” says Will Swenson, who plays Diamond as a young man and is the only import in the Australian cast. “It was weird for me to just go out, first notes out of my mouth and have the audience completely won over and happy and screaming, and it threw me. “But I was like, ‘Oh, this is love for Neil, and I’m just this lucky guy that gets to be the recipient of all of this adoration.’ I will happily take it. But it’s a head trip to go like, ‘Oh wait, Will, you didn’t earn this. Neil earned this, and you are standing in his shoes to get to receive it.’ Neil Diamond performing in Sydney in 2005 Domino Postiglione “Neil Diamond was my dad’s favourite singer of all time,” Swenson says. “I knew these songs when I was six years old.”



But if it’s one thing to perform these songs in front of 1200 Neil Diamond fans a night on Broadway, it’s very different performing them in front of the man himself, as Swenson did in a tiny room in Nashville. “He just sat five feet away from me, and we played through the songs and read the script, just hoping that he would like it enough. It was one of the more surreal things I’ve ever done in my life. It was completely nerve-wracking, and luckily, about halfway through, he started raising his hand and started singing along and you’re like, ‘oh, I think he likes it’.” Related Article Performing arts Waitress is gone, Beetlejuice too. Where is the next Hamilton? Diamond isn’t the only one singing along. As anyone who has ever heard Sweet Caroline in a pub knows, it’s impossible not to join in the “ba ba ba!″⁣s. “We were careful crafting the show because it is a musical,” Regan says. “It’s not a concert, so we want people to be able to engage with the story and the play of it, but there are some moments where we know you have to release the pressure valve and let people sing along because how could you not with Song Sung Blue and with Sweet Caroline and all these songs? They’re iconic melodies, and you can’t help but join in.” The show ran on Broadway for just under two years, where, as in Australia, musical theatre has struggled to find its feet after lockdowns. The New York Times reported late last year that only three musicals that had opened since the pandemic had made a profit. A Beautiful Noise was not one of them. “We would have loved to have run longer, but I think we were all really, really proud that we got almost two years out of the show,” says Regan. “Most shows these days close after just a few months. It’s very, very hard to make a show work on Broadway, and I think of all the musicals in our season we ran the second longest of any production, which feels pretty great.”

World.title: ‘This is just the beginning’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.73m
World.content:
PropertyNewsSydney house prices ‘This is just the beginning’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.73m Alice Uribe July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost to buy the typical Sydney property has started to fall over recent months, with buyers beginning to get the upper hand as muted confidence, affordability pressures and higher interest rates combine to dent the property market. Sydney’s median house price dropped 3.3 per cent, or about $60,000 over three months to December to $1,733,891, the latest Domain House Price Report, released on Thursday, showed. This was a fall from the previous quarter’s record high and the largest fall of all the capital cities. Over the year, house price growth slowed to 1.1 per cent. The city’s median unit price was also down, falling 1.5 per cent to $849,068 over the quarter to June. This was also a drop from the previous quarter’s peak and the first quarterly decline in two years. Over the year, growth eased to 2.5 per cent.



Three rate hikes had affected borrowing capacity, while cost of living pressures and weak consumer sentiment was helping to constrain activity. Recent falls are signalling the “next stage” of the property cycle, Dr Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief residential economist, said. “This is just the beginning,” she said of negative growth. More drops are expected during 2026. Selling conditions in Sydney had weakened materially, Domain said. Clearance rates are at their lowest level since April 2020 (48 per cent), while withdrawn auctions were at a record 29.3 per cent. Powell said that alongside weaker clearance rates and withdrawn auction levels, there were longer selling times, higher discounting and rising supply.



“The element of increased choice is just taking that urgency away from buyers, and giving them the power,” she said. The federal budget in May introduced negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions reforms that Powell said would have a greater impact in markets such as Sydney, which has a larger proportion of investor activity than other states. “It’s vulnerable to changes in investor participation. And ultimately, I think we are going to see fewer investors partaking in Sydney’s housing market.” For first home buyers, too, there would be an “absolute element of caution to purchase in a falling market,” Powell said.



“Market conditions have shifted rapidly ... First time buyers are sensitive to changes in affordability, and we have to consider the mortgage serviceability aspect.” Independent economist Saul Eslake said even though the budget’s property reforms did not come into effect until July 1 next year, they were having an impact on the way people think about the property market and what they were doing in “anticipation of those changes”. Both investors and first home buyers are cautious about buying property in a falling market, experts say. James Brickwood This was at the same time, he added, as borrowing was becoming “significantly” more expensive thanks to higher interest rates, and banks were tipping further property price falls of between around 5 and 10 per cent nationally. “Given that there may well be another increase in interest rates as well, and the full effects of the changes to the tax system on investors are yet to play out, it would make sense for prospective buyers to hold back.”



Related Article NSW residential property ‘We never really needed to move’: Sydney suburbs where home owners stick around According to the latest Equifax Consumer Market Pulse, overall mortgage demand plunged 14 per cent over the year to June, driven by a 17.2 per cent drop in first home buyer applications. With affordability pressures ongoing, the areas recording the biggest declines in price over the past 12 months across Sydney have been at the upper end, while more affordable areas have retained buoyancy. The strongest median price growth for houses over the year to June was in the outer south west, up 12.5 per cent to $1,125,000) over the year. That was followed by the outer west and Blue Mountains (up 9.4 per cent to $1,110,000). By comparison, it was North Sydney and Hornsby which fell the most, dropping 12.1 per cent to $2,767,500. Despite a downturn, every region of Sydney still has a median house price of at least $1 million.



For units, the biggest growth for the same period was on the Central Coast – part of Greater Sydney – up 11.9 per cent to $730,000, followed by the outer south west, which jumped 10.3 per cent to $642,500. Alana Pasikala, 25, recently bought a one-bedroom apartment in the St George area after realising that repayments may not be much more than her rent, which had spiked over recent years. Even so, the aviation people leader, who started looking for a property in January after getting her pre-approval, noticed a high level of competition. She noticed queues to view properties and steepening prices over the course of her hunt. First home buyer Alana Pasikala avoided auctions on her property hunt. STEVEN SIEWERT



“When you’re a first-time buyer, auctions are quite difficult … so I completely avoided auctions,” she said. “For the properties I was looking at, they were going for more than what they were initially advertised, or asking for, at that time.” Pasikala, who is soon moving into her new home, is happy she stayed within her budget after putting in offers for a few properties. “Ultimately, it’s a step in the right direction for something for myself, and my future.” Pasikala says buying a unit in the St George area was a “step in the right direction” for her future. STEVEN SIEWERT



The more affordable parts of Sydney, Powell said, were likely to remain firmer in price and may even see modest rates of price growth. “I think it says a lot about who is active and the lack of affordable supply,” she said. “The upper end of the market is leading the downturn.” Related Article NSW residential property ‘A bit more laid-back’: The family-friendly Sydney suburb that soared Julian Finch, principal mortgage broker at Finch Financial Services who worked with Pasikala, said inquiries for all types of lending had “quieted down exponentially” since the federal budget after a stronger start to 2026. “I think what we’ve got is just a situation where everybody’s lost confidence in what the market is doing,” he said. “The reality is, of course, the buyers are in a stronger position to negotiate, or at least take their time.”



As the property cycle turns, NAB senior economist Taylor Nugent said the lender was forecasting Sydney house price declines of around 7 per cent over 2026. “At the moment, it would be fair to say that recent momentum suggests the risk might be to a slightly larger decline over the course of the year than that.”

World.title: Revealed: The NSW children spending years on psychiatry wait lists
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWMental health Revealed: The NSW children spending years on psychiatry wait lists Rachel Rasker July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content Ethan Annetts was 11 when he started self-harming. By the time he saw a psychiatrist, he was an adult and suicidal. Ethan spent years on the waitlist for an assessment, and was trapped in an unending cycle of hospital presentations and discharges without any ongoing care, his mother, Jo Cockle said. Jo Cockle’s children Ethan (left) and Grace have spent years waiting for child and adolescent psychiatric support. Wolter Peeters With no other options, an extremely distressed Cockle enrolled in suicide prevention classes herself. If she hadn’t: “I don’t think he’d be here,” she said.



NSW has the worst child and adolescent psychiatrist shortage in the country, a shortfall projected to almost double in the next two decades, a new analysis of federal government data revealed. The federal government’s Thriving Kids policy, which will shift demand from the NDIS to state-based services, risks exacerbating the problem, leaving more families without timely access to treatment, the peak body for psychiatrists has warned. Before medication, Ethan couldn’t leave his room. Now, he enjoys fishing in nature. Wolter Peeters An extra 64.3 full-time child and adolescent (CAD) psychiatrists are needed just to meet the current demand of families across NSW, found a report released by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. By 2048, that shortfall will have grown to 119, the report found.



The state’s psychiatrists shortage is almost triple that of Victoria’s, which needs an additional 21.5 full-time clinicians, it read. Nationwide, there is just one specialist for every 571 children with moderate to severe mental illness. Professor Valsamma Eapen, a psychiatrist who led the report, said resourcing constraints mean children can only access help after their condition has become severe, and Thriving Kids could “add more pressures onto the already stressed system”. Cockle put Ethan on a wait list to see a paediatrician when he was 13. “When he finally got called up, he was 17 and a half, and they actually said: We can no longer see you because you’re too old now,” Cockle said.



Ethan’s sister, 12-year-old Grace, was granted funding to see a specialised counsellor two years ago, but still hasn’t been given an appointment. “There aren’t any available, or if they are available, they’re full,” Cockle said. “It’s my job to provide for my children, and not being able to provide for their basic human rights, I can’t even put it into words. It’s heartbreaking,” she said. Jo (left) has studied suicide prevention and psychology to help her son and other vulnerable people. Wolter Peeters Dr Joel Killey, who ran a CAD psychiatric unit at a public hospital in Sydney’s north, said it was “frustrating, exhausting and quite sad” to see the mental health of young people deteriorate as they repeatedly returned to hospital with progressively severe presentations.





He hoped new NSW rules that allow trained GPs to prescribe ADHD medication will ease the burden on psychiatrists, and said investing in child and adolescent mental health provides “the biggest bang for our buck”. “If we get people when they’re in the early stages of their illness, that’s where we can have the biggest impact,” he said. “We can get them essentially back to normal levels of functioning, rather than having the morbidity that has occurred from long periods of untreated mental health problems.” In a statement, a federal government spokesperson said more than $2.8 billion is currently invested in youth mental health, including $490.3 million for 20 new psychiatrist-led youth specialist care centres across Australia, and training programs for specialist psychiatrists. NSW Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said in a statement that she recognised the growing demand, and acknowledged there was “always more work” needed to meet it. Jackson said her government had invested in recruitment, training and new models of care to strengthen the mental health workforce and improve access to support for children and young people. The report found that each additional full-time CAD psychiatrist generated an estimated $5.85 million in lifetime social and economic benefits, including reduced mental health system use, increased parental workforce participation due to a lower care burden, and improved education and lifetime productivity.



Related Article Mental health Carly couldn’t get the healthcare she needed. She almost didn’t make it home Thriving Kids will move children with mild-to-moderate developmental delays or autism off the NDIS and into state-based mental health systems. Autistic children are more likely to have a co-occuring mental health condition like anxiety, depression or ADHD, and the introduction of an early identification screening is also expected to lead to increased demand. The RANZCP said details about the transition have not been finalised, despite its rollout date of October 2026. “Where and how this will fit in, and how state interpreters are going to fund and deliver these services, is really not yet known,” Eapen said. A federal government spokesperson said, “significant implementation work has been completed” on Thriving Kids, while the NSW government said they were working closely with the Commonwealth and monitoring potential impacts on demand, access and wait times. Now that Ethan has been able to see a psychiatrist and get the right medication, “everything [is] a bit easier for me to handle in terms of getting a job, going to work, education, going to TAFE; I was able to do that stuff again,” he said.



“Life is a lot easier to manage with the right resources.” For urgent, free and confidential support, contact Lifeline on 13 11 14, Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636 or the NSW Mental Health Line on 1800 011 511. World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street mixed; Oil continues to climb Stan Choe July 23, 2026 — 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is drifting in mixed trading, while oil prices climb another 3 per cent as fighting continues in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 slipped less than 0.1 per cent, coming off its best day in three weeks, after swinging between modest losses and gains for much of the day. The Dow Jones was up 61 points, or 0.1 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street swung between gains and losses throughout the session. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to climb, with futures pointing to a gain of 75 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.99¢. The majority of stocks in the S&P 500 rose after more companies reported strong profits for the spring. Expectations are high for the reports, and companies will need to match them after their stock prices already neared records on anticipation for them.



Philip Morris International rose 2.4 per cent after the seller of Marlboro cigarettes reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Its shipments of smoke-free products rose 7.5 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist AT&T climbed 2.7 per cent after reporting a stronger profit than analysts expected. CEO John Stankey also said the telecom is accelerating plans to send roughly $US10 billion ($14.3 billion) to its shareholders this year through the buybacks of its stock. Super Micro Computer soared 21.1 per cent after the seller of AI servers said it expects to report stronger profit margins for the latest quarter than it had earlier forecast. It, though, also said that revenue will likely come in at the low end of its forecasted range of $US11 billion to $US12.5 billion. They helped offset a 7.9 per cent drop for GE Vernova, which reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.



Alphabet ticked 0.1 per cent higher ahead of its earnings report, which is scheduled to arrive after trading ends for the day. Anticipation is high, and not just because the parent company of Google is one of the largest stocks on Wall Street. It’s also one of the biggest spenders on artificial-intelligence technology. Investors are looking for signs that the deluge of dollars going into processors, computer memory and other building blocks of the AI boom are producing the kinds of productivity and profits that would make the investments worth it. If that isn’t the case, stocks of chip companies and other AI winners would look very expensive following their rushes higher. Such worries have kept AI stocks at the center of Wall Street’s swings for weeks. Micron Technology swung between a loss of 3.6 per cent and a gain of 0.8 per cent Wednesday. That’s after it jumped 14.4 per cent in the first two days of this week to reclaim nearly all its 13.3 per cent plunge from the week before. It’s still up roughly 241 per cent for the year so far. Stocks broadly also felt pressure from continuing climbs for oil prices, which raise costs for most businesses and erode their profits.



The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 3.3 per cent to $US94 after briefly topping $US95 in the morning to touch its highest price in nearly six weeks. That’s up from less than $US72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Related Article Opinion

Media & marketing It’s News Corp v the ‘byte burglars’: Murdochs fire up in AI content battle Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Rising oil prices are threatening a reacceleration of inflation. That in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.66 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Tuesday and from just 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran began. It’s already helped bring long-term US mortgage rates to their highest levels in nearly a year. Oil prices have climbed as fighting across the Middle East keeps oil tankers from using the Strait of Hormuz to exit the Persian Gulf. Normally, a fifth of all oil and natural gas traded passes through the narrow strait.



The auto club AAA said Wednesday that the average price for a gallon of regular gas in the US jumped again overnight to $US4.06. That’s still below highs of around $US4.56 per gallon in May, but it had been below $US3 before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. In stock markets abroad, indexes climbed in Europe following a mixed session in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 rose 1.2 per cent, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘That moment gave me perspective like nothing else’: The encounter that changed Lisa Gorman Long before she started her eponymous fashion label or her more recent role as kikki.K creative director, the designer learnt a lesson that’s served her well in life. Jane Rocca July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I meet Lisa Gorman inside kikki.K’s new retail store in Fitzroy, in the heart of Melbourne’s cosmopolitan inner north. A vintage workshop bench greets you on arrival – it feels more co-working space than retail – and it’s where they’ll host masterclasses, the first being a sketch series inspired by a calligraphy book that Gorman’s father gave her when she was eight years old. A cash register anchors the lifestyle and stationery brand’s space in a nod to preserve the past, while a moss-green cork floor screams of her love of ’80s decor. There’s a lived-in, homely feel here: a space where Gorman invites you to linger longer. Oh, and the green racks are the same shade as her Laminex kitchen at home, while oranges and browns in the retail space also show her allegiance to bygone eras. Kikki.K’s Lisa Gorman: “Heading up the rejuvenation of a known and existing brand nowadays requires a very different approach than what was required to start a label in the ’90s.” Peter Tarasiuk You’ll find journals, pens, and mix-and-match covers on display, but garments also feature throughout: pops of lemon-coloured denim, shrub-green jeans and hard-yakka blue tones are curated alongside boxy knits, shirts and jackets that show us Gorman the fashion designer, version 2.0, is back. Gorman has been kikki.K’s creative director for three years now and setting up shop on Gertrude Street is the latest move under her watch. It’s a role she came to after leaving her eponymous brand in 2021, her signature bright prints having established her as one of Australia’s most popular fashion designers.



During her tenure, Gorman has doubled down on kikki.K’s distinctive stationery, developed its travel accessories and introduced some fashion into the mix. Now, she’s hoping to tap into the love of neighbourhood shopping with kikki.K’s first foray into the high street – a notable shift from shopping centres, where the brand’s outlets have long resided. Gorman outside kikki.K’s first “high street” shop. Peter Tarasiuk Gorman has been instrumental in shaping the look and feel of the new retail space. Fitzroy is familiar stomping ground for Gorman, who has lived in the neighbourhood for 20 years with her husband, Dean Angelucci – a mid-century furniture dealer who owns a store around the corner on Smith Street – and their two daughters, now aged 17 and 20. Wearing a cinnamon jumpsuit that she designed (it’ll be available in-store from August), Gorman says the decision to join the high street was not accidental timing; there have been many discussions around how to grow a brand and introduce new fans at a time when brand loyalty is dwindling. “The focus on community and localised shopping is what we’re about,” says Gorman. “While shopping centres are a really important part of retail in Australia, and have been for the best part of 30 to 40 years, there’s a shift happening in the way people shop. Gertrude Street felt like the spot to move into and give this a go.



“Fitzroy is where I live, work and have traded over the years, so I understand the area and enjoy the product mix in this street. This felt really homely for us. It’s popular with locals and tourists, it has a mix of independent designer labels, such as from my best friend Megan Park to Northside Records; it’s a nostalgia trip for me. It’s a textured street that made sense to be part of.” Gorman (at right) with a model at the 2006 Australian Fashion Week. AAP Fashion has quietly found its place in kikki.K under Gorman, but it’s less about high volume; it feels more like the Benetton era of the 1980 and 1990s. “We’re not about putting out a new collection every four weeks and being stuck in the fashion cycle,” Gorman says. “That’s not useful anymore; people are focusing on building a wardrobe that lasts longer. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns, such as the classic bandanna or a simple plaid. I am also bringing coloured denim back. This reminds me of growing up in the ’80s. There are barrel jean shapes, cropped oversized denim jackets and patching – it’s an ode to the time that reminds me of my childhood.” Lisa Gorman has added colourful apparel to kikki.K’s range. “I’m inspired by nostalgic patterns,” she says. @kikki.k/Instagram



That childhood was spent in the Victorian coastal town of Warrnambool. Gorman is the eldest of four daughters, and she went on to become a nurse before becoming a fashion designer. She followed in the footsteps of her late father, Brian, who went back to TAFE to study English when she was in high school. (English was one of the requirements needed for him to become a nurse.) He had left school at 14 to go to work to help support his mum and siblings. Gorman’s maternal relatives worked at Warrnambool’s Fletcher Jones: her grandfather was the company’s accountant while her mother, Jane, and aunts all worked on the department’s shop floor. Fabric swatches became a part-time obsession; the warp and weft would inspire her own solo exhibition, Fluorescence, held at Warrnambool Art Gallery three years ago. Related Article Fashion designers The women who walked away from fashion to find something more As a child, Gorman loved sewing clothes for her Barbie dolls with her sisters. They’d fill Tupperware bowls with hand-sewn rah-rah (ruffled, tiered) skirts and boob-tube tops for their imaginary poolside Barbie runway shows. She also spent hours at the kitchen table tracing calligraphy. “I am still quite analogue myself,” Gorman says. “I don’t use the Adobe suite. I still sketch, and it goes back to my time as a kid when I just loved that feeling of drawing.”



Gorman arrived in Melbourne in the 1990s to start work as a nurse at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. One day, strolling through the city after work, wearing her nursing whites and dreaming about fashion, she stumbled upon a sign in the window of the Mariana Hardwick bridal store on Bourke Street. “They were looking for two trainees,” she says. “What drew me in was the sheer scale and architecture of the [wedding] dresses, and the hours, thought and hand-finishing touches put into those sculptural pieces. I walked in, had a good chat with Mariana and got the job.” Gorman ultimately left nursing, but says her experiences at the time have stayed with her. “When I was 18, I was looking after a terminally ill girl of the same age who was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer,” Gorman says. “One day, she asked me to cut off her long hair and I remember sitting at the end of her bed and thinking, this woman is my age – it didn’t feel right. It was really eye-opening for me. ‘I’ve never been the type of person to let go of opportunities, so saying yes to this job felt right.’ Lisa Gorman “It was the first time I’d ever cared for someone my age that had a life that was about to be shortened. That moment gave me perspective like nothing else and that has always stuck with me. What I saw and experienced gave me such a level head when it came to the fashion industry. It kept everything in perspective and served me well in life.”



Gorman is adamant that letter-writing is not dead, and neither is keeping a journal – they’re both part of the increasing appreciation for slowing down and finding the analogue element in an age of digital fatigue. “People are returning to writing things down, so there’s still 100 per cent a place for paper in our society,” says Gorman. “But the value around paper is changing and we’d be fools not to realise that. Related Article Australian fashion What Gorman did next: the designer weaving new patterns “In this digital age, a quality notebook and pen are viewed almost as luxury items. It’s the time, thought and permanency that stationery can provide that I feel is the luxury in paper these days, and without it carrying a luxury price tag – at least not at kikki.K. The value is in what it provides to you, rather than what it costs you to buy.” Despite coming from the era of Australian fashion that gave us high-octane labels such as Sass & Bide and Zimmermann, Gorman has always been an advocate for applying a more measured pace to work and life. In her 20s, a two-week visit to New York turned into a stay that lasted a few years while she took on a number of jobs. Meanwhile, she says kikki.K’s DNA, which lies in its heritage of quality stationery, is firmly staying put. She’s well versed in running a business, having done so for 21 years, and has quietly found her feet at the helm of kikki.K, which is celebrating 25 years of operation after being bought out from voluntary administration in 2020.

World.title: There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder
World.content:
InspirationNew Zealand There’s one major flaw with new ‘business class’ day trip to a world wonder Natasha Bazika July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anyone who has ever flown business class knows the real luxury isn’t the wider seat or the gourmet meals (though they’re definitely perks). It’s the curtain, a visual barrier that separates you from the frantic, elbow-to-elbow situation of the main cabin. RealNZ and Altitude Tours have essentially pulled that velvet curtain across the day trip from Queenstown to Milford Sound with their new premium tour, Milford Sound Business Class. Milford Sound on the MV Sinbad. The upgrade starts at 7.30am. Instead of the typical 50-seat coach, I’m in a 14-seat Mercedes Sprinter. A lambswool blanket is left on my seat and a ginger tonic waits in the pocket, a preemptive strike against the notoriously winding roads ahead. Our driver, Ash, handles the two-hour stretch to Te Anau with a running commentary of fast facts. My favourite is the Maori legend of Lake Wakatipu, New Zealand’s longest lake, said to have been formed by the burning body of a giant taniwha named Matau. “Some say you can still see his heart beating with the rise and fall of the lake level,” she says over the microphone. “It pulses around 12 centimetres every half hour.”



By our morning tea stop in Te Anau, I’m entirely sold on the road experience. But the weight of the $NZ699 ($575) a person ticket rests on the cruise and the five-course tasting menu. To deliver it, they’ve partnered with chef Tom Hishon from Auckland’s acclaimed seafood restaurant, kingi, to bring the sensibility of a high-end urban restaurant and set it afloat in the middle of Fiordland. 



I sit down for a course, spot a waterfall spilling down the cliffs, and run to the top deck. I come down for the next dish, paua served in-shell with black garlic, only for the captain to steer us beneath Stirling Falls moments later for what she calls a “glacial facial”. Another few bites arrive, Mount Cook Alpine caviar served on a potato rosti with sour cream and a Titi (muttonbird) croquette with a delightful citrus spin. The menu is by chef Tom Hishon of the acclaimed Auckland restaurant kingi. For the main, we scoop up Fiordland wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps, and swallow in one bite smoked eel under a slice of beetroot. The windows at each table frame the landscape, but on this unusually bright day, they mostly reflect glare and streaks of salt. Besides, no one comes to Milford Sound to stare at it through a window. Someone shouts “dolphins!” at the bow, and every passenger clears out. No one comes back in a hurry, prompting the staff to bring dessert up instead, a flat white-inspired dish served in a glass.



The food is well executed, exactly what you would expect from Hishon, but the portions are too light for a 12-hour day. That becomes most obvious during the optional wine pairing, where generous pours arrive, two at a time, alongside one-bite courses. Related Article Opinion

Adventure holidays I went on my first big hike in my 40s. It changed the way I see travel Bianca O'Neill Contributor Drinking like that on an empty stomach before a three-hour drive back to Queenstown is a tough sell. For a faster return, you can skip the road and fly back by plane ($NZ500) or helicopter ($NZ1000), but that doesn’t fix the issue. There just isn’t quite enough food for the day. A more substantial main would have made a real difference here. Those of us who skip the scenic flight back load onto the van and find a packet of chips and a chocolate bar waiting on our seats. The crinkle of packets being opened and finished fills the van before we’ve even passed the edge of the national park. THE DETAILS



CRUISE

RealNZ Milford Sound Business Class starts from $NZ699 a person and includes return transfers from selected Queenstown accommodation, morning tea and coffee in Te Anau, a five-course tasting menu, and a two-hour Milford Sound cruise. Guests can upgrade to a scenic fixed-wing flight back from around $NZ500, or a helicopter flight with optional alpine landing from around $NZ1000, weather permitting. The optional wine pairing is $NZ65 a person, payable on the day. See realnz.com STAY

QT Queenstown (qthotels.com) has rooms from around $NZ450 a night. In Te Anau, Tasman Holiday Parks (tasmanholidayparks.com) has self-contained cabins, apartments and powered sites; one-bedroom apartments from around $NZ275 a night. See tasmanholidayparks.com; qthotels.com/queenstown FLY

Air New Zealand, Qantas and Virgin Australia operate direct flights from Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne to Queenstown. HIRE CAR

Snap Rentals has a branch five minutes from Queenstown Airport with a free shuttle service. It’s also one of the few rental companies offering one-way hires, so you don’t need to return the car to Queenstown if you plan to drive elsewhere. See snaprentals.co.nz The writer travelled as a guest of Luxury New Zealand Collection. See luxurynewzealandcollection.com

World.title: Inside Queensland’s bid to claw back $66 million from Fortescue
World.content:
Queensland lost several economic opportunities, including the potential to foster an emerging export hydrogen industry worth $1.7 billion a year, the state government will argue as part of its $66 million claim against mining giant Fortescue. The government has now called in several experts, including major consulting firm KordaMentha, to prove its economic loss in its fight against Fortescue, owned by iron ore billionaire Andrew Forrest. Fortescue is fighting against claims it breached its funding agreement with the state for its green hydrogen facility in Gladstone, central Queensland. Fortescue boss Andrew Forrest in Gladstone alongside former premier Annastacia Palaszczuk and her then deputy, Steven Miles. The resources giant dumped the project at the same time it canned a similar one in Arizona in 2025, when US President Donald Trump slashed tax breaks for clean energy investments.



The Queensland site has previously been described as a “vanity project” and a “terrible deal” by Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie. Related Article Exclusive

Energy ‘Dud project’: How Andrew Forrest’s green dreams cost taxpayers $80m As part of Supreme Court documents filed in recent weeks and seen by this masthead, the state has indicated it will file an amended claim. An order made by the court late last month gave Fortescue until July 22 to apply to have the new claim struck out. The government has indicated it would argue for damages based on claims that it lost multiple economic opportunities, including the potential to foster an emerging hydrogen industry worth $1.7 billion in exports annually, according to recent submissions. If Fortescue had upheld its end of the deal, it would have meant the electrolyser manufacturing facility would have continued to operate until 2032, Queensland claims.



That facility would have enabled Queensland to potentially become a global leader in the production of green hydrogen for export. Queensland would also have been well placed to capture the opportunity of future increases in international demand for green hydrogen, according to the documents. A former government source familiar with Fortescue’s original pitch but not authorised to speak on the record told this masthead the mining giant said the project would support 48 ongoing high-end manufacturing roles. Andrew Forrest and former Labor leader Annastacia Palaszczuk in 2021. Queensland was also told the site at Aldoga, central Queensland, could potentially lead to the company securing various future projects, such as manufacturing for battery, wind turbines, cables and solar power systems. In the state government’s claim, it said the development of the industry in Queensland would have enabled it to capture emerging large-scale hydrogen markets in Asia, particularly in South Korea and Japan.



The state said it had become apparent following a first review hearing of the case that Fortescue had “misconstrued” the nature of the government’s case, which was that it would seek to prove the economic benefits flagged from helping to get the industry off the ground were reasonably expected. The funding agreement came after Fortescue sent a letter to the government in May 2021 regarding the project, to which the state responded that Fortescue’s plan aligned closely with Queensland’s policy priorities. The proposed manufacturing facility near Gladstone. The agreement came against a backdrop of the then Labor government, led by Annastacia Palaszczuk, implementing the Queensland Advanced Manufacturing 10-year road map and action plan. According to Supreme Court documents, the then premier said: “Now the world is looking to hydrogen, and we want them to get it from Queensland so we can create even more jobs in our regions.”



Palaszczuk also spoke of the emerging industry having enormous economic benefits for Australia, pointing to the $1.7 billion export figure. Fortescue claims, however, the government has no leg to stand on. It says the funding agreement did not refer to the Hydrogen Industry Strategy or the 10-year road map. In launching its defence, the company said the alleged loss and damage did not flow from the claimed breach of the funding agreement. Fortescue said the Hydrogen Industry Strategy was only expressed to apply between 2019 and 2024 and came to an end in 2024.



Related Article Investigation

Philanthropy ‘Next shiny thing’: Inside Twiggy Forrest’s $7 billion charity “The state would have, in any event, abandoned the Hydrogen Industry Strategy as it, in fact, did in or around October 2024, or alternatively February 2025, or alternatively October 2025,” documents filed on behalf of Fortescue state. Those dates coincided with the October 2024 state election, which resulted in a change of government. The new administration, under LNP leader David Crisafulli, removed the strategy from the government’s website. According to Fortescue, in February 2025, the state withdrew financial support for the Central Queensland Hydrogen Hub – the state’s flagship $12.4 billion green hydrogen project led by Stanwell Corporation. And in October 2025, the state released the Queensland Energy Roadmap, which made no mention of any hydrogen industry policies. “The state would have, in any event, abandoned the 10-year road map as it, in fact, did in or around September 2025,” the documents state.



Fortescue also pointed to how in September 2025, the state released the Transforming Queensland Manufacturing Strategy 2025-30, which made no reference to any hydrogen industry strategies and said the state had not suffered the alleged loss because it had obtained the benefit of at least $37,222,506 in site work costs from stage 1 of the project. The company’s legal team also questioned why another company would not take up the commercial opportunity at the site, and it pressed the state as to why it would not take up the opportunity, given that it had now exercised the buyback right. The industrial site in central Queensland remains abandoned and there are no current plans to either sell or contract a new company to work there, this masthead has confirmed. According to documents recently filed by the state, the government’s identified witnesses to be brought in would include an economic expert to analyse the financial benefits that were expected to flow to Queensland from the agreement. The state said it had already engaged Synergies Economic Consulting to provide an expert economic report, in addition to KordaMentha’s expert accounting context.



Other expected witnesses include a hydrogen industry expert to give evidence concerning the market and potential market for the electrolyser technology and for green hydrogen internationally, both at the time the agreement was entered into and the likely trajectory and future prospects of the market through to 2032 and beyond. The state’s documents say in the six months ending in December 2020, Fortescue had a net profit after tax of $US4.1 billion. World.title: I thought I was getting more open-minded as I got older. Until I saw this at the shops
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life Opinion I thought I was getting more open-minded as I got older. Until I saw this at the shops Kerri Sackville Columnist and author July 23, 2026 — 5:00am

July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As I have edged past middle age and moved towards, well, later middle age, I have noticed myself becoming less judgmental. I don’t care about a person’s life choices, as long as they are nice human and do no harm to others. Just the other day, for example, I was listening to a podcast about polyamory as I was climbing the escalator at my local Westfield. Wouldn’t be my cup of tea, I thought, as a woman described her relationships with her three partners, but hey, good for her! As I congratulated myself on my open-mindedness, I spotted a man standing on the wrong side of the escalator, blocking my path. What a moron, I thought, as I stomped pointedly around him. How hard is it to stand to the left? Live and let live? Sure. Just don’t stand on the wrong side of the escalator. iStock I realised, at that moment, that I have found myself in a rather contradictory state of mind. As much as I wholeheartedly accept people from all walks of life, I will turn on them in an instant if they inconvenience me in any way.



I am both wonderfully compassionate and intensely intolerant. You breastfed your son until he was eight and you only eat white foods? My, how fascinating. You do you! You stand stock still on the wrong side of the escalator? I want to call the police and have you banned from the shops. Life is tough, so whatever brings you joy or fulfillment is fine, whether it is selling jewellery made from semen (it’s a thing!) or marrying a chatbot on your phone. KERRI SACKVILLE You identify as a Wiccan and changed your name to Goddess Spirit Love? Cool, sounds interesting, tell me about it. You ride an e-bike without a helmet with your mate on the back? I want to scream at you for your idiocy and smack you in the head. I truly do not care what lifestyle you adopt, as long as it does not impact negatively on others. Life is tough, so whatever brings you joy or fulfillment is fine, whether it is selling jewellery made from semen (it’s a thing!) or marrying a chatbot on your phone. But life is also short and people’s choices keep impacting negatively on me! And I don’t want to waste a minute of the (increasingly limited) time I have left on this planet being stuck behind some dude standing on the wrong side of the escalator, or veering out of the way of a cyclist who is riding without a bloody helmet in peak-hour traffic.



I don’t want to be so intolerant of other human beings. I want to be a good and serene person, particularly as I get older. I don’t want to be that grumpy old lady who mutters angrily at passers-by. I want to radiate love and acceptance for all. Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life The day I offered to cut my partner’s hair marked our first fight. It’s still going Kerri Sackville Columnist and author And I’d be able to, if the other people in the world weren’t so insanely irritating. Drivers who fail to let me into their lane. Customers who make interminable small talk with the cashier while I’m standing in a queue behind them. Acquaintances who post ridiculous conspiracy theories online, clogging up my Facebook feed with their nonsense. Patrons who get out their phones in the cinemas and distract me when I’m watching a movie. Groups of pedestrians hogging the footpath when I’m on my morning walk. Neighbours who put food scraps in the yellow recycle bin instead of the green. The list goes on. They all make me incensed. I know what the younger people would say because three of them are my children, and they say it to me. They’d say, “Hey, Boomer, don’t sweat the small stuff!” (And for the record, I’m not a Boomer, I’m Gen X, thank you very much.)



Thing is, though, the small stuff is all I can sweat. The big stuff is just too big. I have worked very hard in recent times not to dwell too much on massive, intractable problems. Related Article Opinion

Sunday Life How far would you go to retrieve a missing phone? As far as it takes, I learnt Kerri Sackville Columnist and author Perhaps my aggravation at minor inconveniences is just redirected anger at the state of the world. Perhaps the rage I feel at the woman who didn’t clean up her dog poop is actually sublimated rage at climate change and the evils of technology. Perhaps my urge to hunt down the call-centre operator who disconnected me after I’d been on hold for 23 minutes is simply displaced grief at global conflicts and injustices. Or perhaps I really am just a grumpy old lady, all out of patience after 57 years of life on this chaotic planet among this crazy species. Either way, be careful if you see me at the shops. I will honour your gender identity. I will respect your religious beliefs. I will not judge your sexual preferences or your parenting style or your appearance or your work. But if you push in front of me in a queue, or take too long to order your coffee, or let your silly dog lick my ankles, or block the supermarket aisle with your trolley, you’d better be prepared for the consequences.



I will roll my eyes at you. I will sigh. I will mutter. Watch out. I am going to be cross. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning. Sign up here for our free newsletter.

World.title: If you love Neil Diamond, you’ll love this show. Just try not to sing along
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s a blustery Monday morning, and inside Opera Australia’s Southbank rehearsal studios, the cast and crew of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical are starting their second week of rehearsals. About a dozen young dancers in exercise gear are working with associate choreographer Yasmine Lee, traversing the space in exaggerated, slow-motion movements. In the rehearsal space next door, associate director Austin Regan is giving notes to the cast as they run scenes. The show opens with an elderly Diamond (Terence Crawford), talking to a psychologist about being depressed that his failing health – the singer was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease in 2018 – has put an end to his touring career. As he muses that songwriting gave him a ticket out of the working-class Brooklyn neighbourhood of Flatbush, the music changes, with the background piano chords suddenly turning into the instantly recognisable opening of Diamond’s 1967 hit, Shilo. With the first preview about three weeks away, the cast members are fizzing with energy. Dancers during rehearsals for A Beautiful Noise. Justin McManus A Beautiful Noise would never have come about were it not for another musical biopic, Jersey Boys, the story of the Four Seasons – Frankie Valli, Tommy DeVito, Nick Massi and Bob Gaudio. When Gaudio, a friend of Diamond’s, left the Four Seasons, he became a record producer, producing some of Diamond’s biggest hits. A Beautiful Noise musical supervisor Sonny Paladino says: “Neil was a fan of Jersey Boys, and he saw it a bunch in New York. And one time he said to Bob afterwards, ‘Could I have one of these?’” Music supervisor Sonny Paladino watches rehearsals. Justin McManus The answer was yes. But with 38 top 40 singles and 33 studio albums, winnowing down Diamond’s back catalogue for the show was a daunting task. “What makes this musical work so well is that there’s nothing superfluous,” Paladino says. “If the song is in the show, it has to be part of the show and make the audience care about what’s happening.



“Even in act two, we do a sequence that we call stadium medley, where he’s basically touring the world as he did, and even those songs are part of the narrative. There’s a great song called Heartlight, which we tried to get in there, but it just didn’t work.” Plenty of songs did make the cut, though – there are 25 tracks on the soundtrack, and a few are medleys. The musical opened in Boston in 2022 and has been touring the US since. Audience members turn up in tour T-shirts, aware that this is the closest they will get to seeing the man himself perform. Will Swenson told his agent to be on the lookout for a Neil Diamond musical. Justin McManus “I think a lot of people are coming to see the show, particularly just to have like a Neil concert experience,” says Will Swenson, who plays Diamond as a young man and is the only import in the Australian cast. “It was weird for me to just go out, first notes out of my mouth and have the audience completely won over and happy and screaming, and it threw me. “But I was like, ‘Oh, this is love for Neil, and I’m just this lucky guy that gets to be the recipient of all of this adoration.’ I will happily take it. But it’s a head trip to go like, ‘Oh wait, Will, you didn’t earn this. Neil earned this, and you are standing in his shoes to get to receive it.’ Neil Diamond performing in Sydney in 2005 Domino Postiglione “Neil Diamond was my dad’s favourite singer of all time,” Swenson says. “I knew these songs when I was six years old.”



But if it’s one thing to perform these songs in front of 1200 Neil Diamond fans a night on Broadway, it’s very different performing them in front of the man himself, as Swenson did in a tiny room in Nashville. “He just sat five feet away from me, and we played through the songs and read the script, just hoping that he would like it enough. It was one of the more surreal things I’ve ever done in my life. It was completely nerve-wracking, and luckily, about halfway through, he started raising his hand and started singing along and you’re like, ‘oh, I think he likes it’.” Related Article Performing arts Waitress is gone, Beetlejuice too. Where is the next Hamilton? Diamond isn’t the only one singing along. As anyone who has ever heard Sweet Caroline in a pub knows, it’s impossible not to join in the “ba ba ba!″⁣s. “We were careful crafting the show because it is a musical,” Regan says. “It’s not a concert, so we want people to be able to engage with the story and the play of it, but there are some moments where we know you have to release the pressure valve and let people sing along because how could you not with Song Sung Blue and with Sweet Caroline and all these songs? They’re iconic melodies, and you can’t help but join in.” The show ran on Broadway for just under two years, where, as in Australia, musical theatre has struggled to find its feet after lockdowns. The New York Times reported late last year that only three musicals that had opened since the pandemic had made a profit. A Beautiful Noise was not one of them. “We would have loved to have run longer, but I think we were all really, really proud that we got almost two years out of the show,” says Regan. “Most shows these days close after just a few months. It’s very, very hard to make a show work on Broadway, and I think of all the musicals in our season we ran the second longest of any production, which feels pretty great.”

World.title: ‘This is just the beginning’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.73m
World.content:
PropertyNewsSydney house prices ‘This is just the beginning’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.73m Alice Uribe July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost to buy the typical Sydney property has started to fall over recent months, with buyers beginning to get the upper hand as muted confidence, affordability pressures and higher interest rates combine to dent the property market. Sydney’s median house price dropped 3.3 per cent, or about $60,000 over three months to December to $1,733,891, the latest Domain House Price Report, released on Thursday, showed. This was a fall from the previous quarter’s record high and the largest fall of all the capital cities. Over the year, house price growth slowed to 1.1 per cent. The city’s median unit price was also down, falling 1.5 per cent to $849,068 over the quarter to June. This was also a drop from the previous quarter’s peak and the first quarterly decline in two years. Over the year, growth eased to 2.5 per cent.



Three rate hikes had affected borrowing capacity, while cost of living pressures and weak consumer sentiment was helping to constrain activity. Recent falls are signalling the “next stage” of the property cycle, Dr Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief residential economist, said. “This is just the beginning,” she said of negative growth. More drops are expected during 2026. Selling conditions in Sydney had weakened materially, Domain said. Clearance rates are at their lowest level since April 2020 (48 per cent), while withdrawn auctions were at a record 29.3 per cent. Powell said that alongside weaker clearance rates and withdrawn auction levels, there were longer selling times, higher discounting and rising supply.



“The element of increased choice is just taking that urgency away from buyers, and giving them the power,” she said. The federal budget in May introduced negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions reforms that Powell said would have a greater impact in markets such as Sydney, which has a larger proportion of investor activity than other states. “It’s vulnerable to changes in investor participation. And ultimately, I think we are going to see fewer investors partaking in Sydney’s housing market.” For first home buyers, too, there would be an “absolute element of caution to purchase in a falling market,” Powell said.



“Market conditions have shifted rapidly ... First time buyers are sensitive to changes in affordability, and we have to consider the mortgage serviceability aspect.” Independent economist Saul Eslake said even though the budget’s property reforms did not come into effect until July 1 next year, they were having an impact on the way people think about the property market and what they were doing in “anticipation of those changes”. Both investors and first home buyers are cautious about buying property in a falling market, experts say. James Brickwood This was at the same time, he added, as borrowing was becoming “significantly” more expensive thanks to higher interest rates, and banks were tipping further property price falls of between around 5 and 10 per cent nationally. “Given that there may well be another increase in interest rates as well, and the full effects of the changes to the tax system on investors are yet to play out, it would make sense for prospective buyers to hold back.”



Related Article NSW residential property ‘We never really needed to move’: Sydney suburbs where home owners stick around According to the latest Equifax Consumer Market Pulse, overall mortgage demand plunged 14 per cent over the year to June, driven by a 17.2 per cent drop in first home buyer applications. With affordability pressures ongoing, the areas recording the biggest declines in price over the past 12 months across Sydney have been at the upper end, while more affordable areas have retained buoyancy. The strongest median price growth for houses over the year to June was in the outer south west, up 12.5 per cent to $1,125,000) over the year. That was followed by the outer west and Blue Mountains (up 9.4 per cent to $1,110,000). By comparison, it was North Sydney and Hornsby which fell the most, dropping 12.1 per cent to $2,767,500. Despite a downturn, every region of Sydney still has a median house price of at least $1 million.



For units, the biggest growth for the same period was on the Central Coast – part of Greater Sydney – up 11.9 per cent to $730,000, followed by the outer south west, which jumped 10.3 per cent to $642,500. Alana Pasikala, 25, recently bought a one-bedroom apartment in the St George area after realising that repayments may not be much more than her rent, which had spiked over recent years. Even so, the aviation people leader, who started looking for a property in January after getting her pre-approval, noticed a high level of competition. She noticed queues to view properties and steepening prices over the course of her hunt. First home buyer Alana Pasikala avoided auctions on her property hunt. STEVEN SIEWERT



“When you’re a first-time buyer, auctions are quite difficult … so I completely avoided auctions,” she said. “For the properties I was looking at, they were going for more than what they were initially advertised, or asking for, at that time.” Pasikala, who is soon moving into her new home, is happy she stayed within her budget after putting in offers for a few properties. “Ultimately, it’s a step in the right direction for something for myself, and my future.” Pasikala says buying a unit in the St George area was a “step in the right direction” for her future. STEVEN SIEWERT



The more affordable parts of Sydney, Powell said, were likely to remain firmer in price and may even see modest rates of price growth. “I think it says a lot about who is active and the lack of affordable supply,” she said. “The upper end of the market is leading the downturn.” Related Article NSW residential property ‘A bit more laid-back’: The family-friendly Sydney suburb that soared Julian Finch, principal mortgage broker at Finch Financial Services who worked with Pasikala, said inquiries for all types of lending had “quieted down exponentially” since the federal budget after a stronger start to 2026. “I think what we’ve got is just a situation where everybody’s lost confidence in what the market is doing,” he said. “The reality is, of course, the buyers are in a stronger position to negotiate, or at least take their time.”



As the property cycle turns, NAB senior economist Taylor Nugent said the lender was forecasting Sydney house price declines of around 7 per cent over 2026. “At the moment, it would be fair to say that recent momentum suggests the risk might be to a slightly larger decline over the course of the year than that.”

World.title: Revealed: The NSW children spending years on psychiatry wait lists
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWMental health Revealed: The NSW children spending years on psychiatry wait lists Rachel Rasker July 23, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content Ethan Annetts was 11 when he started self-harming. By the time he saw a psychiatrist, he was an adult and suicidal. Ethan spent years on the waitlist for an assessment, and was trapped in an unending cycle of hospital presentations and discharges without any ongoing care, his mother, Jo Cockle said. Jo Cockle’s children Ethan (left) and Grace have spent years waiting for child and adolescent psychiatric support. Wolter Peeters With no other options, an extremely distressed Cockle enrolled in suicide prevention classes herself. If she hadn’t: “I don’t think he’d be here,” she said.



NSW has the worst child and adolescent psychiatrist shortage in the country, a shortfall projected to almost double in the next two decades, a new analysis of federal government data revealed. The federal government’s Thriving Kids policy, which will shift demand from the NDIS to state-based services, risks exacerbating the problem, leaving more families without timely access to treatment, the peak body for psychiatrists has warned. Before medication, Ethan couldn’t leave his room. Now, he enjoys fishing in nature. Wolter Peeters An extra 64.3 full-time child and adolescent (CAD) psychiatrists are needed just to meet the current demand of families across NSW, found a report released by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. By 2048, that shortfall will have grown to 119, the report found.



The state’s psychiatrists shortage is almost triple that of Victoria’s, which needs an additional 21.5 full-time clinicians, it read. Nationwide, there is just one specialist for every 571 children with moderate to severe mental illness. Professor Valsamma Eapen, a psychiatrist who led the report, said resourcing constraints mean children can only access help after their condition has become severe, and Thriving Kids could “add more pressures onto the already stressed system”. Cockle put Ethan on a wait list to see a paediatrician when he was 13. “When he finally got called up, he was 17 and a half, and they actually said: We can no longer see you because you’re too old now,” Cockle said.



Ethan’s sister, 12-year-old Grace, was granted funding to see a specialised counsellor two years ago, but still hasn’t been given an appointment. “There aren’t any available, or if they are available, they’re full,” Cockle said. “It’s my job to provide for my children, and not being able to provide for their basic human rights, I can’t even put it into words. It’s heartbreaking,” she said. Jo (left) has studied suicide prevention and psychology to help her son and other vulnerable people. Wolter Peeters Dr Joel Killey, who ran a CAD psychiatric unit at a public hospital in Sydney’s north, said it was “frustrating, exhausting and quite sad” to see the mental health of young people deteriorate as they repeatedly returned to hospital with progressively severe presentations.





He hoped new NSW rules that allow trained GPs to prescribe ADHD medication will ease the burden on psychiatrists, and said investing in child and adolescent mental health provides “the biggest bang for our buck”. “If we get people when they’re in the early stages of their illness, that’s where we can have the biggest impact,” he said. “We can get them essentially back to normal levels of functioning, rather than having the morbidity that has occurred from long periods of untreated mental health problems.” In a statement, a federal government spokesperson said more than $2.8 billion is currently invested in youth mental health, including $490.3 million for 20 new psychiatrist-led youth specialist care centres across Australia, and training programs for specialist psychiatrists. NSW Mental Health Minister Rose Jackson said in a statement that she recognised the growing demand, and acknowledged there was “always more work” needed to meet it. Jackson said her government had invested in recruitment, training and new models of care to strengthen the mental health workforce and improve access to support for children and young people. The report found that each additional full-time CAD psychiatrist generated an estimated $5.85 million in lifetime social and economic benefits, including reduced mental health system use, increased parental workforce participation due to a lower care burden, and improved education and lifetime productivity.



Related Article Mental health Carly couldn’t get the healthcare she needed. She almost didn’t make it home Thriving Kids will move children with mild-to-moderate developmental delays or autism off the NDIS and into state-based mental health systems. Autistic children are more likely to have a co-occuring mental health condition like anxiety, depression or ADHD, and the introduction of an early identification screening is also expected to lead to increased demand. The RANZCP said details about the transition have not been finalised, despite its rollout date of October 2026. “Where and how this will fit in, and how state interpreters are going to fund and deliver these services, is really not yet known,” Eapen said. A federal government spokesperson said, “significant implementation work has been completed” on Thriving Kids, while the NSW government said they were working closely with the Commonwealth and monitoring potential impacts on demand, access and wait times. Now that Ethan has been able to see a psychiatrist and get the right medication, “everything [is] a bit easier for me to handle in terms of getting a job, going to work, education, going to TAFE; I was able to do that stuff again,” he said.



“Life is a lot easier to manage with the right resources.” For urgent, free and confidential support, contact Lifeline on 13 11 14, Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636 or the NSW Mental Health Line on 1800 011 511.
